title: Love Is In The Little Things
author: Tas.R
excerpt: "Read to me, will you?"
imageAlt: Cover image for Love Is In The Little Things
content: "Read to me, will you?"
Looking up from his book, he glanced over at her from his desk. She was lying on the carpet in front of the fireplace. Her head was turned towards him, waiting for an answer.
"Really? It's a little boring."
"What are you reading?"
He held up his book so she could see the cover. "Advanced Chemistry."

"Do you honestly think I can see that?" She asked, squinting so much that her eyes were nearly shut. "One of the reasons I asked you to read to me was the fact that I don't have glasses and I desperately need them." She whined.
The other reason is that I love hearing your voice.

"How bad is your vision?" He asked in astonishment. The fact genuinely took him by surprise, since he was used to seeing her read. He never could've guessed that her narrowed eyes during reading wasn't because of concentration, but poor eyesight.
"I can see distant things better than near ones."
"Why didn't you get glasses then?"
"Couldn't make time."
Of course she couldn't make any time. Knowing her circumstances, he couldn't help but feel sympathy for her. She never really had time for herself, always on edge, always on high alert.
"Okay, okay, whatever. Will you read to me now?" She requested impatiently.
"Of course."

Under the light of the desk lamp, he began to read. Every now and then he would steal a glance at her. Her eyes were closed as she lay on her back, face towards the ceiling. He was sure she was listening though. The orange glow of the fire lit up one side of her face. Her features were illuminated clearly, her long lashes against her cheeks, her slim face, her pink lips. He could see clearly why the nurses at the hospital had called her a doll.

He'd been reading for a good while before she interrupted him. "You should add a little emotion to your reading." She said suddenly, propping herself up on her elbow. "The whole time you've been reading, it sounded like some boring monologue."
"This— is a chemistry book. Not some sort of fantasy story." He said in disbelief.

"I know that. Just because it's a chemistry book doesn't mean you can't use your imagination like,"  She sat up in excitement. "You could pretend you're reading something sent from the future." She took on the tone of someone in awe, yet at the same time distressed. "The atoms form a bond which is very difficult to break, like in diamond." Her tone returned to normal. "Like that."
He mimicked her tone. "Like this?"

"Yes!" She approved enthusiastically, not realizing he was teasing her. "Or like you're reading the last words of a famous sea captain or a love letter sent to you anonymously or the diary of your secret lover who never confessed." She gushed on excitedly.
He couldn't help but smile at her enthusiasm. "Well, aren't you a romantic?" He commented, amused.

She chuckled, "I guess." Her back towards the fireplace, her figure was outlined by the warm light of the flames but her face was mostly in darkness.  As if she were the sun in the midst of an eclipse. "It's foolish though."
"Why is that?"
"It's a foolish thing in general, romance. Even more so for me."
If only she knew how much that last sentence hurt him. "Susan loves you." He pointed out.

"Because she knows me." She sounded small. "And I love her too but I'm saying that no one else would ever even want to get too close." She stretched her arms out in front of her, examining her knuckles. The bruising on them wasn't visible in the low light, but he knew how severe it was anyway. He had been there at the hospital as the doctor after all.

He didn't really know what he could say in response, especially after how small she sounded. She was always so lively and cheerful and all this time, he didn't really think she was ever concerned about such matters. He didn't really think she'd ever regretted doing everything she had to for Susan's protection but she was still human after all, it must've hurt.

She sighed. "It's not that I regret anything. I did what I had to. But sometimes the consequences really set in." She pushed her bangs back from her forehead. "Still, at least Susan has never had to worry about perverts."

"I'm sure there's someone out there for you," he tried to reassure her, "Someone who loves all your energy, someone who loves your smile," He thought of all the things someone could love about her, and everything came to mind. All the little insecurities she had about herself, all the miniscule details she probably didn't even know about herself were the things he loved.

"Someone out there loves your slender figure, your loud laughter, your love for reading." He said more confidently, "Someone loves all the strange things you paint, the voices and faces you make, how loud you get when you're excited, but how quiet and contemplative you are otherwise. Someone who loves you."

She didn't answer at first. She was glad he couldn't see her face right now, because she was sure she'd turned pink. He'd just picked out all the things she was insecure about and told her they were things someone would love.
Is that someone you?
Her silence was making him anxious. Had he said too much? Did she realize who that 'someone' he was talking about was?
I'm that someone.
Finally, she let out a chuckle. "Thanks."
"You're welcome."
There was a minute of silence between them before he remembered something. "Do you want to get your eyes checked tomorrow? I can take you."
She smiled. "I'd appreciate that."

title: That's All it Took
author: Zyvaran
excerpt: The machines all around the shop beeped and blinked as if alive. The ACs winked, the washing machines made faces, the TVs even became angry and left. Some bleeped, some clicked, so
imageAlt: Cover image for That's All it Took
content: The machines all around the shop beeped and blinked as if alive. The ACs winked, the washing machines made faces, the TVs even became angry and left. Some bleeped, some clicked, some even hummed. If a person were to stand in the middle of the shop with their eyes closed, they would think they were inside a toy shop, not a home appliances showroom (it would also look like a toy shop if everything inside were more than grey and black).

Presently, a woman somewhere between late 30s and early 40s approached the showroom accompanied by a teenager. She could not figure out how to open the door. A salesman made his way towards her, but the teenager told her something, so she took out her ID card and scanned it. The receptionist gave it a pass and the door unlocked.
The salesman received them anyway. The two women gazed around the shop in wonder. The older woman exclaimed in confusion, “Machines have faces these days!”
Both the teenager and the salesman stifled their laughter. The woman asked, “Are these really eyes? Can the machines see us?”
The teenager was visibly embarrassed. The salesman explained that these were only graphics. Once put to use, they usually showed digits or other selected displays.
She said they wanted to buy an air conditioner for the living room. So he led them to the AC section.

The salesman attentively listened to their requirements and made recommendations. He added that all of these devices could be connected to their home cloud and controlled by the family members with their phones.
Both of the customers looked a bit confused. “I have heard of ACs you can connect to your phone,” said the young lady. “But ‘home cloud'?”

“This is how it works,” the salesman explained patiently. “You must have a wi-fi connection in your home? -Yes? -So you can connect this device with your router. All devices connected to your router will automatically have access to the AC. You can change the temperature, turn it on or off the moment you come into the range of your wi-fi. You can also broaden the range with some extra tinkering. Suppose you are away on a holiday and suddenly wonder, ‘Did I turn off the oven? How about the AC?’ Well, I cannot say about the oven, but you can take your phone out and immediately check! Is it really on? Then ‘bam!’ within a second it's off. Works like a charm for a stress-free vacation! And, if you want to switch your oven and fridge with these newest smart MSD models, we also have a big discount offer going on!”
The teenager was as excited as the salesman wanted her to be. “That’s sooo cool! Mom, let's take one!”
The woman said, “That sounds ridiculous. I can already see more fights between you and your brother. Even the guests will change the temperature all the time.”
The salesman humbly said, “Ma'am, you can set one smartphone as a ‘parent device'. Then you can control it and even lock the temperature.”
The girl's eyes started twinkling again. “See, Mom? They think of everything! It will be fine! And it will be fancy!”

“Next month they will make a fridge with a tongue and that will be fancy. Then we will have to buy another one because ours will be ‘too old' and ‘burning too much electricity'. Be practical, will you? This ‘smart’ thing probably won't last two years.”
“But you will have stress-free vacations for next two years, at least,” another salesman threw playfully in the conversation. The girl nodded vigorously.

The woman impatiently said, “But we don't need it! Why would I control my AC when I am not even home? And when do we even go on vacations? Besides, having everything on the internet is dangerous! You connect this to the internet, next thing you know, someone has hacked our AC!”
“But Mom,” the girl was getting irritated. “What use is hacking an AC?”

“I don’t know. What if our neighbours hack it and turn it up and burn all the electricity? What if-” she stopped and gasped loudly, as if she just realized something big, “what if they keep an eye on us through the machines? Oh my god, no, no no no no no, we don’t need this.”
“But Mom,” the girl started giggling now. “How will they look at us? There aren’t any cameras inside. Will they install a camera through the internet?”
“I don’t know. I wouldn’t put it past them.”
The girl started laughing loudly. The woman spoke again, as if to interrupt her daughter.
“We will take a normal, un-smart AC, please. No internet connection required.”
The salesman said, “We only have the latest smart appliances here, ma'm. For such old products you will have to look in other shops.”
She left. Her daughter found this conversation more fun than the fancy AC. She followed suit while laughing quietly.
The salesman made a call. “I can confirm she is a civilian. This is bad. It means there are ordinary people who can guess.”
She died two days later. A drunk driver ran her over.

She was no spy, no assassin, not even a government worker. This barely literate housewife thrived on common sense and making the best choices for her family. She was skilled at making reasonable guesses.
We still don’t know which part she guessed correctly that terrified someone to the point of eliminating a common woman.

title: The Rift
author: Samreen Maliha Rouf
excerpt: Fariha’s fingertips hesitantly press on the calling bell of the flat. The thudding rain had steadily
imageAlt: Cover image for The Rift
content: Fariha’s fingertips hesitantly press on the calling bell of the flat. The thudding rain had steadily
intensified as the day progressed, which made the appearance of thunder seem inevitable. She let
out a breath, anxiety twisting at the pit of her stomach. A part of her wants to turn around, to
escape, but she stays firmly in place.
“Coming!” A voice calls out. Fariha is able to recognise it as Kabir’s wife, Khushi. Kabir
is Fariha’s maternal uncle, the one who stood by her side when her mother passed and all hell
broke loose. With his guidance she was able to process her passing, and simultaneously manage
to overcome the ruthless legal battles which followed. While others circled her like vultures, he
ensured she never had to fend them off alone.
Distracted by her thoughts, Fariha is startled when the door swings open, revealing a
disheveled Khushi.
“Fariha, it’s been so long! You never said you were coming?” Fariha offers a small smile,
“well, come in.” Khushi steps aside, making way for her niece to step in.
“How have you been Aunty?” Fariha asks, as she walks into the home. She scans Khushi
who looks utterly exhausted; messy hair tied away from her face, with a few strands loose, and
sunken circles visible beneath her eyes. Her eyes fall on a plate of rice on top of the dinner table,
set next to a skillet with fish curry. She suddenly feels guilty for coming unannounced; she is
disturbing the single moment of quiet Khushi can afford.
“Well,” she laughs, “I’m as good as I can be.” She runs her hands through the knots in her
hair. Fariha feels her shoulders slump. “Your uncle is in his room, you should go and see him. He
always asks Lutfar about you.”
“Ah.” She flinches slightly, suddenly reminded why she decided to come. “Yes, um,” she
spoke slowly, as she hands a plastic bag to Khushi, “this is for Uncle, it’s just some fruits.
Apples.”
Khushi smiles softly, thanking Fariha, telling her she didn’t have to. Fariha only laughs in
reply.
As Khushi walks into the kitchen, Fariha glances around the expanse of the room. She
could barely recall the last time she had been here. However the familiar wooden dining table her
mother had gifted her uncle as a wedding gift still stood strong years later. She pictures her
mother sitting across from her uncle, laughing over a cup of tea.
The bittersweet image lingers in her mind as she walks into Kabir’s room, only to stop
short at the sight of him. Witnessing his once agile figure slumped on the bed, she is able to
understand now that her uncle was no longer the active man he once was. He is now withered
and languid, while his face wears an expression of dejection. His mouth is slightly parted, with
his eyes unfocused, unaware of her entrance.
“Uncle,” Fariha was afraid her voice would crack if she spoke too much. Kabir’s
despondent expression was brightened with a small grin and sparkling eyes. She smiles as she
continues, “Hello.”
“Fariha, my girl.” He extends a shaking hand, gesturing for her to take a seat. He puts his
hand on hers, and its shakiness makes her world quake.
“How have you been?” His voice, too, was weak and trembling.
Fariha clears her throat, afraid to break down. She forces a genial smile to paint her
expression. “Good, Uncle. How about you?”
He takes a moment to respond, something unfamiliar to Fariha. Before, whenever she
asked him about his health before, he would merely gesture at himself as though it was obvious:
he was fantastic. That same man now sits frail, supported by a combination of his bed frame and
pillows, feebly responding after long pauses.
“Better,” he says. Fariha waits, expecting more, however nothing more comes. The
silence is broken by Khushi’s entrance.
“Look at who’s come to visit you!” Khushi exclaims to Kabir while holding a tray with
sweets and water.
“Oh, Aunty!” says Fariha, “You didn’t have to. I only came to see Uncle, this wasn’t
necessary!” She becomes aware of the weight on Khushi’s shoulders, she doesn’t want to add to
the burden.
“Oh, be quiet. This is nothing,” she says dismissively. Fariha smiles meekly, thanking
her. She takes a seat on the bed, opposite to where Fariha sits on a plastic chair. “Your Uncle was
in the hospital, if you didn’t hear.”
Guilt gnaws at Fariha’s stomach, “Lutfar told me. I couldn’t go since I was in London for
work.” Fariha wasn’t completely lying. The truth is, her work was done by the time Kabir was
admitted to the hospital. However, for some reason, she couldn’t bring herself to cut an early
ticket. Even today, she came with much reluctance. She wonders what caused her to have this
awful feeling.
“Yes, Lutfar told us you were busy,” Fariha’s guilt intensifies. She allowed others to get
caught in her web of lies. “Your uncle was doing much worse. He—” Kabir suddenly interrupts,
raising an arm.
“Enough. There’s no point in talking about that.”
Khushi frowns at the interruption but says nothing more.
Fariha glances around the room awkwardly, unsure of what to say in response. Her eyes
suddenly spot a frame hanging on the wall. A picture of a young Kabir; she remembers him
showing her this picture. It was from his time in Ireland during the 1980’s. The black and white
finish reflects its age, however his smile radiates colour, carrying a sense of freedom she could
no longer see.
Khushi traces Fariha’s gaze, and softly sighs. Her voice breaks her out of her trance.
“Let me prepare the tea!”
Before Fariha can respond, she rushes out, leaving the two alone once again. They both
stare at Khushi’s figure as she disappears through the doorway.
“When were you discharged, Uncle?” Fariha asks, attempting conversation. She takes the
bowl with sweets in her hand, roshmalay; her favourite.
“This Monday.” He answers easily. Fariha nods, and what follows after is dreadful
silence. Fariha plays with the hem of her shirt, straightening her back as silence thrums in her
ears, causing her to shift in place. Abruptly, Kabir speaks up, looking up at Fariha’s face.
“A life where I’m chained to my bed, unable to do anything for myself, well, is that kind
of life even worth living?” he asks, his face expressionless, but eyes glistening and voice shaky.
Fariha stares at her uncle for a long while, even after he glances away. His lips quiver
ever so slightly.
“Uncle!” A familiar voice breaks Fariha out of her trance. “Looking fresh.”
Fariha watches carefully as her uncle grins at Lutfar’s appearance.
“Grab a chair,” Kabir instructs. Lutfar’s eyes fall on Fariha, who continues to look at their
uncle.
Lutfar acknowledges her with a greeting, however, it goes unheard by Fariha as she
begins to speak. “Why do you think so uncle?”
His gaze returns to her immediately, but he responds after some time.
“Fariha, whenever I think about who I used to be and what I am now, I just can’t help but
feel helpless. My life has lost its value.”
“How can you say this uncle?” Fariha’s voice rises more than she would like it to as she
realises she could no longer deny the reality. The reality that her beloved uncle was now an ailing
man; and that the uncle who breathed the will to live into her had lost it himself.
“Fariha, you just won’t get it.” He let out a breathless, and cruelly amused laugh. Fariha
sits still, demanding him to elaborate with her silence. “You see, I’m no more than a liability.
Look at the state of your aunt, it’s not like she’s young enough to be running around for a grown
man like me. I’ve become a burden.”
“Uncle, did you think this of my mother as well?” Her voice remains low with much
restraint, afraid to alert the whole neighbourhood. “Did you think she was some unbearable
burden?” She bites her lip to shield a sob, feeling Lutfar’s reassuring hand on her shoulder,
forcing down her nerves.
Kabir remains quiet under her heavy gaze. “No,” he replies.
“So then why are you assuming you are?”
No response.
“Uncle, you know what I’m endlessly grateful for? That I was able to be there for my
mother during her final days. Being able to be there for someone, to take care of them, that itself
is a privilege.” Fariha speaks with feigned composure, her voice broken and her spirit shattered.
Fariha’s gaze lingers on her uncle’s trembling hands, his slumped posture, his downcast
expression, and she understands why she was so reluctant to meet Kabir; he mirrors her mother’s
final days, an inescapable memory which has now resurfaced. Her beautiful mother, so vibrant
and kind, became immobile and fixed to a bed. A woman who everyone knew to be energetic
and lively became so unrecognisable.
In her mind, Kabir reflects the painful decline in health her mother had also faced. Fariha
was afraid of death; she was afraid of loss, of being abandoned. By avoiding it she can deny its
existence. It was nothing but childish, and she realizes it must have only brought pain to her
Uncle.
Fariha’s father had passed away when she was too young to discern different faces, so
growing up Kabir was Fariha’s only father figure, and neglected that responsibility. When the
doctor pronounced her mother dead, Fariha was all by herself. However Kabir had never allowed
her to realise that, and she basked in that feeling naively.
Kabir dodges Fariha’s sentiment, placing his palm to her face. “You’ve grown so much,
my Fariha.” He smiles, and without being able to constrain herself, Fariha returns the favour.
“Uncle, please, don’t lose hope.” She pleads. She grasps her uncle’s hands, gently
squeezing them.
Lutfar speaks up, “Uncle, I hope you understand that all of us care deeply for you. We all
are grateful to you, so when you say this, it makes us feel incompetent as well.”
Kabir laughs. “Is that so? Okay, I’ll keep that in mind.”
Despite his sincere tone, Fariha assumes he only says this to keep them quiet. Then, as if
on cue, Khushi makes her entrance, holding a tray with four tea cups.
“Sorry to keep you waiting!” Khushi enthusiastically jogs towards them, placing the tray
on the side table.
“Thank you, Aunty.” Fariha had then let out a genuine smile for the first time since she
stepped through the flat’s front door.
As Fariha bids farewell, she promises her uncle she will visit again as soon as possible.
Kabir only nods with a small smile. Stepping out of Kabir’s room Fariha spots the long-forgotten
plate of rice, and reprimands Khushi.
“Aunty, you have to make sure to eat well,” she says, which only earns a hum from
Khushi, who hands her a box of sweets. “Aunty–”.
“Fariha, thank you.” Khushi’s eyes appear to have a glossy shield, it makes Fariha’s heart
swell. “Your uncle appreciates it as well.” She smiles, as Fariha frowns.
“How has your health been aunty?” Fariha asks, concern dripping from her voice.
“Oh, I’m fine.” Khushi waves it off casually, earning a disapproving look from Fariha.
“Fariha dear, I have to be fine.” Khushi says with a resigned tone. Fariha is unable to conjure a
rebuttal.
As Fariha steps out of the flat, she lingers at the door for a moment, and suddenly wraps
her arms around Khushi. Despite the unresolved tension and unspoken conversations, for a
moment, they had shared laughter and warmth. And as she stood in front of the elevator, a box of
sweets in her hand, she understands that it is enough.

runs.text: Fariha’s fingertips hesitantly press on the calling bell of the flat. The thudding rain had steadily
intensified as the day progressed, which made the appearance of thunder seem inevitable. She let
out a breath, anxiety twisting at the pit of her stomach. A part of her wants to turn around, to
escape, but she stays firmly in place.
“Coming!” A voice calls out. Fariha is able to recognise it as Kabir’s wife, Khushi. Kabir
is Fariha’s maternal uncle, the one who stood by her side when her mother passed and all hell
broke loose. With his guidance she was able to process her passing, and simultaneously manage
to overcome the ruthless legal battles which followed. While others circled her like vultures, he
ensured she never had to fend them off alone.
Distracted by her thoughts, Fariha is startled when the door swings open, revealing a
disheveled Khushi.
“Fariha, it’s been so long! You never said you were coming?” Fariha offers a small smile,
“well, come in.” Khushi steps aside, making way for her niece to step in.
“How have you been Aunty?” Fariha asks, as she walks into the home. She scans Khushi
who looks utterly exhausted; messy hair tied away from her face, with a few strands loose, and
sunken circles visible beneath her eyes. Her eyes fall on a plate of rice on top of the dinner table,
set next to a skillet with fish curry. She suddenly feels guilty for coming unannounced; she is
disturbing the single moment of quiet Khushi can afford.
“Well,” she laughs, “I’m as good as I can be.” She runs her hands through the knots in her
hair. Fariha feels her shoulders slump. “Your uncle is in his room, you should go and see him. He
always asks Lutfar about you.”
“Ah.” She flinches slightly, suddenly reminded why she decided to come. “Yes, um,” she
spoke slowly, as she hands a plastic bag to Khushi, “this is for Uncle, it’s just some fruits.
Apples.”
Khushi smiles softly, thanking Fariha, telling her she didn’t have to. Fariha only laughs in
reply.
As Khushi walks into the kitchen, Fariha glances around the expanse of the room. She
could barely recall the last time she had been here. However the familiar wooden dining table her
mother had gifted her uncle as a wedding gift still stood strong years later. She pictures her
mother sitting across from her uncle, laughing over a cup of tea.
The bittersweet image lingers in her mind as she walks into Kabir’s room, only to stop
short at the sight of him. Witnessing his once agile figure slumped on the bed, she is able to
understand now that her uncle was no longer the active man he once was. He is now withered
and languid, while his face wears an expression of dejection. His mouth is slightly parted, with
his eyes unfocused, unaware of her entrance.
“Uncle,” Fariha was afraid her voice would crack if she spoke too much. Kabir’s
despondent expression was brightened with a small grin and sparkling eyes. She smiles as she
continues, “Hello.”
“Fariha, my girl.” He extends a shaking hand, gesturing for her to take a seat. He puts his
hand on hers, and its shakiness makes her world quake.
“How have you been?” His voice, too, was weak and trembling.
Fariha clears her throat, afraid to break down. She forces a genial smile to paint her
expression. “Good, Uncle. How about you?”
He takes a moment to respond, something unfamiliar to Fariha. Before, whenever she
asked him about his health before, he would merely gesture at himself as though it was obvious:
he was fantastic. That same man now sits frail, supported by a combination of his bed frame and
pillows, feebly responding after long pauses.
“Better,” he says. Fariha waits, expecting more, however nothing more comes. The
silence is broken by Khushi’s entrance.
“Look at who’s come to visit you!” Khushi exclaims to Kabir while holding a tray with
sweets and water.
“Oh, Aunty!” says Fariha, “You didn’t have to. I only came to see Uncle, this wasn’t
necessary!” She becomes aware of the weight on Khushi’s shoulders, she doesn’t want to add to
the burden.
“Oh, be quiet. This is nothing,” she says dismissively. Fariha smiles meekly, thanking
her. She takes a seat on the bed, opposite to where Fariha sits on a plastic chair. “Your Uncle was
in the hospital, if you didn’t hear.”
Guilt gnaws at Fariha’s stomach, “Lutfar told me. I couldn’t go since I was in London for
work.” Fariha wasn’t completely lying. The truth is, her work was done by the time Kabir was
admitted to the hospital. However, for some reason, she couldn’t bring herself to cut an early
ticket. Even today, she came with much reluctance. She wonders what caused her to have this
awful feeling.
“Yes, Lutfar told us you were busy,” Fariha’s guilt intensifies. She allowed others to get
caught in her web of lies. “Your uncle was doing much worse. He—” Kabir suddenly interrupts,
raising an arm.
“Enough. There’s no point in talking about that.”
Khushi frowns at the interruption but says nothing more.
Fariha glances around the room awkwardly, unsure of what to say in response. Her eyes
suddenly spot a frame hanging on the wall. A picture of a young Kabir; she remembers him
showing her this picture. It was from his time in Ireland during the 1980’s. The black and white
finish reflects its age, however his smile radiates colour, carrying a sense of freedom she could
no longer see.
Khushi traces Fariha’s gaze, and softly sighs. Her voice breaks her out of her trance.
“Let me prepare the tea!”
Before Fariha can respond, she rushes out, leaving the two alone once again. They both
stare at Khushi’s figure as she disappears through the doorway.
“When were you discharged, Uncle?” Fariha asks, attempting conversation. She takes the
bowl with sweets in her hand,
roshmalay
; her favourite.
“This Monday.” He answers easily. Fariha nods, and what follows after is dreadful
silence. Fariha plays with the hem of her shirt, straightening her back as silence thrums in her
ears, causing her to shift in place. Abruptly, Kabir speaks up, looking up at Fariha’s face.
“A life where I’m chained to my bed, unable to do anything for myself, well, is that kind
of life even worth living?” he asks, his face expressionless, but eyes glistening and voice shaky.
Fariha stares at her uncle for a long while, even after he glances away. His lips quiver
ever so slightly.
“Uncle!” A familiar voice breaks Fariha out of her trance. “Looking fresh.”
Fariha watches carefully as her uncle grins at Lutfar’s appearance.
“Grab a chair,” Kabir instructs. Lutfar’s eyes fall on Fariha, who continues to look at their
uncle.
Lutfar acknowledges her with a greeting, however, it goes unheard by Fariha as she
begins to speak. “Why do you think so uncle?”
His gaze returns to her immediately, but he responds after some time.
“Fariha, whenever I think about who I used to be and what I am now, I just can’t help but
feel helpless. My life has lost its value.”
“How can you say this uncle?” Fariha’s voice rises more than she would like it to as she
realises she could no longer deny the reality. The reality that her beloved uncle was now an ailing
man; and that the uncle who breathed the will to live into her had lost it himself.
“Fariha, you just won’t get it.” He let out a breathless, and cruelly amused laugh. Fariha
sits still, demanding him to elaborate with her silence. “You see, I’m no more than a liability.
Look at the state of your aunt, it’s not like she’s young enough to be running around for a grown
man like me. I’ve become a burden.”
“Uncle, did you think this of my mother as well?” Her voice remains low with much
restraint, afraid to alert the whole neighbourhood. “Did you think she was some unbearable
burden?” She bites her lip to shield a sob, feeling Lutfar’s reassuring hand on her shoulder,
forcing down her nerves.
Kabir remains quiet under her heavy gaze. “No,” he replies.
“So then why are you assuming you are?”
No response.
“Uncle, you know what I’m endlessly grateful for? That I was able to be there for my
mother during her final days. Being able to be there for someone, to take care of them, that itself
is a privilege.” Fariha speaks with feigned composure, her voice broken and her spirit shattered.
Fariha’s gaze lingers on her uncle’s trembling hands, his slumped posture, his downcast
expression, and she understands why she was so reluctant to meet Kabir; he mirrors her mother’s
final days, an inescapable memory which has now resurfaced. Her beautiful mother, so vibrant
and kind, became immobile and fixed to a bed. A woman who everyone knew to be energetic
and lively became so unrecognisable.
In her mind, Kabir reflects the painful decline in health her mother had also faced. Fariha
was afraid of death; she was afraid of loss, of being abandoned. By avoiding it she can deny its
existence. It was nothing but childish, and she realizes it must have only brought pain to her
Uncle.
Fariha’s father had passed away when she was too young to discern different faces, so
growing up Kabir was Fariha’s only father figure, and neglected that responsibility. When the
doctor pronounced her mother dead, Fariha was all by herself. However Kabir had never allowed
her to realise that, and she basked in that feeling naively.
Kabir dodges Fariha’s sentiment, placing his palm to her face. “You’ve grown so much,
my Fariha.” He smiles, and without being able to constrain herself, Fariha returns the favour.
“Uncle, please, don’t lose hope.” She pleads. She grasps her uncle’s hands, gently
squeezing them.
Lutfar speaks up, “Uncle, I hope you understand that all of us care deeply for you. We all
are grateful to you, so when you say this, it makes us feel incompetent as well.”
Kabir laughs. “Is that so? Okay, I’ll keep that in mind.”
Despite his sincere tone, Fariha assumes he only says this to keep them quiet. Then, as if
on cue, Khushi makes her entrance, holding a tray with four tea cups.
“Sorry to keep you waiting!” Khushi enthusiastically jogs towards them, placing the tray
on the side table.
“Thank you, Aunty.” Fariha had then let out a genuine smile for the first time since she
stepped through the flat’s front door.
As Fariha bids farewell, she promises her uncle she will visit again as soon as possible.
Kabir only nods with a small smile. Stepping out of Kabir’s room Fariha spots the long-forgotten
plate of rice, and reprimands Khushi.
“Aunty, you have to make sure to eat well,” she says, which only earns a hum from
Khushi, who hands her a box of sweets. “Aunty–”.
“Fariha, thank you.” Khushi’s eyes appear to have a glossy shield, it makes Fariha’s heart
swell. “Your uncle appreciates it as well.” She smiles, as Fariha frowns.
“How has your health been aunty?” Fariha asks, concern dripping from her voice.
“Oh, I’m fine.” Khushi waves it off casually, earning a disapproving look from Fariha.
“Fariha dear, I have to be fine.” Khushi says with a resigned tone. Fariha is unable to conjure a
rebuttal.
As Fariha steps out of the flat, she lingers at the door for a moment, and suddenly wraps
her arms around Khushi. Despite the unresolved tension and unspoken conversations, for a
moment, they had shared laughter and warmth. And as she stood in front of the elevator, a box of
sweets in her hand, she understands that it is enough.

title: A Letter from an Unrequited Lover
author: wallflower
excerpt: Dear Marie,
imageAlt: Cover image for A Letter from an Unrequited Lover
content: Dear Marie,
I miss you terribly.
I write to you not to mock you nor do I write to you to salvage my conscience, no matter how
terribly it aches me, especially when night falls. I write to you to keep you alive in both memory
and spirit. The contents of this letter will be the same as the others before this, and it will be
stored in the same manner, under my bed in the dusty wooden box of guilt and self-hatred.
Will you ever return?
There are days when I cannot look myself in the mirror. There is not a bigger thief than I for who
can steal something greater than someone else’s vivacity. Yet, I battle through the impulsive, the
obsessive and the disgusting reality that is my existence. You see I never wanted to hurt you, it
was only a mistake. Oh, I am defending myself again, maybe I should have driven myself into the
oak woods. Never mind I am rambling again…
I still reminisce about two summers ago- when we first met, you in that fancy powder blue dress
and I looking shamelessly at your incomprehensible beauty. The thing about beauty is it can kill, I
tried to make you understand so many times Marie. You must understand I really tried, I really
did.
Beauty can nourish ones soul while taking away all other sources of sustenance, the cruelest
thing about beauty especially if it is fidgety like you is that it doesn’t like to stay. So how did you
leave me? Broken, rejected, and withering like the ugliest flower amongst the green grass of
envy.
You must understand I had to do what I did. More to save you rather than make you mine
forever. To save you from the embarrassment of piling away your beauty to another man,
another problem.
The night that everything went wrong you told me you love him, that I should stop my attempts
because you’ll never be mine. I couldn’t help but smile at how silly the words coming out of your
pretty mouth were, you didn’t know it yet but I was the only meant for you. I saved you…. You
just did see it yet.
But then, when you didn’t stop talking and I could see your cheeks getting more flushed at the
sound of that pest of a man’s name with a certain sort of passion in your gorgeous eyes. I
couldn’t help but wonder why it was that you never not once looked at me like that. All of a
sudden, every fiber of my being was on fire, I couldn’t control the weighs of my hand reaching
out for some closure in order to save you from your own destruction, our destruction. My hands
touched the cold bronze of the Baroque candlestick on the mantelpiece. As I fingered the
excellent craftsmanship of the casters I imagined my life without you whilst you went on
rambling about your plans to marry him.
I couldn’t take it anymore, this wasn’t supposed to happen, it’s supposed to be our story. My
eyesight grew blurry, I clutched onto the heavy rage of the candlestick and struck oppressively
until I felt your beautiful warmth splatter across my wretched face. Your one last gracefulness
towards me before your depart.
In that moment Marie, I swear I saw us sitting in our usual spot, the damned white bench in the
park. The heavenliest place on earth. Your face so near to me I could hear the pattern of your
breathing. Your face red from the cold air and the smoke evading your mouth, often I’d like to
wonder how it would feel to catch it with my mouth. The thing is, a monster like me is not for
the likes of you. I think we were always meant to be like this, side by side like an instrument, or
complimentary showpieces. You always told me I understood you the best. And I do. But Marie,
my girl, I can’t say the same about you. Yet, how I still love you so!
You come to me in my dreams, in my waking and in my death. I may not be reunited with you in
death for there’s blood on my hands no matter how pure it is. Thus any thoughts of surrendering
my soul has evaded me thus far.
For now, I am content with the fact that the ravaging hands of that man will seek you only to find
absence. In the same landscape I see myself deserving purgatory for hurting you so badly to the
point of disfiguration. You see, it is only a tactic to preserve your beauty in my memories and
nowhere else.
They never found your body and I pray to god that they never will. I am sitting on our potentiality
and lost promises whilst suffering from the asthmatic reactions from soul searching through
clouds of smoke of redemption. There will never be another like you. I promise.
I look for you in the sunlight peaking through the morning mist, little strands of heaven, your
reaching out to me or looking down on me I do not know. I only know that I miss you ….. I am
terribly sorry. Forgive me not, so that I can keep writing you letters begging.
Rest well, my love
Yours for eternity,

title: Sanctity of a Sanctuary
author: Aristocrat
excerpt: A house that eats memories
imageAlt: Cover image for Sanctity of a Sanctuary
content: A house that eats memories
Soaking my despair in all its glory
Yet, an unclaimed property
Muddled with its unkemptness
Vast in its territory
But tell me, were you ever just an abode with all your bounty?
Bounty in reminiscence, bounty in laughter
Was it all in sincerity, or in mindless chatter?
I ponder, I mull, I sit in contemplation
For to me, it was all but simple recollection
Dwelling of closeness, dwelling of proximity
Seldom melancholic, seldom wistful
Now I sit while I ruminate over your ephemerality
Fleeting and ever tristful
What once was mine, now merely remains.
A relic of a self I no longer recognise.
The remnants of a life once inhabited.
Familiarity surrendered to the passage of time.

title: She
author: NAFIZ-BIN-HAFIZ
excerpt: Meadows passed me by as I cruised along her side,
imageAlt: Cover image for She
content: Meadows passed me by as I cruised along her side,
Amber rays of the winter sun caressed her silky hair.
Radiant clouds smiled where the gleaming stars reside
When the world goes to sleep at night,
And flakes of dreamdust fill the air.
Morning birds flew and came to greet us with their song,
All around the sky played their gleeful tunes of grace.
Raging through the trees, raced a river, fierce and strong,
Wild and mighty it marched on
And yet seraphic was its face.
Mountains stood tall with their heads amidst the clouds,
Around a valley painted green with scattered purple, blue and red;
Rocky roads roamed through the dense, charming woods;
While waterfalls from heaven’s peaks
Arched down like mystic threads.
Myriads of epitomes of beauty had rained
As if the goblet of divinity had poured out onto me,
Realm of the mortals became one with the one above,
With angelic mist it was unchained; from despair it was free.
And yet the only thing that had enthralled my dazzled mind — was she.

title: Did It Make Sense?
author: R.A.N. — Remember A Name.
excerpt: Late evening. The rain had stopped, but the city remained restless.
imageAlt: Cover image for Did It Make Sense?
content: Late evening. The rain had stopped, but the city remained restless.
Rickshaws surrounded the area, trying to profit from the restlessness. One stood on all four wheels,
antique-looking but wrapped in its waterproof jacket. Water dripped from the blue sheet covering the
rickshaw.
One drop.
Then another.
And another.
The old man sat beneath it, waiting, with no particular thought in his head.
He did not know whom he was waiting for, or what.
Was he waiting?
Did he need to wait?
Why?
Perhaps he was waiting for a passenger.
Or simply for the night to grow late enough that nobody would bother asking him for directions.
In a world that loves answers, he was always looking for questions.
But never their answers, though.
What an odd man.
Could the moon ever rise without the sun setting?
The answer was obviously no.
He rejected it.
He had never been fond of answers.
Called them unnecessary.
A little girl appeared beside the rickshaw.
Her clothes were shaggy and torn, yet modest.
Her hair was tangled, and, surprisingly enough, her feet seemed to shine despite her being barefoot.
She stared at the rickshaw's blue plastic sheet with her big doe eyes, almost as if she were seeing the
world for the first time.
"Does it know where it's going?"
The man gave her a disheartened look.
"No."
She watched another drop gather at the edge.
"Wow."
She followed it until it disappeared into the puddle beneath the rickshaw.
"And the world accepted it anyway."
"What do you mean?"
"It didn't know where to go, and the world still gave it a place."
He simply stared at the puddle.
She climbed onto the rickshaw.
"Yes."
"Where?"
"Home."
"Where's that?"
She pointed down the road.
"Over there."
He started driving.
They passed a tea stall.
It was lively, with a group of men bursting into laughter, almost as if music were pouring from their
hearts.
The girl huffed in annoyance.
"Why do they do that?"
"Do what?"
"Make those noises."
"Laughing?"
"Yes."
"Something was funny."
"What was funny?"
"I don't know."
She chose to sit with that for a while.
"Isn't it weird?"
"What?"
"Humans. They sound like animals when they're happy."
The man laughed.
"You do that too."
"Yeah, I do. Maybe because they're too used to their human voices. They experiment with different
animal sounds when they're happy."
She nodded.
The water continued dripping from the sheet.
She eyed it with curiosity.
"It's still falling."
"Yeah, it tends to do that. It'll stop eventually."
"Does everything?"
The man thought it best not to answer.
They passed A middle aged women was hanging clothes from a alcony
The girl reached for a loose thread on the old mans clothes
She held it with her two hands, carefully, gently.
“Was this alive?”
Stunned the man looked back while driving.
What?
This.
She lifted the thread.
Was this alive before it turned into this?
Its just a piece of cloth.
But it was something else before and came from somewhere
She looked at the trees beside the road.
Why do they tear up their mother to make clothes for themself?
I mean they need clothes
More than their mother?
The man chose to not answer again
And the mother still chose to make more people?
The old man almost laughed.
She looked at him.
“Why?”
He shook his head.
“Nothing.”
She let the thread fall.
“People are sometimes weird.”
The old man looked at her.
“Why?”
“Greed.”
She looked at the flowers growing beside the road.
“They take away all the beauty from nature.”
She pointed at a flower someone had picked and left on the pavement.
They exchange plant for plant.

The World Accepted It Anyway
Late evening. The rain had stopped, but the city remained restless.
Rickshaws surrounded the area, trying to profit from the restlessness. One stood on all four wheels,
antique-looking but wrapped in its waterproof jacket. Water dripped from the blue sheet covering the
rickshaw.
One drop.
Then another.
And another.
The old man sat beneath it, waiting, with no particular thought in his head.
He did not know whom he was waiting for, or what.
Was he waiting?
Did he need to wait?
Why?
Perhaps he was waiting for a passenger. Or simply for the night to grow late enough that nobody would
bother asking him for directions.
In a world that loved answers, he was always looking for questions.
But never their answers, though.
What an odd man.
Could the moon ever rise without the sun setting?
The answer was obviously no.
He rejected it.
He had never been fond of answers. He considered them unnecessary.
A little girl appeared beside the rickshaw.
Her clothes were shaggy and torn, yet modest. Her hair was tangled, and, surprisingly enough, her feet
seemed to shine despite her being barefoot.
She stared at the rickshaw's blue plastic sheet with her big doe eyes, almost as if she were seeing the
world for the first time.
"Does it know where it's going?"
The man gave her a disheartened look.
"No."
She watched another drop gather at the edge.
"Wow."
She followed it until it disappeared into the puddle beneath the rickshaw.
"And the world accepted it anyway."
"What do you mean?"
"It didn't know where to go, and the world still gave it a place."
He simply stared at the puddle.
She climbed onto the rickshaw.
"Where to?"
"Home."
"Where's that?"
She pointed down the road.
"Over there."
He started driving.
They passed a tea stall. It was lively, with a group of men bursting into laughter, almost as if music were
pouring from their hearts.
The girl huffed in annoyance.
"Why do they do that?"
"Do what?"
"Make those noises."
"Laughing?"
"Yes."
"Something was funny."
"What was funny?"
"I don't know."
She chose to sit with that for a while.
"Isn't it weird?"
"What?"
"Humans. They sound like animals when they're happy."
The man laughed.
"You do that too."
"Yeah, I do. Maybe because they're too used to their human voices. They experiment with different
animal sounds when they're happy."
She nodded.
The water continued dripping from the sheet.
She eyed it with curiosity.
"It's still falling."
"Yeah, it tends to do that. It'll stop eventually."
"Does everything?"
The man thought it best not to answer.
They passed a middle-aged woman hanging clothes from a balcony.
The girl reached for a loose thread on the old man's clothes. She held it with both hands, carefully, gently.
"Was this alive?"
Stunned, the man looked back while driving.
"What?"
"This."
She lifted the thread.
"Was this alive before it turned into this?"
"It's just a piece of cloth."
"But it was something else before. It came from somewhere."
She looked at the trees beside the road.
"Why do they tear up their mother to make clothes for themselves?"
"I mean, they need clothes."
"More than their mother?"
The man chose not to answer again.
"And the mother still chose to make more people?"
The old man almost laughed.
She looked at him.
"Why?"
He shook his head.
"Nothing."
She let the thread fall.
"People are sometimes weird."
The old man looked at her.
"Why?"
"Greed."
She looked at the flowers growing beside the road.
"They take away all the beauty from nature."
She pointed at a flower someone had picked and left on the pavement.
"They exchange plant for plant."
"What?"
"They give money for it."
"Yeah, that's what is usually done."
"Do you like flowers?"
"To some extent, yes."
"Which part of them?"
"Hm?"
"Would you want the flower's body or its head?"
"Um, the head? It's not a flower without the head, is it?"
"But you still think money is more valuable?"
"Yes?"
"But it's the flower's body!"
"Humans exchange the head for the body."
She paused again.
She looked at the flowers.
"Humans hate themselves."
"Why do you think that?"
"They find happiness in exchanging heads with bodies."
"How can one live with that?"
The man chose not to answer.
They passed a bakery.
"What are those?"
"Cakes?"
"Yeah, cakes. What do they do?"
"Um, people eat them on their birthdays."
"Oh? They need cakes to remember the 365 days they've lived? How unique."
"Why is there fire on top of that one?"
"Those are lit candles."
"And they're not scared of the fire?"
"They choose to make fire a part of their special day?"
The man had no answer.
He kept driving.
The girl was quiet for a while.
"Do you have a home?"
The old man kept his eyes on the road.
"No."
She nodded.
"I don't either."
She studied him for a while.
"Did you go?"
"I don't go. I take you to places."
"You haven't?"
"Where are you talking about?"
"To your funeral."
He frowned.
"I'm not dead."
She tilted her head.
"You look like someone who died without needing mortality."
The old man looked away, no longer interested in answering.
They passed a party centre.
Fireworks were being set off.
"Fireworks."
The girl stood beside the rickshaw, her eyes reflecting the colours above.
Blue.
White.
Gold.
She watched them disappear, one after another.
"I love the world."
The old man looked at her.
"They made me like a night filled with fireworks."
She smiled.
"It's funny, though."
"What?"
"When I talked to a firework, it told me fireworks are a nightmare to the night."
Another burst of light opened above them.
She watched the darkness return.
"Am I a nightmare?"
The old man stopped the rickshaw.
He struggled not to answer, but remained quiet.
Then
Drip.
A drop of water fell from the blue plastic sheet.
The girl looked up.
Another gathered at the edge.
She watched it tremble.
Then fall.
She looked at the old man.
"Do I make sense?”

title: When every man is dead
author: SUN
excerpt: When the night falls on the bloody mud,
imageAlt: Cover image for When every man is dead
content: When the night falls on the bloody mud,
The earth knows who bloodied it.
When the children stop crying in the tender age,
The walls know every bit.
When even the river is shackled by the fresh blood,
The water knows who shackled it.
And,
When they are done laughing on their high chairs,
Might they stop this horrific?
When will their hearts start to ache,
Burdened shoulders by every death.
When will their hearts cry out loud,
Not even knowing what was it about.
Might it be late?
It’s already late,
“What good stopping now?”
They say with a destined fate.
When every man will die,
Who will we send to wars?
Might we make robots,
To fight those wars.
As it’s too late,
Already,
It’s too late,
“What will the good be if we stop it now?”
“Who will we fight with now?
No man left to die”
The robots may ask,
With an angry sigh.
No but really,
When every man is dead,
Dead is every woman and children,
God may ask,
“What was your sin?
Why were you put to death?”
Indeed he knows, yet he still asks,
So give them the answer before you pull the trigger.
Before you pull the trigger to blow up the brains,
Before you press the button to obliterate the states,
Before you order your army to kill those little lives,
Before the fire gets cold and hot is the ice.
Give them the answer.

title: Love
author: R.A.N. — Remember A Name.
excerpt: When I say I love myself, I don't just mean when I'm happy or proud of myself.
imageAlt: Cover image for Love
content: When I say I love myself, I don't just mean when I'm happy or proud of myself.
I genuinely never thought of me without I.
I have experienced happiness, pride, sadness, fear, anger, disgust and distrust. Yet, at the end of the day, I
know that no one will ever replace the connection I have with myself. The love I have for myself makes
the word connection feel inadequate. When things don't go as expected, I am the first person to enter my
own inner monologue, with or without room for judgement.
All the lies I've told,
the truths I've hidden,
The sins I've committed,
The things I wasn't supposed to be proud of, but am,
The admiration, not the pride, I have for myself,
The silhouette of my past, which I don't appreciate but grudgingly respect
I love all of it.
I won't wait for someone to make me their muse.
I take pride in being the one who creates. I am not just a writer, painter or reader.
I am, solely, an imaginator.
In every moment of my life.
For any creative, love for the world they have created is the highest form of love there is.
But even more so when I am the world.
We have come so far in seeking to be understood that we have forgotten how to understand ourselves.
The usual being is built from the air they breathe in,
But I don't trust that air.
Instead, I choose to inhale the air I am built of.
Even when it runs out, I refuse to breathe anything else.
Even when I know it will poison me.
Perhaps there is a price to being one's own world.
But all this love doesn't excuse the mistakes I've made.
I still love how I judge myself,
How I hold myself accountable for the guilt of being indecisive.
Even so, I love myself for being willing to pay the price of being me.
Whether a blessing or a curse.
Even with an empty pocket.
Love.
ME.

title: My Favorite TV show
author: Rihah Abeer
excerpt: I was born in the mid-2000s and spent my formative years growing up in the city. During that
imageAlt: Cover image for My Favorite TV show
content: I was born in the mid-2000s and spent my formative years growing up in the city. During that
time, TV was one of the primary sources of entertainment for the children growing up in the
urban area. Confined in the urban density, TV became the centrepiece in my world. I have
watched a lot of programs during those times. Some of them have shaped my imagination
more than anything else in those years. But there was one show that captivated and
impacted me more than the other and it was an animated TV show called Dragon Ball Z.
Dragon Ball Z is my favorite TV show.
Dragon Ball Z is a Japanese animation TV show. It was hugely popular among the kids and
teenagers at that time. There was something about its universe, replete with impossible
strength, loyalty, and rivalry, that transcended age divisions in a way few other programs did.
For me it wasn’t just about a cartoon filled with amazing fights and superpowers. It is
because of the characters themselves and how they resolve the conflicts, their
competitiveness, and friendship building between them that kept pushing their limits.
Moreover, beyond the story, I was particularly intrigued by a character of the show named:
Vegeta.
Vegeta was not the hero of the series. This role belonged to Goku, who exhibited unbridled
optimism and pure goodness effortlessly. But Vegeta had pride and a bad temper, and for
much of the show, he was downright villainous. It is precisely this depth of character that
intrigued me about him. Now that time has passed, I understand that seeing him develop
throughout all of those episodes subconsciously taught me things that I have only fully
understood more recently in my life. During my childhood years when I met Vegeta, I got
attracted towards his confidence and determination. He was a very competitive individual
and did not want to be inferior to anyone, particularly Goku. Vegeta's rivalry with Goku is a
captivating storyline in the series. Back then when I was a child, the concept was fascinating
to me because I was thinking of who would be more powerful. However, now that I have
grown up, I see Vegeta differently, especially his personality. His personality has taught me
lessons of ambition, competitiveness, humility, failure, and personal growth.
The first lesson that I learned from Vegeta was the importance of healthy competition.
Vegeta always kept on competing with himself since he wanted to become better than he
had been before. While the rivalry between Vegeta and Goku was fueled by envy and
egocentrism, it also motivated him to try his best and improve himself. This is an example
that taught me that the success of others serves as motivation rather than the reason for
insecurity about myself. In case I realize that others are doing well and I am lagging behind,
then I need to focus on the success of others and achieve success through hard work.
Vegeta also showed me a lesson about the problems that can develop from having too much
pride. Throughout the series, Vegeta had a hard time accepting the fact that another person
could be better at something than he was himself. This is one problem that I have
encountered in real life as well. Admitting the fact that one needs help or that another person
is better at something than oneself can be uncomfortable. However, recognizing one’s
weaknesses is frequently the beginning of overcoming them. Vegeta’s development allowed
me to understand the significance of confidence; however, without humility, confidence may
be the very thing that hinders your development.
The most significant thing about his character was the way that he grew in humility. Vegeta
started off as an arrogant fighter who cared about little more than proving that he was better
than anyone else. But as time went on, things were different for him. He began to form
relationships with other people, including Bulma and his own children, and became someone
who would sacrifice himself for the benefit of others. This realization made me realize that
humility doesn’t necessarily equate to the absence of ambition. A person can retain his
ambition and yet be aware of the significance of others around him. In fact, humility will
enable us to be more open to meeting many people that we could not have otherwise
encountered had we been prideful. This is because humility will enable us to listen to and
learn from people, even take their advice when they know better than us.
Another lesson I learned from Vegeta was how to handle failure. Vegeta suffered many
failures over the course of the series. While his attempts at beating Goku continuously failed,
he kept on training and striving nonetheless. These failures played an important role in his
growth process and were just a step in the journey for him. This gave me a lesson on how
failure does not necessarily imply that one does not have the ability to accomplish
something. It may only imply that the individual has not achieved their objective. Maybe the
most inspiring thing about Vegeta is that he evolves. He does not come across as a perfect
hero. In fact, he is an arrogant and selfish individual with questionable moral standards at
first. However, through his experiences, his ability to be loyal, loving, responsible and
self-sacrificing is brought out. This made me realize that one’s worst traits do not define him
or her all the time.
Looking back, I can now see how Dragon Ball Z played a major part in my life during my
early days, and this is not only because of the enjoyment that it provided me with, but
because of the journeys of the characters in the show that helped me understand various
aspects of life based on my growth to an adult. This is why, despite my growing older and
having watched various other types of television shows, Dragon Ball Z remains the best TV
show for me.

title: Savour
author: wallflower
excerpt: I feel his eyes staring into me from across the table. Has he sensed anything yet? No, I cannot take any
imageAlt: Cover image for Savour
content: I feel his eyes staring into me from across the table. Has he sensed anything yet? No, I cannot take any
chances. I must be over with it as soon as possible. I stand up from my chair and walk slowly towards the
kitchen, his eyes keep following me from his seat. Nothing I can do about it, nothing he can do to run,
not any more at least.
I bring out the dishes. It took me hours to prepare the meat with wine, pearl onions and smoky
mushrooms. All my life I’ve had people of many statures compliment my cooking, and at one point of I
started taking pride in this skill. What was left unnoticed and hiding in plain sight is that cooking would
turn out to be the vilest and also the most advantageous skill for someone like me. My dear father, may
his soul rot in peace, wanted me to become a butcher ever since I started speaking but I never let that
old hag get in the way of my true passion, food. Specifically meats- meats of all kinds. Even the kinds
that may make your stomach turn. He really did try though, my father. He even went as far as dressing
me up in boy clothes and cutting my hair short. As if cutting meat had anything to do with what sex I
was.
I’ve tried all sorts of meats, beef, chicken, goat, buffalo, rabbit blah blah…even alligator meat. Basically
all the socially acceptable kinds. But there’s one type of meat I haven’t had the luxury of tasting yet and
that is…human meat. Now I know what you might be thinking, that that’s undoable or absolutely
disgusting. But my god, my conscience has failed me so terribly all my life and curiosity has gripped me
forever. I can’t let it suffocate me anymore. So I made a plan to fulfill my desires.
I love tender meat the same way I love the unruly coarseness of wild meat. I can talk for hours about
that. Which is exactly what I was doing with this particular guest. We met at a banquet party that was
serving the nastiest steak I’ve ever had, that’s when I noticed him right in front of me sharing the same
look of disgust on his face. He seemed younger than me, perhaps in his late twenties. We locked eyes
and for no reason at all shared a laugh together. That was my cue. I got up and sat beside him and
immediately we started talking about our hatred for the food here. I told him with a rather strange
voracity that we should get out of here and get better food. “But where?” he asked me with this
confused but excited look on his face. “Let’s go to my place, people always tell me I’ve got a knack for
cooking meat”, I reply. Now you might be thinking what sort of man would be willing to go to a strangers
place for a home cooked meal? Answer to that would be any desperate young man who’s got their
intentions warped between hunger for the body and an appetite for good food. Yes, I felt him staring at
me with his lusty eyes and a certain hunger in the way his body twitched around me; he wants me more
than the meal. That’s when I knew he must be the first victim. The best way to begin my first time
should be with a lusting bitch who’s got balls for appetite.
Anyways, I bring out the boeuf bourguignon with a glass of red wine and serve it to him. I bet that makes
him hot. Fucking repulsive. “What about your plate?” he asks me with an attempted caring tone. In my
head I scoff at this question but reply with “oh I’m already full. Go ahead and take a bite. I’d love to see
you eat.” He seems to be pleased with my last remark seeing him blush slightly. Ughh makes me
revolted. He picks up the fork and starts biting into the meal slowly, at the first bite his eyes widen as he
looks at me with amazement. “This is so good… Are you a cook or something?” I look at the mignon
sauce dripping down his lips, crimson red, like blood. He even eats like an ogre. “Oh you flatter me too
much, I only cook for the joy of it. I’m glad you like it…” He doesn’t look up and keeps eating fast and
greedily, without control. I know why he’s hurrying, I knew why the moment he looked at me with such
greed. He finishes the meal and starts drinking the wine. Halfway through the glass I saw his eyes glazing
over and losing control of his hands. “Wha- what’s happening?” he asks me stupefied, his words tripping
on his own tongue. A tremendous smile creeps into my face, etched from one corner to the other
almost reaching my eyes.
For my first time, I didn’t think I would be getting this much pleasure out of it rather than feeling guilt or
fear. Whatever it was, I was feeling cathartic. I could do this forever is what I thought of. Now comes the
hard part. I pick up the butcher knife from underneath the table and approach him slowly. He looks up
at me with a frantic look on his eyes. He cannot move, he cannot speak, he can only watch me. I ask him,
“By the way, what’s your name?” He opens his mouth, to speak or to scream I don’t know, but not a
single sound escapes from his mouth before I strike down the knife on him. And then…silence.
I hadn’t for the life of me had any idea it would be this hard to cut human meat. At this point I am
running strictly on adrenaline, nothing else works, it’s been about 11 hours since I froze his body using
my old rusty freezer that father used to store his deer meat in. Finally, something of his came to use. I
prepared all the spices, pans, oils, containers I require for the dish I’m about to cook. For the past 11
hours I contemplated which part I wanted to taste first. I have decided for it to be the thighs. So I
separated some of the upper thigh meat from the body. And cut it precisely into rectangular shapes. I
can only imagine how he might taste…
The juicy seared steak besides the sirloin displayed on the fine Chinas, garnished with the finest
rosemary and caramelized onion stared back at me. I added the finishing touches, sprinkling some flaky
sea salt on top. Not being able to contain myself any longer, I cut into the dish with my knife and the
meat seemed to melt off right away. What a delicacy! I have never tasted meat richer than this, the
taste seemed to be stuck onto the tip of my tongue with the likes of never letting go. I enjoyed every
single bite and with each bite my prayer for it to never end grew stronger. But alas! Everything good has
to end and end it did. Before this I could never tell you what bliss could be. This is a drug that I could
never tire of, I’ll go to the ends of my life to get this high, I am sure of that much. No matter the
repercussions. Does love ever go wasted? My own, personal debauchery.
I wake up in the dead of the night, by the sounds emerging from my stomach. It has been but only three
hours since I experienced heaven, yet it seems like my body wants to end my happiness. I run to the
bathroom clutching at my stomach with my accusing hands. The dimly lit walls of my bathroom
welcome me and with a desperate plea my basin looks back at me. I cannot help it, I clutch down into
the basin and let the contents of my stomach flood out into the basin. I didn’t vomit due to any sort of
guilt experienced by a murderer or a cannibal. I vomited unwillingly, uninhabited by any emotions,
almost as if my body rejected the idea of any such consumption. I looked at the basin and the mouth fell
open at the sight I saw. A blood bath is all saw. “What the fuck?” I thought to myself. This is not what I
ate what the hell is this, am I vomiting blood? A sudden fear tugs at me from behind but I am not one to
look back, so I turn off the lights and go back to sleep.
I wake up at 4 p.m. in the afternoon with sore spots all over my body. It takes me half an hour before I
can carry myself to the mirror by my bed. Standing in front of the mirror I notice something absurd, I
seem… taller, no, I grew taller by a few inches. “What?” I murmur slowly under my breath, I look down
at my ankles and gape at the purple swollen marks around them. I don’t know how they appeared. My
feet seemed bigger than usual as well with hair as sharp as razor sticking out. Am I seeing things now? I
run to the bathroom to take my chemise off and what I see in the mirror haunts me, my body has
clumps of meat hanging out, with skin lazily lathered onto it. Almost like it was sewn onto them by an
unskilled hand. The only thing normal about me is my face. I grab my car keys and make a run for the
door. “I need to get fresh air, I’m seeing things,” I tell myself. The sun hits my face and immediately I feel
my face burning with a passion, almost like I didn’t have any skin to protect me. Just bare and
vulnerable. I walk to the park it and it takes me about 3 minutes. I see people all around me. It comforts
me to see that no one can see the freakish design that my body has taken overnight. I take deep breaths
and long strolls trying to clear my mind. Is what I saw real? I walk and try to feel my body, I can feel the
clumps underneath my top moving with the rhythm of my legs. The sensation rises bile up to my
throats. I zoom to the nearest bush and vomit. All I see is hair, his hair and something else…nails. Before
I can understand anything I hear a guttural scream erupting and soon realize that the sound is coming
from me. People rush towards me to but stop dead midway upon seeing me. Have they noticed
something peculiar about me? Did they notice the vomit? I scramble for my phone and open my camera
to see my eyes are turning red and hollow. A woman near me screams at the sight of me. I can’t stay
here, I make a run for it.
I lock myself in my apartment. What’s happening to me? My eyesight becomes blurry as I get visions of
the man in his drugged state. All I see is red, like blood is leaking into my eyes. I muffle a scream begging
to come out of me. This is all a bad dream I keep repeating to myself until everything goes blank.
It’s dark here. I don’t know where the light switches are, I cannot move. I can smell myself and I smell
like rotten meat. I cannot speak, I can only see. I look down at myself and all I see is a slab of rotten,
piling meat with leakages of sweat and pus oozing through the rolls of my mass. I get visions of the man
I consumed, he almost always speaks to me. He keeps rambling about us being one and the same. I think
if I could speak I would hear his voice instead of mine. He never cusses at me though. He never shows
any distaste towards me. He only laughs at me. Mocks me. At first I loathed him, but I can never shut
him off. Now I am him. There are no parts of me that belong to the person I was. One time he told me
something that I’ll never forget, “Your father would be so happy to see you right now, you’ve finally
become the boy he always wanted“
I don’t know how long it has been. It feels like an eternity. All I know is when the unjustifiable chains of
hope choke my soul for one last time begging for freedom, his voice will always whisper into my ears the
unmistakable words:
You are what you eat.
