content: My father's lifeline stops halfway down his palm, at a clean pale scar where the rest of it used to
be. When I was small I used to trace it at dinner, all the way from the edge of his hand to the
place where it just stopped, like a road that runs into the sea. He'd close his fingers around mine
and say, Dhorechi, dhorechi, and I'd shriek like it was the best joke in the world. I didn't know
what the scar was then. I thought everybody's father had one. Most of them do.
The marks office is three floors above Sunrise Coaching Centre, past a photocopy shop and a
man who laminates certificates. The rates are taped to the wall beside the stairs, the tape gone
yellow and curling at the corners. Sixty to seventy, a month a mark. Ninety to ninety-five, a year.
Nobody bothers to print the price of a hundred. I've walked past that wall twice a week since I
was twelve, on my way up to physics tuition, and I could recite the whole thing to you now the
way Sheila recites K-pop.
Tonight my mother is reading my palm at the kitchen table. She doesn't ask. She just takes my
hand off the table, turns it over, and runs her thumb down the line, all the way around the base
of my thumb to my wrist. Then she sighs.
"So long," she says. "Like a girl who never studies."
"I study," I tell her. "I study so much I dream in organic chemistry. Last night a benzene ring
proposed to me."
"And?"
"I said I'd think about it."
"Not the benzene. The mock."
"Ninety-one."
"Ninety-one," she says, the way she sniffs milk to see if it's turned.
"Ninety-one is a good number," Dadi says from her mat by the window. She is shelling peas into
a steel bowl and pretending not to listen, which is how she listens to everything. "In my day
they'd have put a garland on you for ninety-one. They'd have walked you round the whole
neighbourhood like a bride."
"In your day, Amma, they'd garland anyone who could spell cat," my mother says.
"In my day I failed my matriculation twice, and look at me."
"Yes, look at you. Shelling peas."
"Shelling peas at eighty-four," Dadi says, and holds up her hand.
You have to see Dadi's hand to understand our house. Her lifeline runs all the way to her wrist
and keeps going past it, faint, like a river on a map that doesn't know where the border is.
Nobody her age bought anything, because when she was a girl there was nothing to buy. You
failed or you passed, and then you lived, apparently, forever.
She goes back to her peas. It's a good argument. There just isn't a box for it on a form.
What you can put on a form is a number. The number for the medical colleges was ninety-six
last year. The year before that, ninety-four. The year before that I don't remember, but it was
lower. Next year it will be higher, because every mark somebody buys pushes the line up for
everyone who didn't. My chemistry teacher calls this simple economics. He likes the phrase. He
says it with his whole chest, simple economics, like he invented it. He has a scar where most of
his line should be, and halfway through writing an equation on the board he has to pull out the
chair and sit down for a minute. We all wait. Nobody says anything. Isn't it simple economics?
My father comes home at nine with a bag of oranges and the evening paper, complaining before
he's through the door.
"Ajke abar shutki niye ashche."
"Shuru hoise," my mother says to the ceiling.
The man at the next desk brings shutki to the office every day, which my father considers an act
of war.
Before he sits down he washes his hands at the basin for a long time, soap all the way up to the
wrists, twice. He has always done this. When I was little I thought it was the dust from the office
files. I think a lot of things about my father that turn out to be something else.
"Ninety-one," my mother tells him, before he's even sat down.
"Ninety-one what? Degrees? It's hot, but it isn't that hot."
"Don't be funny. Your daughter got ninety-one in the mock."
"My daughter got ninety-one with her own head." He sits and pulls the oranges toward him. "Do
you know what I got in my mock? Seventy-four. Seventy-four, and I was so frightened I couldn't
eat for a week. My mother had to feed me rice with her own hand like a baby."
"I did," says Dadi. "He cried into it."
"I did not cry into it."
"He cried into it, and then he ate it, so it was very salty."
"And then what did you do?" my mother asks him, though she knows. We all know.
He doesn't answer right away. He peels an orange in one long spiral, the way he has my whole
life, so the peel comes away in a single curling ribbon he can stand back up on the plate, as if
the orange were still inside it. Then he puts the segments on my plate one at a time.
"Then I did what everyone did," he says.
"And now you have a desk and a pension and a fan that works," my mother says. "Honest is a
teacher at the girls' school. Honest takes the bus."
"I take the bus."
"You take the bus because you're cheap, not because you're honest."
He laughs, and she almost laughs, and this is how my parents love each other: by arguing
about whose fault it is that they love each other.
"We'll go in March," my mother says, firmly. "After the pre-test. Five. Six at the very most."
My father reaches for another orange. He doesn't say anything at all.
I eat my orange and do the maths in my head. Ninety-one to ninety-five, a year a mark. Four
years. Above ninety-five the wall doesn't say, and nobody I know has ever said it out loud, which
tells you everything.
Everyone knows what happens on results day. The newspaper puts the toppers on the front
page, arms up, palms to the camera, the way you show a teacher your hands are clean before
lunch. The shorter the line, the bigger the photo. That's not a rule; it's just how it works out,
because the short lines are the high numbers and the high numbers are the news. Last year's
first place was a boy from the cadet college whose line was a stub no longer than a grain of rice.
He was grinning so hard you could see his back teeth. I cut that photo out and stuck it inside my
wardrobe door, next to the ones from the year before, and the year before that. I'm not proud of
it. I'm telling you so you understand I wasn't some girl who didn't want it. I wanted it the way you
want air.
So I make a plan, and I don't tell anyone. I'm going to learn everything, every single thing, so
that there's nothing left to buy and nobody in my house has to climb those stairs for me. I start
that night, my hands still sticky from the oranges.
Sheila bought back in October, before the pre-tests. Her parents are both engineers, and they
believe in investing early, the way they believe in fixed deposits and getting your eyes tested
every year. She showed me in the girls' toilets on the second floor, the ones where the latch
doesn't work, so one of us always had to hold the door shut with a foot.
"Look, look. Ish, don't touch it, it's still tender. Eight. Eight marks, and they said I'd hardly feel it,
and I hardly do. Is it ugly? Tell me honestly. Actually, don't tell me honestly."
"It's not ugly."
"It's a little bit ugly."
"You said to not tell you honestly!" I smirked.
"Shaitan. Aare dhur, I changed my mind. I'm allowed to change my mind. I'm going to be a
doctor now," she said. She closed her hand and held it against her school shirt like something
warm, and I kept my foot against the door and didn't ask her how many years.
The years come off the end. That's what the office says, what the clerk tells every family on the
stairs: you won't feel a thing until you're old, and by then you'll have a good life to be old in. It's
on a laminated sign behind her desk. The man downstairs probably laminated it.
But by December, Sheila is falling asleep in physics with her eyes open. I don't mean she looks
sleepy. I mean her eyes are open and pointed at the board and she isn't in there. When I pinch
her, she comes back up from somewhere very deep and says, "What, what, I'm listening!"
At home I study at the dining table now, because my desk has run out of room. There are books
on both chairs and on the floor in a ring around my feet, and after dinner my father sits across
from me and peels his orange. I don't watch him. I've heard that sound every night of my life, the
peel coming away in one long piece, and I could do differentiation to it in my sleep.
Then I don't hear it.
I don't know why I look up. Nothing has fallen, and nobody has said anything. It has just gone
quiet.
My father is sitting there with half the peel in one hand and the orange in the other.
In January I start finding white hairs on our bench before assembly. Sheila sits with a little
compact mirror in her lap and pulls them out of her parting one at a time, frowning like she's
threading a needle, and lays them on the desk in a row.
"Don't," she says, without looking up. "Don't say anything."
"I didn't say anything."
"You were going to. I can hear you thinking." Another one. She lays it beside the others. "Ammu
says it's the shampoo. We changed the shampoo."
I watch the row get longer, neat and white on the dark wood, as if she's counting something.
Then she sweeps them all off the edge of the desk into her palm, closes her hand, and the bell
goes.
One night Dadi stops shelling peas with a pod still open in her fingers.
"Ei," she says to my father. "Tor mathai eto paka chul kobe theke?"
My father touches his head like he's checking for a hat. "Office-er tension, Amma."
"Tension," Dadi says, as if it's a curse.
I look up from my book. There's grey at his temples, grey in his eyebrows, grey in the stubble
along his jaw. I look at it for a long time. Then I look down at the books on the chairs and on the
floor around my feet, and at the highlighter in my hand, and I read the same line about electron
shells four times and can't make it mean anything. The whole time I can feel Dadi watching me
over her peas, the way she used to watch me when I was small and climbing something.
Ayan's older brother lives inside my wardrobe door.
He's the photo from three years ago, the one on the left, its corner curling where the tape gave
up: a thin boy in a white shirt, arm up, a line like a full stop, grinning so hard his eyes have
disappeared. Zayan Hassan, first place, Dhaka Board. Ayan sits behind me at physics tuition
and has the longest line in the whole batch. Everyone knows why. Nobody says it.
"Your brother," I say to him one evening in February, on the stairs past the rate wall. "Can I meet
him?"
Ayan stops on the step. "Keno? Autograph nibi?"
"I want to ask him something."
"Ask me. I'm his brother, I know all his secrets. He's scared of lizards and he cried at the end of
Titanic."
"Ayan."
He looks at the rates on the wall for a long time, the way you look at a relative you don't like
across a wedding. "Friday," he says. "After Jumma. Ammu will make you eat. Don't say no to
anything, she takes it personally."
Their flat is on the fourth floor of a building with no lift, and on every landing Ayan waits for me
without saying he's waiting. His mother opens the door before we knock. She's already smiling.
She has the face of a woman who's been smiling at that door for three years.
The photo is in the drawing room. Not cut out of the paper like mine: the whole front page, in a
gold frame, hung above the showcase with the good plates in it.
"Our Zayan," his mother says, as if I could have missed it. "Dhaka Board. First." She says it the
way you say a phone number you've had for years. Then she goes to make tea, and she doesn't
say anything about Ayan at all.
Zayan bhaia is on the sofa under a shawl, an anatomy book open face-down on his chest like a
little roof. He's twenty-one. I know, because I've done the maths on that photo a hundred times.
His hair is grey. Not a streak. All of it, the colour of the ash in an agarbatti stand. When he sits
up to say hello, he does it in two stages, like an old man getting down from a rickshaw.
"You're the one with the wardrobe," he says.
I look at Ayan. Ayan looks at the ceiling fan.
"He tells me everything," Zayan bhaia says. "It's fine… I used to have the whole cricket team in
mine."
He's nice. That's the thing that feels wrong. I climbed four floors ready for a hero or a warning,
and he's just nice, and tired, and a little bit funny. He asks about my mocks. He remembers the
name of my chemistry teacher, and does an impression of him pulling out the chair to sit down
that makes Ayan snort tea through his nose.
"Anatomy is beautiful, actually," he says. "Everything has a name. Every little bone. There are
eight in your wrist." He holds up his hand but doesn't look at it. "Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum,
pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate." He says them fast and flat, the way you give a
rickshaw-wala your address. Then he smiles, carefully, with his mouth closed, so you can't see
any of his teeth at all.
I brought a list of questions, written in the back of my physics copy. Did it hurt. How many. Who
signed. When you sit at your desk at night, does what you know feel like yours. I don't ask any
of them. I ask the only one I can manage.
"Would you do it again?"
He looks past me at the wall: the gold frame and the thin boy with his arm up, grinning so hard
his eyes are gone.
"He would," he says, and nods at the photo. "Ask him."
Then, while his mother is still bringing in the tea, he falls asleep. Just like that, sitting up, in the
middle of niceties. His mother doesn't even stop talking. She tucks the shawl under his chin with
one hand and sets a plate of shingara in front of me with the other.
"Always tired," she says, proud. "Doctor manush."
Ayan walks me to the end of the lane. Neither of us says anything until the corner, where a man
is frying jilapi in a pan as wide as a satellite dish.
"Ammu wanted me to buy," Ayan says. "Twenty. She had the form filled in, my name and
everything."
"What did you say?"
"I said I'd go when Bhaia could climb our stairs without stopping." He holds up his palm in the
light from the jilapi stall, the long line running all the way round to his pulse. "She doesn't
introduce me to people now. She says I'm taking a different path. Like I've joined a cult."
"You'll get eighty-something."
"Eighty-something," he agrees. "And a long, boring life. I'll be a bank officer. I'll be the best bank
officer. I'll have the longest line in the bank."
"Ayan."
"Tui-o kinbi, dekhish," he says. He isn't being cruel. He says it the way you'd tell someone it's
going to rain. "Everyone says they won't. Then March comes."
I go home and cry the whole afternoon, in the bathroom with the tap running so nobody hears,
until the tank on the roof runs dry and Ma bangs on the door wanting to know who's wasting
water. I can't tell you exactly what I'm crying about. Not about Bhaia. Bhaia seemed fine. And
Auntie was happy, so happy. I keep seeing her at that door, smiling. Then I keep seeing Ma.
That night I don't take the photos off my wardrobe door. I just stop opening that side.
By the end of February I've done every past paper back to 2012. I know every footnote in the
textbook, and the mistakes in the footnotes. I didn't go to my cousin's wedding. I gave up
sleeping the way other people give up sugar.
The pre-test results come on the last day of the month. Our chemistry teacher reads them out
the way he always does, from the front, in order, so that everyone knows exactly where
everyone is.
"Sheila. Ninety-eight."
The class claps. Sheila smiles with her mouth closed and doesn't stand up.
He goes down the list. When he gets to me he looks at the paper, then at me, and something
happens on his face that I don't like.
"Ninety-three. Good effort."
Halfway down the list he has to pull out the chair and sit, and we wait. I wait, my hand clenched
under the desk.
On the school stairs afterwards Sheila stops at every landing with one hand on the rail.
"Aare, ei goromta…" she says, fanning herself with the result sheet.
"It's February," I tell her.
"Then it's February. February makes me tired. Don't look at me like that. You're giving me the
auntie look."
"I am not."
"You are. You're doing it right now. Stop it, you'll get wrinkles."
By now there are too many white hairs to pluck. There's a thin, pale patch along her parting, and
she's started wearing her hair a new way to cover it. Nobody asks about her hair. Everybody
asks about the ninety-eight. Her mother brings sweets to the staff room.
"Sheila koto paise?" my mother asks at dinner, before I've even sat down.
I tell her. She doesn't say anything. She doesn't have to. That night my father falls asleep in his
chair before the ten o'clock news is over, the paper open on his chest, and she goes in and
takes his glasses off his face very carefully, the way you'd take a cup out of a sleeping child's
hands, and turns the television down instead of off.
In March my mother's back hurts, so I do the laundry. In the pocket of my father's office shirt, the
blue one with the frayed collar he won't let her throw away, there's a slip of paper gone soft in
the water. It's a carbon copy, the blue ink bleeding out into the fibres, but most of it's still there if
I hold it up to the window. SUNRISE. TRANSFER. 3 YRS. And my name, in the box marked
BENEFICIARY—Nilima Nabarun Nabilah—spelled correctly.
That's the part that gets me, standing in the bathroom with wet hands and the bucket at my feet.
Nobody spells my name right. Teachers don't, the exam board doesn't, my own friends don't on
my birthday cards. He must have stood at that desk under that little laminated sign and spelled it
out for the clerk, letter by letter, and watched to make sure she got it right. Then he gave her
three years. Then he came home, washed his hands for a long time, and peeled me an orange.
That night at dinner I take his hand the way I used to, to trace it. He lets me. He doesn't even
look surprised, which means he knows I know, or he doesn't care if I know, or he's too tired to do
anything about it. The scar at the end of his line isn't pale anymore. It's pink and new and a little
shiny, and it's closer to the middle of his palm than it was at the start of the year. I press the end
of it with my fingertip, right where the line stops.
"Dhorechi," he says.
But he doesn't close his hand.
We talk on the roof after dinner, where my mother can't hear us over the neighbour's generator.
It has been running since the power went off at eight, and it sounds like the pigeons rumbling in
their chests.
"How many more are you going to buy me?" I ask him.
He doesn't pretend. That's the thing about my father: he has never once been good at
pretending. It's probably why he's still at the same desk after twenty-two years while the shutki
man got promoted twice.
"I was going to tell you," he says.
"When? At my wedding? In your speech?"
He laughs a little, at the water tanks rather than at me. "Something like that."
"Baba."
"Shono. Mamoni, ek minute shono, without making that face." He puts both hands flat on the
parapet, side by side, so I can see them both, the short line and the shorter line. "I bought mine
for a desk and a pension. Every single morning I sit down at that desk and I think, I paid for this
with the end of my life. You know what the end of my life was supposed to be? Sitting up here
with your children. Making them peel their own oranges."
"You'd peel them anyway."
"I would peel them anyway," he agrees. "So let me buy yours for something. Something worth
the years. You'll be a doctor. You'll cut people open and close them back up, and they'll walk
home. That's worth three years. That's worth all of them."
"I won't take them," I say. "Whatever you buy. I'll write my own paper with my own head, and I'll
leave the rest on the desk."
"You don't have to take them, Mamoni." He says it gently, the way you'd explain to a child why
the moon follows the car. "That's not how it works. You don't have to do anything at all. You only
have to sit the exam."
"They don't give them back. You know they don't give them back."
"I know."
"Then why—"
"Because I know," he says, "and you're my daughter," as if that were an answer. The terrible
thing is that standing on the roof with the generator going and the whole city orange under the
smog, it sounds like one.
I look at his hands on the parapet and understand the plan, which isn't really a plan so much as
a direction. He's going to keep climbing those stairs until I have a hundred or he has nothing,
whichever comes first. He isn't going to tell me. He's going to keep washing his hands for a long
time at the basin when he comes home.
That night I lie on my bed with the books stacked around me like sandbags and do the sum
every way it can be done.
If I refuse, he buys anyway. He doesn't need my signature, or my approval, only my name, and
he already knows how to spell it.
If I buy five, the way Ma wants, it won't be enough, because ninety-six last year means ninety-
eight this year, and he'll go back for the rest.
If I study harder… my mouth grows dry. Ninety-three.
If I tell Ma, she'll fight him, and she'll lose, because some part of her wants him to win.
Every way I do it, it comes out the same: my father on those stairs, one hand on the rail,
stopping at every landing, his breathing laboured, whispering it's the heat.
And under the sum there's the other thing. Zayan bhaia asleep in the middle of a conversation.
Sheila's white hairs in a row on the desk. All these people, going back, month after month, year
after year. Climbing the same stairs. I don't want to spend my life on those stairs. I don't want to
stand at a basin for twenty years, washing my hands for too long. I don't want a daughter of
mine to find a slip in my pocket.
I think about what my mother says when she's haggling in the market: never let the other person
name the price first.
Simple psychology.
Minors need a parent's signature, so I take my mother. I tell her it's for five. She's so pleased
she buys me a mango ice cream from a cart on the way, which she has never once in my life
allowed, because thanda lagbe.
The clerk has reading glasses on a chain and a little fan clipped to the edge of her desk that
turns its face from side to side, slowly, like it's refusing something over and over again. There's a
calendar from a pharmaceutical company on the wall, and the laminated sign about having a
good life to be old in. She measures my line with a white thread and a steel ruler and writes the
length into a ledger as long as my arm.
"How many?"
"A hundred," I say.
My mother's head turns. She is still holding the stick from the ice cream. For the first time in my
life she looks like a woman who would settle for ninety-one.
The clerk doesn't even look up. "Every year somebody," she says. "Last year two. You'll want
tea after." She slides a card across the desk, the only rate that isn't taped up on the wall. I read
it. I don't read it out. I don't need to.
"We always leave a little," the clerk says. "Regulations."
"A little for what?" my mother says. Her voice comes out wrong, too high, like it belongs to a
frightened girl.
The clerk shrugs, not unkindly. "Enough to see her photo in the paper."
My mother puts the pen down. "Na. Shona, na, we said five. We said six at the very most, we
said—"
"You said six," I tell her. "Baba never said a number. Baba just went. I'm saying a hundred, so
nobody in our house, ever, has to utter those numbers again."
"Your father doesn't—"
"He does. He did. Three years, last week." I hold my hand out across the desk, palm up: the
long line, the whole stupid river of it. "Sign it, Ma. Or he will."
She looks at my hand for a long time. Then she picks the pen back up and signs, pressing so
hard the nib tears through the paper and the clerk has to tape the back of the form.
It doesn't hurt the way I expected. First it's a paper cut, a quick bright sting that makes my eyes
water. Then it's something else. A pulling. It's like a thread being drawn out of me from
somewhere very far away, from a room at the end of a long corridor I'll never get to walk down,
and I can feel it coming the whole way, through my elbow and my wrist and out. The clerk
presses cotton wool to it, bandages it neatly, and tells me not to get it wet for three days, and
not to tell my friends the rate, because it upsets people.
I don't have the tea.
My mother doesn't say one word the whole rickshaw ride home, which has never once
happened before in recorded history. She holds my bandaged hand in her lap with both of hers,
like it's something she bought at the market and doesn't trust the rickshaw driver not to take.
My father finds out the way everyone in our house finds out everything: Dadi announces it at
dinner as if she's reporting the price of onions.
"The girl bought a hundred," she says, reaching for the dal.
My father puts his orange down. He doesn't peel it. He doesn't say anything at all, not that night
and not the next day or the day after that. For a week there are no oranges in our house. I didn't
know until then that silence could have a smell, but it does. It smells like a kitchen where
nobody's peeled anything.
Dadi is the one who unwraps the bandage, the third night, when nobody's looking. She rubs
mustard oil into the edges of my palm, around the cut, the way she rubbed it into the soles of my
feet when I had fevers as a child. Then she holds my hand between both of hers, her long lines
pressed against my short one, and closes her eyes, as if she could pour some of hers in.
"It doesn't work like that," I tell her.
"I know how it works," she says. "Buri hoisi, tar mane ki mathai sense nai?" She holds on
anyway. After a while I let her, and after a longer while I put my head on her shoulder, which
smells like mustard oil and peas and talcum powder. In other words, like the whole of my life
before any of this.
On the eighth night there's an orange on my desk when I come back from washing. It's peeled in
one long spiral, the peel stood back up around it, so it looks whole until you touch it.
I sit the exam in April, in a boys' school across the city, in a hall with the basketball hoops tied
up with rope and two hundred desks in rows so straight they look ruled. My roll number is taped
to the corner of my desk. Sheila's is taped to the desk three to my left. For the first papers she's
there, a little greyer each morning, writing fast and then putting her head down on her arms
between questions like a child asleep in the back of a car.
The last paper is chemistry, and Sheila's desk is empty. Halfway through the first hour the
invigilator stops beside it, checks his list, and writes something down. Her mother phoned,
someone whispers. A fever.
I write until my hand aches along the new scar, and then past the aching into something flat and
far away. I know answers I barely glanced at. That's the strangest part, the part nobody warned
me about. Every time I reach back for something, it's already there, neatly arranged, as if
someone has tidied my head while I slept.
Ayan is two rows in front of me, by the window. On question nine he stops writing. I'm done
thirty minutes early and I've never finished early in my life. I watch the back of his neck. He
reads the question, and reads it again, and puts the end of his pen in his mouth the way he
does at tuition when he's stuck. His hand lies flat on the desk beside the paper, the long line
running all the way round to his pulse.
I know the answer. I know it the way you know your own phone number. I could lean forward
and say it, six words, and the invigilator is at the far end of the hall peeling a banana. I don't. I
put my head down and look at my own paper, at the answer already there in handwriting that's
mine and partly isn't, and I don't look up again until the bell.
With every page I finish, I feel a little more used at the edges, a paper folded too many times.
Results come out on a Thursday in June.
I know before anyone tells me. I've known since the clerk turned that card over. But the
message still comes to my mother's phone at 8:14. She reads it, goes into the kitchen, and
starts crying in a way that could mean anything, and she goes on crying while she makes tea
that nobody drinks.
By nine there are men with cameras at our gate: three newspapers and a television van that's
too wide for our lane, so it's parked crooked at the corner with two wheels up on the drain. Boys
from the neighbourhood are sitting on our wall with their legs dangling, the same boys who used
to throw mangoes at me from that wall, and now they're shouting my name like it's a cricket
score. Some uncle is selling cold drinks out of a bucket.
One of the boys on the wall shouts that Sheila came second, ninety-nine, and the
photographers are already at the hospital. For a minute I can see it as clearly as if it were
already printed: Sheila sitting up in a hospital bed with a drip in one arm and the other hand
raised high for the camera, smiling with her back teeth. And I hope she's happy. I mean that. I
hope it was what she wanted. I hope it was worth it to her.
My father is standing in the doorway holding the newspaper. Somebody brought it round early,
still warm from the press. He hasn't unfolded it. He doesn't need to.
"They want you to show them," he says.
"I know, Baba."
"You don't have to." He's looking at the paper in his hands, not at me. "Nobody can make you.
I'll go out and tell them you're sleeping. I'll tell them you've got a fever."
"Everyone's got a fever this year."
He almost laughs. It's the closest he's come since March. Then he steps out of the doorway so I
can go by, and as I pass him he puts his hand on the top of my head for just a second, the short
line against my hair.
The light outside is so bright it's white. The second I step off the step it's all noise: the boys on
the wall, a rickshaw bell somewhere stuck on one long ring, the shutters going like rain on a tin
roof, a microphone pushed so close to my face I can see the dents in its foam, and a man from
the television van calling to me in the voice you'd use to coax a dog out from under a car. Here,
here, look here. Hold it up. Show us. Hold it up high, good girl, palm to the camera, let's see it.
I know exactly what they want, because I want it too. Some part of me still does. When I was
thirteen I drew a line on my palm with my father's blue ballpoint, a short one that stopped right in
the middle, and stood in front of the wardrobe mirror with my hand up. Palm out. Chin up. Back
teeth showing, although I never smiled with my teeth. I practised until Ma caught me and
scrubbed my hand at the basin with laundry soap and lectured me about dreaming useless
things, and I cried later, in private, not because it hurt but because I was embarrassed. I wanted
strangers to know my face. I wanted to be the photo inside some girl's wardrobe door. I want to
raise my hand the way the cadet college boy did, the way Sheila is doing right now in a hospital
bed across the city, and show everyone how much I was willing to pay. That's what the picture is
for. That's what the picture has always been for.
But I don't raise my hand.
I hold it against my chest instead, palm in, fingers closed, the way you hold a letter you haven't
decided whether to send. The shutters keep going. They'll print it anyway. Tomorrow on the front
page there'll be a girl with her hand over her heart and her eyes half shut against the sun, and
people will think it's gratitude, or modesty, or a prayer. It isn't any of those. It's a game we used
to play at dinner, and only three people in the world know the rules: one of them shelling peas
by the window, one crying into the tea, and one standing in the doorway behind me, holding a
newspaper he will never unfold.
Under my fingers, in the middle of my palm, there's a line no longer than an eyelash.
It's enough to see my photo in the paper, the clerk said. She didn't say how much more than
that. I didn't ask, and I won't, and I don't want anyone to measure it ever again.
I close my hand around it, the way my father taught me.
Dhorechi, I tell it. Dhorechi.

runs.text: My father's lifeline stops halfway down his palm, at a clean pale scar where the rest of it used to
be. When I was small I used to trace it at dinner, all the way from the edge of his hand to the
place where it just stopped, like a road that runs into the sea. He'd close his fingers around mine
and say,
Dhorechi, dhorechi
, and I'd shriek like it was the best joke in the world. I didn't know
what the scar was then. I thought everybody's father had one. Most of them do.
The marks office is three floors above Sunrise Coaching Centre, past a photocopy shop and a
man who laminates certificates. The rates are taped to the wall beside the stairs, the tape gone
yellow and curling at the corners. Sixty to seventy, a month a mark. Ninety to ninety-five, a year.
Nobody bothers to print the price of a hundred. I've walked past that wall twice a week since I
was twelve, on my way up to physics tuition, and I could recite the whole thing to you now the
way Sheila recites K-pop.
Tonight my mother is reading my palm at the kitchen table. She doesn't ask. She just takes my
hand off the table, turns it over, and runs her thumb down the line, all the way around the base
of my thumb to my wrist. Then she sighs.
"So long," she says. "Like a girl who never studies."
"I study," I tell her. "I study so much I dream in organic chemistry. Last night a benzene ring
proposed to me."
"And?"
"I said I'd think about it."
"Not the benzene. The mock."
"Ninety-one."
"Ninety-one," she says, the way she sniffs milk to see if it's turned.
"Ninety-one is a good number," Dadi says from her mat by the window. She is shelling peas into
a steel bowl and pretending not to listen, which is how she listens to everything. "In my day
they'd have put a garland on you for ninety-one. They'd have walked you round the whole
neighbourhood like a bride."
"In your day, Amma, they'd garland anyone who could spell cat," my mother says.
"In my day I failed my matriculation twice, and look at me."
"Yes, look at you. Shelling peas."
"Shelling peas at eighty-four," Dadi says, and holds up her hand.
You have to see Dadi's hand to understand our house. Her lifeline runs all the way to her wrist
and keeps going past it, faint, like a river on a map that doesn't know where the border is.
Nobody her age bought anything, because when she was a girl there was nothing to buy. You
failed or you passed, and then you lived, apparently, forever.
She goes back to her peas. It's a good argument. There just isn't a box for it on a form.
What you can put on a form is a number. The number for the medical colleges was ninety-six
last year. The year before that, ninety-four. The year before that I don't remember, but it was
lower. Next year it will be higher, because every mark somebody buys pushes the line up for
everyone who didn't. My chemistry teacher calls this
simple economics
. He likes the phrase. He
says it with his whole chest, simple economics, like he invented it. He has a scar where most of
his line should be, and halfway through writing an equation on the board he has to pull out the
chair and sit down for a minute. We all wait. Nobody says anything. Isn't it simple economics?
My father comes home at nine with a bag of oranges and the evening paper, complaining before
he's through the door.
"Ajke abar shutki niye ashche."
"Shuru hoise," my mother says to the ceiling.
The man at the next desk brings shutki to the office every day, which my father considers an act
of war.
Before he sits down he washes his hands at the basin for a long time, soap all the way up to the
wrists, twice. He has always done this. When I was little I thought it was the dust from the office
files. I think a lot of things about my father that turn out to be something else.
"Ninety-one," my mother tells him, before he's even sat down.
"Ninety-one what? Degrees? It's hot, but it isn't that hot."
"Don't be funny. Your daughter got ninety-one in the mock."
"My daughter got ninety-one with her own head." He sits and pulls the oranges toward him. "Do
you know what I got in my mock? Seventy-four. Seventy-four, and I was so frightened I couldn't
eat for a week. My mother had to feed me rice with her own hand like a baby."
"I did," says Dadi. "He cried into it."
"I did not cry into it."
"He cried into it, and then he ate it, so it was very salty."
"And then what did you do?" my mother asks him, though she knows. We all know.
He doesn't answer right away. He peels an orange in one long spiral, the way he has my whole
life, so the peel comes away in a single curling ribbon he can stand back up on the plate, as if
the orange were still inside it. Then he puts the segments on my plate one at a time.
"Then I did what everyone did," he says.
"And now you have a desk and a pension and a fan that works," my mother says. "Honest is a
teacher at the girls' school. Honest takes the bus."
"I take the bus."
"You take the bus because you're cheap, not because you're honest."
He laughs, and she almost laughs, and this is how my parents love each other: by arguing
about whose fault it is that they love each other.
"We'll go in March," my mother says, firmly. "After the pre-test. Five. Six at the very most."
My father reaches for another orange. He doesn't say anything at all.
I eat my orange and do the maths in my head. Ninety-one to ninety-five, a year a mark. Four
years. Above ninety-five the wall doesn't say, and nobody I know has ever said it out loud, which
tells you everything.
Everyone knows what happens on results day. The newspaper puts the toppers on the front
page, arms up, palms to the camera, the way you show a teacher your hands are clean before
lunch. The shorter the line, the bigger the photo. That's not a rule; it's just how it works out,
because the short lines are the high numbers and the high numbers are the news. Last year's
first place was a boy from the cadet college whose line was a stub no longer than a grain of rice.
He was grinning so hard you could see his back teeth. I cut that photo out and stuck it inside my
wardrobe door, next to the ones from the year before, and the year before that. I'm not proud of
it. I'm telling you so you understand I wasn't some girl who didn't want it. I wanted it the way you
want air.
So I make a plan, and I don't tell anyone. I'm going to learn everything, every single thing, so
that there's nothing left to buy and nobody in my house has to climb those stairs for me. I start
that night, my hands still sticky from the oranges.
Sheila bought back in October, before the pre-tests. Her parents are both engineers, and they
believe in investing early, the way they believe in fixed deposits and getting your eyes tested
every year. She showed me in the girls' toilets on the second floor, the ones where the latch
doesn't work, so one of us always had to hold the door shut with a foot.
"Look, look. Ish, don't touch it, it's still tender. Eight. Eight marks, and they said I'd hardly feel it,
and I hardly do. Is it ugly? Tell me honestly. Actually, don't tell me honestly."
"It's not ugly."
"It's a little bit ugly."
"You said to not tell you honestly!" I smirked.
"Shaitan. Aare dhur, I changed my mind. I'm allowed to change my mind. I'm going to be a
doctor now," she said. She closed her hand and held it against her school shirt like something
warm, and I kept my foot against the door and didn't ask her how many years.
The years come off the end. That's what the office says, what the clerk tells every family on the
stairs: you won't feel a thing until you're old, and by then you'll have a good life to be old in. It's
on a laminated sign behind her desk. The man downstairs probably laminated it.
But by December, Sheila is falling asleep in physics with her eyes open. I don't mean she looks
sleepy. I mean her eyes are open and pointed at the board and she isn't in there. When I pinch
her, she comes back up from somewhere very deep and says, "What, what, I'm listening!"
At home I study at the dining table now, because my desk has run out of room. There are books
on both chairs and on the floor in a ring around my feet, and after dinner my father sits across
from me and peels his orange. I don't watch him. I've heard that sound every night of my life, the
peel coming away in one long piece, and I could do differentiation to it in my sleep.
Then I don't hear it.
I don't know why I look up. Nothing has fallen, and nobody has said anything. It has just gone
quiet.
My father is sitting there with half the peel in one hand and the orange in the other.
In January I start finding white hairs on our bench before assembly. Sheila sits with a little
compact mirror in her lap and pulls them out of her parting one at a time, frowning like she's
threading a needle, and lays them on the desk in a row.
"Don't," she says, without looking up. "Don't say anything."
"I didn't say anything."
"You were going to. I can hear you thinking." Another one. She lays it beside the others. "Ammu
says it's the shampoo. We changed the shampoo."
I watch the row get longer, neat and white on the dark wood, as if she's counting something.
Then she sweeps them all off the edge of the desk into her palm, closes her hand, and the bell
goes.
One night Dadi stops shelling peas with a pod still open in her fingers.
"Ei," she says to my father. "Tor mathai eto paka chul kobe theke?"
My father touches his head like he's checking for a hat. "Office-er tension, Amma."
"Tension," Dadi says, as if it's a curse.
I look up from my book. There's grey at his temples, grey in his eyebrows, grey in the stubble
along his jaw. I look at it for a long time. Then I look down at the books on the chairs and on the
floor around my feet, and at the highlighter in my hand, and I read the same line about electron
shells four times and can't make it mean anything. The whole time I can feel Dadi watching me
over her peas, the way she used to watch me when I was small and climbing something.
Ayan's older brother lives inside my wardrobe door.
He's the photo from three years ago, the one on the left, its corner curling where the tape gave
up: a thin boy in a white shirt, arm up, a line like a full stop, grinning so hard his eyes have
disappeared. Zayan Hassan, first place, Dhaka Board. Ayan sits behind me at physics tuition
and has the longest line in the whole batch. Everyone knows why. Nobody says it.
"Your brother," I say to him one evening in February, on the stairs past the rate wall. "Can I meet
him?"
Ayan stops on the step. "Keno? Autograph nibi?"
"I want to ask him something."
"Ask me. I'm his brother, I know all his secrets. He's scared of lizards and he cried at the end of
Titanic."
"Ayan."
He looks at the rates on the wall for a long time, the way you look at a relative you don't like
across a wedding. "Friday," he says. "After Jumma. Ammu will make you eat. Don't say no to
anything, she takes it personally."
Their flat is on the fourth floor of a building with no lift, and on every landing Ayan waits for me
without saying he's waiting. His mother opens the door before we knock. She's already smiling.
She has the face of a woman who's been smiling at that door for three years.
The photo is in the drawing room. Not cut out of the paper like mine: the whole front page, in a
gold frame, hung above the showcase with the good plates in it.
"Our Zayan," his mother says, as if I could have missed it. "Dhaka Board. First." She says it the
way you say a phone number you've had for years. Then she goes to make tea, and she doesn't
say anything about Ayan at all.
Zayan bhaia is on the sofa under a shawl, an anatomy book open face-down on his chest like a
little roof. He's twenty-one. I know, because I've done the maths on that photo a hundred times.
His hair is grey. Not a streak. All of it, the colour of the ash in an agarbatti stand. When he sits
up to say hello, he does it in two stages, like an old man getting down from a rickshaw.
"You're the one with the wardrobe," he says.
I look at Ayan. Ayan looks at the ceiling fan.
"He tells me everything," Zayan bhaia says. "It's fine… I used to have the whole cricket team in
mine."
He's nice. That's the thing that feels wrong. I climbed four floors ready for a hero or a warning,
and he's just nice, and tired, and a little bit funny. He asks about my mocks. He remembers the
name of my chemistry teacher, and does an impression of him pulling out the chair to sit down
that makes Ayan snort tea through his nose.
"Anatomy is beautiful, actually," he says. "Everything has a name. Every little bone. There are
eight in your wrist." He holds up his hand but doesn't look at it. "Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum,
pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate." He says them fast and flat, the way you give a
rickshaw-wala your address. Then he smiles, carefully, with his mouth closed, so you can't see
any of his teeth at all.
I brought a list of questions, written in the back of my physics copy. Did it hurt. How many. Who
signed. When you sit at your desk at night, does what you know feel like yours. I don't ask any
of them. I ask the only one I can manage.
"Would you do it again?"
He looks past me at the wall: the gold frame and the thin boy with his arm up, grinning so hard
his eyes are gone.
"He would," he says, and nods at the photo. "Ask him."
Then, while his mother is still bringing in the tea, he falls asleep. Just like that, sitting up, in the
middle of niceties. His mother doesn't even stop talking. She tucks the shawl under his chin with
one hand and sets a plate of shingara in front of me with the other.
"Always tired," she says, proud. "Doctor manush."
Ayan walks me to the end of the lane. Neither of us says anything until the corner, where a man
is frying jilapi in a pan as wide as a satellite dish.
"Ammu wanted me to buy," Ayan says. "Twenty. She had the form filled in, my name and
everything."
"What did you say?"
"I said I'd go when Bhaia could climb our stairs without stopping." He holds up his palm in the
light from the jilapi stall, the long line running all the way round to his pulse. "She doesn't
introduce me to people now. She says I'm taking a different path. Like I've joined a cult."
"You'll get eighty-something."
"Eighty-something," he agrees. "And a long, boring life. I'll be a bank officer. I'll be the best bank
officer. I'll have the longest line in the bank."
"Ayan."
"Tui-o kinbi, dekhish," he says. He isn't being cruel. He says it the way you'd tell someone it's
going to rain. "Everyone says they won't. Then March comes."
I go home and cry the whole afternoon, in the bathroom with the tap running so nobody hears,
until the tank on the roof runs dry and Ma bangs on the door wanting to know who's wasting
water. I can't tell you exactly what I'm crying about. Not about Bhaia. Bhaia seemed fine. And
Auntie was happy, so happy. I keep seeing her at that door, smiling. Then I keep seeing Ma.
That night I don't take the photos off my wardrobe door. I just stop opening that side.
By the end of February I've done every past paper back to 2012. I know every footnote in the
textbook, and the mistakes in the footnotes. I didn't go to my cousin's wedding. I gave up
sleeping the way other people give up sugar.
The pre-test results come on the last day of the month. Our chemistry teacher reads them out
the way he always does, from the front, in order, so that everyone knows exactly where
everyone is.
"Sheila. Ninety-eight."
The class claps. Sheila smiles with her mouth closed and doesn't stand up.
He goes down the list. When he gets to me he looks at the paper, then at me, and something
happens on his face that I don't like.
"Ninety-three. Good effort."
Halfway down the list he has to pull out the chair and sit, and we wait. I wait, my hand clenched
under the desk.
On the school stairs afterwards Sheila stops at every landing with one hand on the rail.
"Aare, ei goromta…" she says, fanning herself with the result sheet.
"It's February," I tell her.
"Then it's February. February makes me tired. Don't look at me like that. You're giving me the
auntie look."
"I am not."
"You are. You're doing it right now. Stop it, you'll get wrinkles."
By now there are too many white hairs to pluck. There's a thin, pale patch along her parting, and
she's started wearing her hair a new way to cover it. Nobody asks about her hair. Everybody
asks about the ninety-eight. Her mother brings sweets to the staff room.
"Sheila koto paise?" my mother asks at dinner, before I've even sat down.
I tell her. She doesn't say anything. She doesn't have to. That night my father falls asleep in his
chair before the ten o'clock news is over, the paper open on his chest, and she goes in and
takes his glasses off his face very carefully, the way you'd take a cup out of a sleeping child's
hands, and turns the television down instead of off.
In March my mother's back hurts, so I do the laundry. In the pocket of my father's office shirt, the
blue one with the frayed collar he won't let her throw away, there's a slip of paper gone soft in
the water. It's a carbon copy, the blue ink bleeding out into the fibres, but most of it's still there if
I hold it up to the window. SUNRISE. TRANSFER. 3 YRS. And my name, in the box marked
BENEFICIARY—Nilima Nabarun Nabilah—spelled correctly.
That's the part that gets me, standing in the bathroom with wet hands and the bucket at my feet.
Nobody spells my name right. Teachers don't, the exam board doesn't, my own friends don't on
my birthday cards. He must have stood at that desk under that little laminated sign and spelled it
out for the clerk, letter by letter, and watched to make sure she got it right. Then he gave her
three years. Then he came home, washed his hands for a long time, and peeled me an orange.
That night at dinner I take his hand the way I used to, to trace it. He lets me. He doesn't even
look surprised, which means he knows I know, or he doesn't care if I know, or he's too tired to do
anything about it. The scar at the end of his line isn't pale anymore. It's pink and new and a little
shiny, and it's closer to the middle of his palm than it was at the start of the year. I press the end
of it with my fingertip, right where the line stops.
"Dhorechi," he says.
But he doesn't close his hand.
We talk on the roof after dinner, where my mother can't hear us over the neighbour's generator.
It has been running since the power went off at eight, and it sounds like the pigeons rumbling in
their chests.
"How many more are you going to buy me?" I ask him.
He doesn't pretend. That's the thing about my father: he has never once been good at
pretending. It's probably why he's still at the same desk after twenty-two years while the shutki
man got promoted twice.
"I was going to tell you," he says.
"When? At my wedding? In your speech?"
He laughs a little, at the water tanks rather than at me. "Something like that."
"Baba."
"Shono. Mamoni, ek minute shono, without making that face." He puts both hands flat on the
parapet, side by side, so I can see them both, the short line and the shorter line. "I bought mine
for a desk and a pension. Every single morning I sit down at that desk and I think, I paid for this
with the end of my life. You know what the end of my life was supposed to be? Sitting up here
with your children. Making them peel their own oranges."
"You'd peel them anyway."
"I would peel them anyway," he agrees. "So let me buy yours for something. Something worth
the years. You'll be a doctor. You'll cut people open and close them back up, and they'll walk
home. That's worth three years. That's worth all of them."
"I won't take them," I say. "Whatever you buy. I'll write my own paper with my own head, and I'll
leave the rest on the desk."
"You don't have to take them, Mamoni." He says it gently, the way you'd explain to a child why
the moon follows the car. "That's not how it works. You don't have to do anything at all. You only
have to sit the exam."
"They don't give them back. You know they don't give them back."
"I know."
"Then why—"
"Because I know," he says, "and you're my daughter," as if that were an answer. The terrible
thing is that standing on the roof with the generator going and the whole city orange under the
smog, it sounds like one.
I look at his hands on the parapet and understand the plan, which isn't really a plan so much as
a direction. He's going to keep climbing those stairs until I have a hundred or he has nothing,
whichever comes first. He isn't going to tell me. He's going to keep washing his hands for a long
time at the basin when he comes home.
That night I lie on my bed with the books stacked around me like sandbags and do the sum
every way it can be done.
If I refuse, he buys anyway. He doesn't need my signature, or my approval, only my name, and
he already knows how to spell it.
If I buy five, the way Ma wants, it won't be enough, because ninety-six last year means ninety-
eight this year, and he'll go back for the rest.
If I study harder… my mouth grows dry.
Ninety-three
If I tell Ma, she'll fight him, and she'll lose, because some part of her wants him to win.
Every way I do it, it comes out the same: my father on those stairs, one hand on the rail,
stopping at every landing, his breathing laboured, whispering it's the heat.
And under the sum there's the other thing. Zayan bhaia asleep in the middle of a conversation.
Sheila's white hairs in a row on the desk. All these people, going back, month after month, year
after year. Climbing the same stairs. I don't want to spend my life on those stairs. I don't want to
stand at a basin for twenty years, washing my hands for too long. I don't want a daughter of
mine to find a slip in my pocket.
I think about what my mother says when she's haggling in the market: never let the other person
name the price first.
Simple
psychology
Minors need a parent's signature, so I take my mother. I tell her it's for five. She's so pleased
she buys me a mango ice cream from a cart on the way, which she has never once in my life
allowed, because thanda lagbe.
The clerk has reading glasses on a chain and a little fan clipped to the edge of her desk that
turns its face from side to side, slowly, like it's refusing something over and over again. There's a
calendar from a pharmaceutical company on the wall, and the laminated sign about having a
good life to be old in. She measures my line with a white thread and a steel ruler and writes the
length into a ledger as long as my arm.
"How many?"
"A hundred," I say.
My mother's head turns. She is still holding the stick from the ice cream. For the first time in my
life she looks like a woman who would settle for ninety-one.
The clerk doesn't even look up. "Every year somebody," she says. "Last year two. You'll want
tea after." She slides a card across the desk, the only rate that isn't taped up on the wall. I read
it. I don't read it out. I don't need to.
"We always leave a little," the clerk says. "Regulations."
"A little for what?" my mother says. Her voice comes out wrong, too high, like it belongs to a
frightened girl.
The clerk shrugs, not unkindly. "Enough to see her photo in the paper."
My mother puts the pen down. "Na. Shona, na, we said five. We said six at the very most, we
said—"
"You said six," I tell her. "Baba never said a number. Baba just went. I'm saying a hundred, so
nobody in our house,
ever
, has to utter those numbers again."
"Your father doesn't—"
"He does. He did. Three years, last week." I hold my hand out across the desk, palm up: the
long line, the whole stupid river of it. "Sign it, Ma. Or he will."
She looks at my hand for a long time. Then she picks the pen back up and signs, pressing so
hard the nib tears through the paper and the clerk has to tape the back of the form.
It doesn't hurt the way I expected. First it's a paper cut, a quick bright sting that makes my eyes
water. Then it's something else. A pulling. It's like a thread being drawn out of me from
somewhere very far away, from a room at the end of a long corridor I'll never get to walk down,
and I can feel it coming the whole way, through my elbow and my wrist and out. The clerk
presses cotton wool to it, bandages it neatly, and tells me not to get it wet for three days, and
not to tell my friends the rate, because it upsets people.
I don't have the tea.
My mother doesn't say one word the whole rickshaw ride home, which has never once
happened before in recorded history. She holds my bandaged hand in her lap with both of hers,
like it's something she bought at the market and doesn't trust the rickshaw driver not to take.
My father finds out the way everyone in our house finds out everything: Dadi announces it at
dinner as if she's reporting the price of onions.
"The girl bought a hundred," she says, reaching for the dal.
My father puts his orange down. He doesn't peel it. He doesn't say anything at all, not that night
and not the next day or the day after that. For a week there are no oranges in our house. I didn't
know until then that silence could have a smell, but it does. It smells like a kitchen where
nobody's peeled anything.
Dadi is the one who unwraps the bandage, the third night, when nobody's looking. She rubs
mustard oil into the edges of my palm, around the cut, the way she rubbed it into the soles of my
feet when I had fevers as a child. Then she holds my hand between both of hers, her long lines
pressed against my short one, and closes her eyes, as if she could pour some of hers in.
"It doesn't work like that," I tell her.
"I know how it works," she says. "Buri hoisi, tar mane ki mathai sense nai?" She holds on
anyway. After a while I let her, and after a longer while I put my head on her shoulder, which
smells like mustard oil and peas and talcum powder. In other words, like the whole of my life
before any of this.
On the eighth night there's an orange on my desk when I come back from washing. It's peeled in
one long spiral, the peel stood back up around it, so it looks whole until you touch it.
I sit the exam in April, in a boys' school across the city, in a hall with the basketball hoops tied
up with rope and two hundred desks in rows so straight they look ruled. My roll number is taped
to the corner of my desk. Sheila's is taped to the desk three to my left. For the first papers she's
there, a little greyer each morning, writing fast and then putting her head down on her arms
between questions like a child asleep in the back of a car.
The last paper is chemistry, and Sheila's desk is empty. Halfway through the first hour the
invigilator stops beside it, checks his list, and writes something down. Her mother phoned,
someone whispers. A fever.
I write until my hand aches along the new scar, and then past the aching into something flat and
far away. I know answers I barely glanced at. That's the strangest part, the part nobody warned
me about. Every time I reach back for something, it's already there, neatly arranged, as if
someone has tidied my head while I slept.
Ayan is two rows in front of me, by the window. On question nine he stops writing. I'm done
thirty minutes early and I've never finished early in my life. I watch the back of his neck. He
reads the question, and reads it again, and puts the end of his pen in his mouth the way he
does at tuition when he's stuck. His hand lies flat on the desk beside the paper, the long line
running all the way round to his pulse.
I know the answer. I know it the way you know your own phone number. I could lean forward
and say it, six words, and the invigilator is at the far end of the hall peeling a banana. I don't. I
put my head down and look at my own paper, at the answer already there in handwriting that's
mine and partly isn't, and I don't look up again until the bell.
With every page I finish, I feel a little more used at the edges, a paper folded too many times.
Results come out on a Thursday in June.
I know before anyone tells me. I've known since the clerk turned that card over. But the
message still comes to my mother's phone at 8:14. She reads it, goes into the kitchen, and
starts crying in a way that could mean anything, and she goes on crying while she makes tea
that nobody drinks.
By nine there are men with cameras at our gate: three newspapers and a television van that's
too wide for our lane, so it's parked crooked at the corner with two wheels up on the drain. Boys
from the neighbourhood are sitting on our wall with their legs dangling, the same boys who used
to throw mangoes at me from that wall, and now they're shouting my name like it's a cricket
score. Some uncle is selling cold drinks out of a bucket.
One of the boys on the wall shouts that Sheila came second, ninety-nine, and the
photographers are already at the hospital. For a minute I can see it as clearly as if it were
already printed: Sheila sitting up in a hospital bed with a drip in one arm and the other hand
raised high for the camera, smiling with her back teeth. And I hope she's happy. I mean that. I
hope it was what she wanted. I hope it was worth it to her.
My father is standing in the doorway holding the newspaper. Somebody brought it round early,
still warm from the press. He hasn't unfolded it. He doesn't need to.
"They want you to show them," he says.
"I know, Baba."
"You don't have to." He's looking at the paper in his hands, not at me. "Nobody can make you.
I'll go out and tell them you're sleeping. I'll tell them you've got a fever."
"Everyone's got a fever this year."
He almost laughs. It's the closest he's come since March. Then he steps out of the doorway so I
can go by, and as I pass him he puts his hand on the top of my head for just a second, the short
line against my hair.
The light outside is so bright it's white. The second I step off the step it's all noise: the boys on
the wall, a rickshaw bell somewhere stuck on one long ring, the shutters going like rain on a tin
roof, a microphone pushed so close to my face I can see the dents in its foam, and a man from
the television van calling to me in the voice you'd use to coax a dog out from under a car.
Here,
here, look here. Hold it up. Show us. Hold it up high, good girl, palm to the camera, let's see it.
I know exactly what they want, because I want it too. Some part of me still does. When I was
thirteen I drew a line on my palm with my father's blue ballpoint, a short one that stopped right in
the middle, and stood in front of the wardrobe mirror with my hand up. Palm out. Chin up. Back
teeth showing, although I never smiled with my teeth. I practised until Ma caught me and
scrubbed my hand at the basin with laundry soap and lectured me about dreaming useless
things, and I cried later, in private, not because it hurt but because I was embarrassed. I wanted
strangers to know my face. I wanted to be the photo inside some girl's wardrobe door. I want to
raise my hand the way the cadet college boy did, the way Sheila is doing right now in a hospital
bed across the city, and show everyone how much I was willing to pay. That's what the picture is
for. That's what the picture has always been for.
But I don't raise my hand.
I hold it against my chest instead, palm in, fingers closed, the way you hold a letter you haven't
decided whether to send. The shutters keep going. They'll print it anyway. Tomorrow on the front
page there'll be a girl with her hand over her heart and her eyes half shut against the sun, and
people will think it's gratitude, or modesty, or a prayer. It isn't any of those. It's a game we used
to play at dinner, and only three people in the world know the rules: one of them shelling peas
by the window, one crying into the tea, and one standing in the doorway behind me, holding a
newspaper he will never unfold.
Under my fingers, in the middle of my palm, there's a line no longer than an eyelash.
It's enough to see my photo in the paper, the clerk said. She didn't say how much more than
that. I didn't ask, and I won't, and I don't want anyone to measure it ever again.
I close my hand around it, the way my father taught me.
Dhorechi
, I tell it.
Dhorechi

title: The Quiet in Between
author: Atheira
excerpt: The house is asleep,
imageAlt: Cover image for The Quiet in Between
content: The house is asleep,
and the night feels wider than usual.
My thoughts drift like curtains in an open window—
moving, pausing, never settling.
I remember when life used to feel softer.
I would laugh without thinking too much,
I loved without wondering how long things would last,
and I never questioned whether I was enough.
back then, I didn’t know
how much I would miss the girl
who could move through a day ever so lightly.
Afterwards, things began to change ever so slowly.
I started speaking lesser,
thinking a little more,
holding my feelings closer than before.
Somewhere inside me,
things started changing without permission,
and I didn’t know how to stop them.
I lost my best friend somewhere in that becoming.
There wasn't any final goodbye,
no moment that could explain the emptiness.
Just the strange realization
that some things can become memories
while you are still trying to understand them.
And some people can be
the best chapters of your life
without becoming a forever part of it.
I started getting slower
slower than others
in the race of life.
Not because i didn't know how to run
I was confused whether I'm on the correct track.
I lost people,
who I imagined myself growing old beside.
For a while, I carried that grief quietly.
Then came the anxiety.
My chest would drum,
my thoughts would race and stumble over.
I began reading too deeply into silence,
checking the room, the faces, myself.
Loneliness curled around me
like a folded blanket—
not heavy,
just there, beside me.
I missed people.
I missed old days.
But sometimes, more than anything,
I missed who I was before
I learned how much could change.
I missed how life felt
without the weight of losses.
Growing up waited patiently,
while my heart kept leaning backward,
asking if it was allowed
to stay soft a little longer.
To stay where names are called softly
and love isn't a deal.
I wanted things to make sense.
I wanted to know what I was becoming,
when would the anxiety finally go quiet,
when would I stop feeling
like I was carrying too much.
I still don’t know.
The anxiety is still here.
Some nights still feel heavier.
I still hold memories carefully,
as if they might fade if I breathe too hard.
But something in me has become quieter too.
There are gentler mornings now.
Sometimes I catch myself laughing a little louder
before I can think about it.
Sometimes the future feels less like a question
and more like an open window.
And tonight,
the house is still asleep.
The curtains move with uncertainty,
the night breeze caresses my skin ever so lightly,
and for once,
I don’t try to make them still.
I just watch them move—
backward, forward,
never quite settling,
and somehow,
still becoming.
Because maybe that's the law of nature,
to shed to become.
Or the way grandma always said.
"The new could never come
if the old never left"
Either way,
I learnt to let things go
without erasing their essence from my life.
And perhaps,
that is the actual becoming.

title: The Photographer
author: Nashid Tahsin
excerpt: The photographer has a hat on his head. One that almost covers his face. He always wears a trench coat no matter the season. Gloves in his hands and shoes are also such a part of h
imageAlt: Cover image for The Photographer
content: The photographer has a hat on his head. One that almost covers his face. He always wears a trench coat no matter the season. Gloves in his hands and shoes are also such a part of his life. As if, he doesn’t want any part of his body revealed.

There he walks on a lonely road. Half of an open green field, the better looking part on the left. While a beautiful mansion is on the right. The architecture of the road barely makes sense. Except for the capture of beauties. Then again, there is an actual Merry-Go-Round in the middle of the road that is glittering with multiple colors but it's not actually active. The photographer keeps on walking. A mosaic river that is actually moving like a real river, origami birds, a tree made of sand with hundreds of shoe prints on it, an ice cream hawker with his ice cream van standing beside the road like a statue, they all pass by. The photographer keeps on walking. He keeps on walking with his gloved hand in his pocket.

Two children playing with each other. They have some kind of yellow fluorescent aura around them. The photographer walks by. The sun is about to set. The children playing at a place where the setting sun and those children’s placement aligns. The photographer takes his camera out, he captures the picture from an appropriate angle. Now they are a collection. Now they are still. The photographer keeps on walking. He is in need of breakfast.
The photographer has some delicious fruit for his breakfast, or does he? Look out for the reflecting glass beside him. You may find the truth.
Let us check the camera, shall we? We got some videos there. Let us see what they are, what is it that it hid.
The video playback begins…

The camera, abandoned in the backyard. It was a beautiful day it seems. The sky looks beautiful in the video, the grasses look shiny. None can say if it really did look that way or if it was the camera. It looks like a day of beautiful solitary. Then suddenly….a boy opened the backdoor roughly and closed it in the same manner. The shadow from a tree beside makes it hard to recognise his face. Though which tree, that cannot be figured out, as it is outside the camera frame. The boy kept on standing  without any movements with his fists clenched. After a while he just stood there looking at a tree upfront. Though his face cannot be seen, surely it could be understood that he was glazing at something. Someone shouted a name. The boy frustratingly went back inside.
Next video….

The boy was sitting in the backyard. Gazing at something outside. At one moment he looked directly at the camera. Almost crawled toward it but stopped at the midpoint and went back to how he was sitting. Continuing his gazing at something.
Third one….

The boy was trying to hang himself on a tree. He did tie the knot. But the moment he tried to swing, the camera, it….it somehow changed its position. A position not possible for a camera to be on its own. A position, from which it wasn't looking like the boy hung himself but was rather floating.
The last one….

The boy was alive. He was quarreling with someone who looked like his parents. The camera is damaged. One can barely hear what they are saying. Even the display is damaged badly. It seems the quarrel at one point became too hot. The boy went back to home from the backyard thudding the door on his ‘could be' parents. The record went on. When the sun set. The boy came back. The sky was looking gorgeous. The setting sun's scattered light and disoriented clouds made a banger scenario. Anyone would want to keep that sky in memory. But the boy seemed desperate to keep his memory of the sky permanently. He was looking for something to keep a hold of the image but found nothing. He kept looking. And that's when he found out. A camera, sitting in the middle of nowhere, in the backyard. He crawled like a drooling child and took it. The camera started glitching and the video, thereby, finished.

The photographer is back at his home. He washed his hand while keeping his gloves on. He opens his bedroom. The wall is filled with all the framed photos that move like Hogwarts school. He opens his trench coat because he will now sleep. Then he opens his shirt. Then the hat. The photographer was moved by the beauty, the beauty helped him to stillness, the stillness was his continuum, for the camera ate him. There is no face, no skin, no trace of human biology in his face and only the part where face usually is for a human being. It was only a giant camera. A camera that took his face. Who is he? He is The Photographer. He had a trip, he is the trip, none shall know his trip, till the end.

title: The Sea's Mercy
author: Tas.R
excerpt: It was during the twilight hours that he came outside. The waves came crashing down on the shore, the water foaming at his feet. The sea was angry today— it was likely that there w
imageAlt: Cover image for The Sea's Mercy
content: It was during the twilight hours that he came outside. The waves came crashing down on the shore, the water foaming at his feet. The sea was angry today— it was likely that there would be a great storm tonight. The type of storm that would toss great ships around as though they were feathers. The type of storm that would send waves as high as buildings crashing down on the beach and take the lives of people both on land and at sea.
If he stayed on the beach long enough, it might take him away too.

The twilight sky had painted everything with a sad blue hue. Everything seemed to be overwhelmingly blue— from the sand under his feet to the surrounding cliffs overlooking the beach. The endless expanse of greenish blue sea would rumble occasionally. From a distance at first, but it had come closer in the quarter hour he had been here. Every now and then a flash of lightning would illuminate the sky briefly and threateningly.

As he watched the violent undulating of the sea, he spotted a sparkle in the distance. He rubbed his eyes and squinted to try and see it more clearly. There it was again, twinkling like a star amidst the water, hovering in front of the horizon. He knew he should go back to the safety of his home. It was only rational that he did, considering how dangerous the weather was today. However, the light looked much too enticing.

Mindlessly, he made his way over to it, reaching out. His body moved of his own accord. He felt the freezing water come up to his ankles, then his knees. The water offered a slight resistance to his movement, which he ignored. He would drown before he could even come close to it.
Stop.
Whether it was his own voice or not, he was not quite certain, but he listened to it and stopped in his tracks. The light had seemingly heard it too, having disappeared.
The rumbling of the sea became louder. The flashes of lightning in the sky became more frequent. Thunder could also be heard in the distance. Something had aggravated both the sky and sea.

He had to leave, and fast. A wave, almost three times as tall as him, came rushing at him as he hurriedly made his way back to shore. The wave was too fast. It would catch him and he would drown. He would be taken away.

Somehow, he reached the shore before the wave reached him. He fell onto his knees on the sand. Without wasting a second, he crawled further onto shore, putting as much distance as he could between him and the sea.

The wave crashed dangerously onto shore after him, the water foaming all the way up to where he sat, just a hair's breadth away from him. He sighed in relief as the water receded like a dangerous snake, ready to strike again.
He stood up. The blue of the twilight had become the green-grey of a stormy night sky. The sky seemed to be weighing down on him, ominous in its appearance.

He began to head back in the direction of home. Glancing back, he swore he saw the sea become completely stationary for the slightest moment, admitting defeat, before it began its violent surging once again.
He had managed to escape the sea this time.
Next time, however, the sea may not be as merciful.

title: The Things a Table Remembers
author: Atheira
excerpt: There was a mango tree at the entrance of my grandparents' home. Their flat stood right across ours, yet my Nana never entered his without first visiting his granddaughters.
imageAlt: Cover image for The Things a Table Remembers
content: There was a mango tree at the entrance of my grandparents' home. Their flat stood right across ours, yet my Nana never entered his without first visiting his granddaughters.

He rarely came empty-handed. Two packets of Mr Twist, sometimes cotton candy, occasionally balloons. He wasn't a wealthy man, but somehow, he made sure we never felt the limitations of what he could afford.

On weekends when Baba went to visit Dadu and returned late, Nana would take me to the stationery shop to make me stop crying. He took me to school, too, never allowing me to carry my little bag until I had reached the school gate. I suppose I was a princess in his kingdom, and he never particularly minded playing the king.

He had his little habits. Every night, he made himself a glass of Horlicks or Bournvita. When he would finish his food and wanted some more, he would gently tap his spoon against his plate. Such insignificant things, I thought. I never knew I would spend years wishing to hear them again.

Being the elder son at a family who had to shoulder the responsibilities of family after his father’s untimely death, he never got to pursue the education he wanted to. Yet he made a study table for his daughter, never imagining that one day his granddaughter would sit at it, studying for the future he so desperately wanted to witness.

Then came the afternoon I learnt that Nana had fainted at work. There were hospital visits, unfamiliar medical terms and assurances that he would recover. I believed every word. I even chose his Pohela Boishakh outfit, telling Maa that the following year we would take him shopping and make him choose one himself.
Seven year old me was kept in the dark, never told what was wrong with her best friend.

His condition worsened. My energetic Nana was confined to bed, and I couldn't understand why my favourite person was suddenly so tired. After lunch, he would still call, "Nanu, now is my head massage time." I would gently caress his forehead, quietly wiping away my tears when he fell asleep.
One day, he couldn't recognise his own son. When Mama pointed towards me and asked, "Abbu, who is this?", he replied, "Ota amar adorer nanu (That’s my beloved grand daughter)."
Twenty-four hours later, I lost my favourite person.
Years have passed, but his home remains a museum of memories. I brought only one thing with me: the study table he made.
Now, I study at it.
He never got to see me become a doctor. He never got to visit the golden Kaaba. And I never got to take him shopping for that following Noboborsho (Bangla New Year).
But perhaps some dreams don't disappear with the people who dream them. Perhaps they quietly find their way into the lives of those they leave behind.
And every day, at a table he once built, I try to become someone he would have been proud to call his Nanumoni.
