. Yet he made a study table for his daughter, never imagining that one day his granddaughter would sit at it, studying for the future he so desperately wanted to witness.
Then came the afternoon I learnt that Nana had fainted at work. There were hospital visits, unfamiliar medical terms and assurances that he would recover. I believed every word. I even chose his
Pohela
Boishakh
outfit
, telling
Maa
that the following year we would take him shopping and
make
him choose one himself.
Seven year old me was kept
in the dark, never told what was wrong with her best friend.
His condition worsened. My energetic Nana was confined to bed, and I couldn't understand why my favourite person was suddenly so tired. After lunch, he would still call, "
Nanu
, now is my head massage time." I would gently caress his forehead, quietly wiping away my tears when he fell asleep.
One day, he couldn't recognise his own son. When Mama pointed towards me and asked, "
Abbu
, who is this?", he replied, "Ota
amar
adorer
nanu
(That’s my beloved grand daughter
Twenty
-four hours later, I lost my favourite person.
Years have passed, but his home remains a museum of memories. I brought only one thing with me: the study table he made.
Now, I study at it.
He never got to see me become a doctor. He never got to visit the golden Kaaba. And I never got to take him shopping for that following
Noboborsho
(Bangla New Year).
But perhaps some dreams don't disappear with the people who dream them. Perhaps they quietly find their way into the lives of those they leave behind.
And every day, at a table he once built, I try to become someone he would have been proud to call his
Nanumoni

Birth certificates.
Death certificates.
Marriage certificates.
School records.
Land deeds.
Copies of copies.
Evidence that you were born.

Married.
Owned.
Lost.
Died.

A little sign above him.

He'd been there for 11 years.
Long enough to know how even if you lived for 70 years you could still be a problem because one letter is missing.
Next.

Wrong date of birth.
Sent him to counter 3.
Next.
A woman and a kid sleeping.
Her husband's last name different on two documents.
To counter 5.
Next.
Old man.
Fingers are too weak for the scanner.
Approved by supervisor.
Next.

He'd started seeing documents.
Facings.
Docs.
Documents were easier.
They're right or wrong.

It took her 20 minutes to come back.
This time she has form.

She came back after lunch.
She has someone has filled her form.

Name of village.
Date of birth.

Was when they realized that their knowledge of themselves had more authority than some stranger’s once-typed machine.
He tried again.
“Do you have anyone who can vouch for you?”
“The people in my neighborhood.”
“ witnesses?”
“They know me.”
“Are their IDs valid?”
“Probably.”
“You’ll need two.”
“They’re in the village.”
“Bring them.”
She turned to the window.
Outside the pavement was bleached white by the afternoon sun.
“It took me six hours to get here.”
Rahim said nothing.
“My knees hurt.”
“I understand.”
“No.”
It was not angry.
Which made it worse.
“You don’t.”
Silence on the line.
Rahim lowered his voice.
“Those are the rules.”
She nodded.
“Yes.”
Now she started to put the papers in her bag.
The hospital slip fell on the floor.
Rahim crouched. Picked it up.
Glanced at it.
Gave it back.
It was from fifteen years ago.
The name of the patient.
With the same wrong spelling.
He looked again at the ration card.
Same spelling.
He looked at the electricity bills.
Same spelling.
That wrong name had dogged her for years.
Not because it was right.
But once they put something wrong in your papers, it became a piece of evidence.
What's your name? - Rahim asked.
She gave him the name.
Slowly.
He said it.
She says how it's pronounced.
He said it.
She nodded.
"That one."
Rahim enters it into the system.
Nothing.
Spelling?
There's one.
He gazes at the screen.
There she is.
Well, almost.
Same husband.
Same village.
About the same age.
Just a different name.
One letter different.
Status:
INACTIVE – BIOMETRIC REVERIFICATION REQUIRED
Rahim stared at the woman.
"I've located your record."
She seemed to light up.
"That means I exist?"
Her words were said with no malice.
However, somehow, that bothered Rahim.
"You are in the database."
"Which means I exist?"
Rahim looked back at the screen.
A box was waiting below.
VERIFY IDENTIY
He couldn't press it.
Procedure demanded documentation or witness confirmation.
Or, it required supervisor approval.
He clicked on supervisor approval.
A notification appeared.
INSUFFICIENT DOCUMENTARY BASIS
He tried it again.
The same notification.
He looked up at the woman.
"Is there a problem?"
Rahim hesitated.
"There is a record of your existence. But I cannot verify it."
"Why?"
"Because I need the proof."
She regarded him for a while.
And then she pointed at herself.
"I am here."
Rahim kept silent.
"Am I standing here?"
"Yes."
"Did you request me to come. I came."
"I am aware."
"You told me the name of my husband."
"Yes."
"And the name of my village?"
"Yes."
"And my age?"
"About twenty-five years."
"And the photo of me?"
Rahim opened the record.
It contained the photo.
That picture had been taken almost twenty years ago.
The woman in the picture looked young.
Full face.
Black hair.
However, it was unmistakably the same woman.
Rahim tilted the screen a little.
She gazed at the photograph.
The expression on her face changed suddenly.
"That was taken before my husband died."
Rahim stared at her.
And she pointed at the screen with her finger.
"I wore that sari."
Then she giggled softly.
"I used to think that I am very fat."
And Rahim found himself smiling involuntarily.
The queue behind her moved once again.
Someone coughed.
Somebody complained about the long wait.
Rahim gazed at the photograph.
And then he looked at the woman.
The system didn't accept resemblance as a proof.
The system didn't accept the memory.
It didn't accept a key which would open a house.
It didn't accept the presence of neighbors if the identity of the latter weren't confirmed as well.
It didn't accept the fact that the woman could stare at a picture taken almost twenty years ago and recognize the sari she had been wearing.
The system required proof.
Rahim knew the reason for that.
In absence of any rules, everybody could become anybody.
Fraud was possible.
Mistakes happened.
People lied.
Documents protected people too.
He knew everything about it.
And this knowledge made the whole process quite hard.
The machine was not cruel in itself – it followed the rules.
The system was cruel sometimes when those rules worked as intended.
“Can you provide two witnesses?” he said.
By that time the woman seemed really exhausted.
“Yes.”
“And when?”
“I don’t know.”
Rahim nods.
The woman started to pack up once again.
Before leaving, she looks at the screen.
"Will she still be there?"
“Who?”
She points at the picture.
“Me.”
Rahim looks at the picture.
“Yes.”
She smiles.
“Good”
Then leaves.
Rahim watches how the lady is going towards the stairs.
Another customer appears almost immediately.
“My certificate contains incorrect district.”
Rahim is staring at the man.
“Sir?”
Rahim turns to the entrance and sees the old woman.
“Sir, my certificate.”
The record of the woman is still opened on the screen.
IDENTITY NOT VERIFIED
Rahim moves the cursor over the button.
There is nothing legal that he could do.
So he closes the record.
Rahim spends his working day processing names.
Correct names.
Incorrect names.
Names without some letters.
Names belonging to dead people but still registered in the system.
Names of living people whose existence cannot be confirmed by the system.
Five o'clock comes.
Everyone is leaving the building.
Rahim turns off his monitor.
For a short moment the black screen reflects his face.
He thinks about the documents in which he will find his name listed.
Certificate of birth.
Identification document.
Work certificate.
Banks account.
Registration of marriage.
Enough paper evidence that even though Rahim Ahmed is absent the proof that the guy exists is still there.
The old woman stands in front of him breathing.
Speaking.
Remembering.
And somehow it is not enough.
Rahim gathers up his bag.
And notices something on the desk.
A little metal key.
She had forgotten.
With the key in his hand.
Brass keys. Cheap.
Key: unofficial.
No picture.
No signature.
No stamp.
No.
No Nothing to verify anything.
Somewhere, six hours away, there is a door it is able to unlock.
Rahim put the key in his pocket.
The next morning, before calling the first number on the list, Rahim writes the woman's name on a piece of paper.
Name not in database.
Her actual name.
The name as she said it.
He placed it under his keyboard.
That didn't prove anything.
But for the time being he decided that that wasn't the same as meaning nothing.

title: Thanatos
author: wallflower
excerpt: I like to believe that everything exists simply due to the existence of its contrastive elements. For
imageAlt: Cover image for Thanatos
content: I like to believe that everything exists simply due to the existence of its contrastive elements. For
example: you can say the night is dark only because you’ve seen how brightly the sun glares at
you during the day. The same can be said about our souls, we like to believe we exist because
there are moments when we are completely numb. Devoid of life. Now here’s the thing I have an
issue with, using this logic we could say that anything good is meaningless without the existence
of anything bad. So what is good and what is bad? Maybe we let society, culture or tradition
dictate that for us. But what I truly mean is everything is meaningless at its core. When the
fundamental things in this world can be defined and understood solely because of the existence
of its parallels or opposites, what do we depend on when they vanish?
In this meaningless world there are moments when the human psyche tends to play with our
minds. Kind of like tugging at the strings of a puppet. You must have heard about self-harm.
Most people I know who do self-harm say the same thing and that is – it is to feel something, to
misdirect the mind, to convert the existing pain to another. All my life I found it terribly hard to
understand the concept of self-harm (one might say I am lucky to have a difficulty as such). But
then I did something to myself that was no less than self-harm. At the end of the day it is you
who gets to dictate what’s good and what’s bad.
I don’t know when my minds’ downfall was manifested unto my soul, but before I knew it, I
would be sitting in the fetal position, spiraling, begging for the thoughts to stop. Which at the
time never did work for me. These thoughts were obsessive and they left stains more persistent
than blood on linen. At first I told myself that it’ll pass, but it didn’t. Not for a long, long time.
That’s when I realized there’s something wrong with me. Not physically, or mentally. More like
there’s a gaping hole in my soul that needs feeding. A huge abyss where there should be
contentment.
I have always been the procrastinating type, any chance I get I procrastinate. Then I got to a
grade where procrastinating was the equivalent to “he who shall not be named” but I was
persistent. I told myself I could do it. Then when the realization finally caught up to me that I am
obliterated by my own idleness my mind decided to distract myself with these excruciating
thoughts. Even in my own privacy I have not yet dared to write down the thoughts I have had.
They are that gruesome. Coming from the deepest depravity known to any human soul. And I
loathe myself for it.
A healthy person will naturally ask why I couldn’t stop thinking immediately. Well, here’s the sick
truth: I liked it. I liked hurting myself. I liked hating myself every second or so. I even at times
enjoyed getting lost in these thought and losing control of myself. There’s nothing more
miserable than a person whose thoughts are not within the whims of their conscience and that
was what I was, I was miserable. I was a massacre in limbo. And I hated every second of my life. I
had some thoughts of self-infliction. But then it’d hit me that no amount of cuts would reach the
sore spot deep inside my soul.
The problems’ solution were on the inside, you see. So I set my mind to it. I thought about how
good it felt to enjoy life in the positive ways. I thought about the person I was before that.
Healthy, creative, happy, thoughtful. And one random day I woke up and decided to stop
destroying myself. It hit me that I am the harbinger of my own happiness and it is I who can
control my mind. And that was the end of my few months of intentional agony.
I thought about this period of my life for a long time. Until I realized that it was nothing if not
intentional. This experience of mine reaffirmed my previous belief that we love to see our own
gradual demise. Maybe it has been biologically instilled within the Homo sapiens species,
perhaps we were designed to be a self-cleaning instrument on a timer. Now when I look back I
understand that the only reason why I pulled back was because I wasn’t done yet, I wanted to do
other things before I cracked myself open and let vultures feast on me.
This tendency starts with the inhale of cigarette smoke, and the slashes of razors between your
thighs. You know you can end it, because you know you can control yourself, but there’s a voice
within that says no. Because there’s pleasure in the discerningly cold hands of torture, especially

one else. If anyone can free me or lock me up- it is me. Even a jailed man can find himself to be

runs.text: I like to believe that everything exists simply due to the existence of its contrastive elements. For
example: you can say the night is dark only because you’ve seen how brightly the sun glares at
you during the day. The same can be said about our souls, we like to believe we exist because
there are moments when we are completely numb. Devoid of life. Now here’s the thing I have an
issue with, using this logic we could say that anything good is meaningless without the existence
of anything bad. So what is good and what is bad? Maybe we let society, culture or tradition
dictate that for us. But what I truly mean is everything is meaningless at its core. When the
fundamental things in this world can be defined and understood solely because of the existence
of its parallels or opposites, what do we depend on when they vanish?

minds. Kind of like tugging at the strings of a puppet. You must have heard about self-harm.

misdirect the mind, to convert the existing pain to another. All my life I found it terribly hard to
understand the concept of self-harm (one might say I am lucky to have a difficulty as such). But
then I did something to myself that was no less than self-harm. At the end of the day it is you
who gets to dictate what’s good and what’s bad.

would be sitting in the fetal position, spiraling, begging for the thoughts to stop. Which at the

contentment.

that
gruesome. Coming from the deepest depravity known to any human soul. And I

intentional
agony.

title: If a God Exists
author: Charlotte Diane
excerpt: If a God exists, why are famine, poverty, terminal illnesses, hate crimes, terrorism, and
imageAlt: Cover image for If a God Exists
content: If a God exists, why are famine, poverty, terminal illnesses, hate crimes, terrorism, and
sexism still present?
If a God exists, why do murderers escape scot-free? Why do pedophiles and abusers get
to live among civilians?
If a God exists, why can’t women walk around at night without fearing for their safety?
Why can’t women simply exist without fear for their safety? Why do child marriages
exist?
Why do trillionaires exist when people are dying of starvation, dehydration, and lack of
healthcare? Why is abortion illegal when it is simply healthcare for a woman?
Is it really about the existence of God or the failure of humanity?
Age 11:
I used to walk around my neighborhood in the afternoons; it was relatively safe, and I had
befriended a few girls my age. The issue? I also attracted the attention of a man. A sixty-
year-old man who was the guard at one of the buildings. He noticed my affection for cats,
and he used it to ‘befriend’ me.
If only naive young me had realized.
I remember that incident vividly. He used to feed an outdoor cat that belonged to a
shopkeeper nearby. The cat had had a litter of kittens, and one of them began to stay at
the guard’s garage.
He lured me in under the guise of petting the cat. As soon as we were inside, he pulled a
chair near to sit down and held my wrist, persuading me—attempting to force me into his
lap. “Come sit, it’s okay, don’t worry. Nobody will mind… The cat is right there, honey.”
I didn’t understand the gravity of the situation, but I was uncomfortable.
So, I broke free. And I ran away.
Age 12:
1. I used to take my cat out on walks; my sweet baby hated it, but I wanted her to learn.
So I would consistently take her out.
Except whenever I did, older guys would stare. Not that it affected me because all sorts of
people stare, so that wasn’t the ‘bad’ part. They would come up to me, call me ‘biral
apu’, and try to flirt; that was the bad part.
Eventually, my brother and his friends stepped in. He’s seven years older than me, a bit
tsundere, acts tough, but he cares a lot. He told me not to bring Puchi out with me
anymore, because his friends kept reporting all the incidents to him.
2. Once, I was playing with the stray dog called Tommy, who had been present from the
first day, after school. I was around a construction site for an upcoming apartment
complex.
I had the school uniform on: standard black school shoes, a bottle-green coat that we
called a kameez, standard white salwar/trousers, and a white ready-made scarf. My
school’s logo was embedded into the sleeve of my kameez, clearly visible to the eye.
This middle-aged man came up to me, talking casually. “What school are you in?”
“Which grade?” “How old are you?” “Which building do you live in?”
I was and am still a friendly, extroverted person, so I replied... Until he lifted his hand and
gently put a stray strand of hair behind my ear.
I made up an excuse and left.
3. Tommy was on the sidewalk that particular afternoon. I went to him and started
playing with him, petting his belly and scruff; he was a very good boy. I remained seated
comfortably in a crouch. Across from us, in front of a garage, a driver was washing a car.
I think it was an SUV; it was one of those big, black cars. I can’t remember the exact
details.
He started hollering at me, something about Tommy. “You’re petting him so much! Do
you feed him? You should bathe him! Take him to your home, and wash him since you
love him so much. You know those shampoo packets? Buy some, and bathe him!”
I had ignored him, wanting to enjoy my time with Tommy.
Eventually, he started throwing digs at my parents. “Wow, what a disrespectful daughter
they’ve raised, cannot even reply when an elder talks.” “Are your parents poor? Can’t
they afford a shampoo for a dog? Do they not make enough money?”
I finally replied—something vague, yet something rude, simply to shut him up, as he was
gaining quite the attention from passersby.
He finished wiping the water droplets off the hood and got in the driver’s seat, slamming
the door shut. Then? He turned the key and started driving slowly, taking a sharp U-turn
and nearly hitting Tommy and me.
I remember freezing up for a moment, then pushing Tommy away. Tommy kept barking
at the car. I scraped my knee, slipping while trying to get out of the way.
The man got out of the car and started laughing.
Laughing.
I remember charging at him, screaming and cursing him out, and trying to jump on him.
But a kind rickshaw driver stopped me and calmed me down.
4. Same driver, same garage. It had been a while since that incident, but I hadn’t forgotten
his face. He decided to buy a piece of bonruti and feed Tommy in front of me, as I had
been playing with him.
“Since I fed you, she should apologize to me, don’t you think, little dog?” He kept
saying.
When I told him I would never apologize for swearing at him, he frowned and mocked
me. So I charged at him yet again, completely ready to throw a punch.
My friends held me back by the arms.
Age 13:
My friend, a fellow woman, and I were walking home when a man came up to us, asking
about our ages. He followed us for ten minutes. We had switched to English to talk, and
we were quite panicked.
He finally stopped two minutes before we reached our house road.
Age 14:
I was walking home after my Chemistry class. It was around 6:30 PM in summer. My
home was only fifteen minutes away, and it was a relatively safe area.
Not many incidents occurred with me except for the following and random stares. Three
minutes away from home, this guy in his mid-twenties began hooting and hollering at me.
He wouldn’t stop, and I took a glance at him.
Blue jersey. One pierced ear. Black slides.
I went straight home and told my brother, who immediately left to confront the man.
The man told him that he had been whistling and hollering at the dog resting near me.
Personal:
1. Verbal: Demon Child, Prostitute, Disgrace.
She told me she would make me ‘disappear’ and ‘bury me alive’ and that they would
ensure not even my siblings found me, after finding out about my online (text-only)
boyfriend from school.
A few weeks ago, she saw me up at 3 AM, writing. She screamed until her throat ached
and ended the conversation by saying, “I hate you!” She then stomped back to her room
and slammed the door on my face. It felt as though she was the teenager, not me.
2. Sexual: Being forced to strip my pants and show the extent of my injuries to her hours
after she had hit me.
3. Physical: Her fingers were curled around my throat, the grip tightening until I started
suffocating. She had no regrets, no mercy. Rather, she dug her nails in and made my
throat bleed. Instead of her fury diminishing, it grew. She grabbed hold of my long locks
of hair and pulled me off the floor, bashing my head against the wall until she calmed
down.
These were the hands that were meant to protect me.
A few months ago, I got the courage to text my beloved uncle to tell him about
everything. He sat there and listened to my quiet words, while my hands shook and tears
slipped down my cheeks.
After I finished, he gave me a hug and told me, “The world is a harsh place.”
If a God exists, how have I been through so much when I am only fifteen? I’m not trying
to be dismissive of the trauma and way more painful histories of other people.
I love my parents, too; they’re good people when they’re calm or in good moods.
Sometimes, though, they hurt me. And that isn’t okay. I’m not perfect either, God knows.
He knows very well. Everyone knows. And I’m not trying to say I am.
All I’m trying to say is—
The world is, indeed, a harsh place, but I also deserved a safe place.

title: Essence
author: Laces&Letters
excerpt: Sometimes,
imageAlt: Cover image for Essence
content: Sometimes,
Looking out of my window in the late afternoons,
I find myself being in a distant past.
The weather often helps me slip into that illusion.
And the sky never leaves my side in doing so.
Instead it stirs my imagination gently.
Making me feel as if I’m living many decades ago,
Even amidst the lifeless modern buildings.
Because, somehow, fragments of a long-gone past
Seem to echo everywhere.
Maybe in the spices soaking the sun and laundry drying on the terraces of the old houses across the street.
Or, maybe, in the ferns dangling whimsically
From their tired yet vibrant verandahs .
But mostly when, despite their fullness of life,
The late afternoon sun becomes the soul of it all,
Pouring itself abundantly,
All over the neighbourhood.
Making all the plants;
From that dense cluster of elderly trees
Beside one of the houses,
To the countless freshly watered shrubs on the terraces glisten and sway to the rhythm so blissful.
In the same way, I feel, it must have long, long ago.
With all the other things, becoming ethereal
Upon witnessing a melody like this.
And then slowly, time starts unraveling itself
Thread by thread,
Pulling me quietly into a time that wasn’t mine
Yet somehow feels deeply mine.
The time that’s carved into history,
Infused with the deep richness of Itr and
Bathed with the golden, buttery warmth of pure Ghee.
It feels as if the somewhat warm yet crisp breeze
And the ever dreamy clouds,
Are connected to when they were pure
And beheld slow lives.
The time I long to have existed in.
And, slowly, magically, for a moment,
That time becomes my present,
While my present becomes invisible.
Even the henna plants on the neighbouring terrace
Seem to whisper to me, “ We feel the same”.
As they faintly rustle, letting their earthly essence
Pass through my lace curtain.
Then, comes to my mind, glimpses of times when I felt the same as a child.
Thinking, on such warm, calm, and golden late afternoons ,
“ This afternoon feels like a time from a very distant past, I know which one, but I didn’t exist back then”.
Just like the past that’s coming to my mind now.
When I was either coming back from or going to the countryside with endless fields on both sides of the road, with my parents and sister.
Or when, back in my childhood home,
I was basking in that same glow
Spilling inside my late grandma’s bedroom
Through the intricately designed white verandah,
Over viewing a plain white mosque,
Surrounded by unkempt trees
With its reflection calmly resting on the pond beside.
Afternoons like these seem to have always been carrying the past with them,
That even when the light insists on fleeing gracefully
Towards dusk,
Time seems to always say to itself
“ let me pause for a moment so she can be in the past for a while”.

title: The Quiet I Choose
author: Tahia Islam
excerpt: People often say that human beings are social beings who need a partner, a
imageAlt: Cover image for The Quiet I Choose
content: People often say that human beings are social beings who need a partner, a
companion, a friend, or someone to confide in. I had the same belief for a long time and
accepted it as an undeniable truth, but someone once told me that, in the end, we are
all alone in this world. The statement may be grim, but the more I thought about it, the
more I realized it carried a quiet kind of wisdom. We came into this world alone and
fight many of our battles alone, and many of the battles that shape us are fought in the
depths of our minds.
Sometimes I like to play with words – like the word women. I look at the word and split
it into wo and men. That’s not how the word is formed, but it reminds me that language,
like people, carries hidden meanings we create for ourselves. Breaking the word, it
represents only half of mankind; the other half of it is lost. Then, considering the lost
half, we just have to add “wo” to “men”. The irony is that the word “wo “ adds meaning
to the word men, carrying emotions like worry, wonder, and woe - and gives our
humanity its emotional depth. Perhaps what was meant to be the afterthought is
actually the missing half of meaning itself. By taking “wo” away, we are left with only
men – alone, unaccompanied. And it leads to a belief that the word admits what cannot
be said aloud; that we were never meant to be whole alone
So, as a woman in this world, where everything is unpredictable, I believed I was
supposed to have a companion. But why does being sociable feel so difficult? I live in a
chaotic world, where noise is mistaken for connection and constant company is
celebrated as happiness. Yet, amidst all the chaos, I enjoy being alone. People love to
gossip about everyone’s lives; yet, I enjoy the silence of a quiet room, where my head is
not filled with constant hesitation, endless conversations, relentless expectations,
worrying about upsetting other people, and the exhausting demand to belong
anywhere.
In a room filled with people celebrating festivals, I find my sanctuary beside a corner
window, where I can observe the supposedly happy people, carrying the fear of being
judged, thinking: do they ever have a thought about being alone? Or am I the only one?
Do they ever fear empty halls, unanswered calls? Or do they fear themselves?
Because for a long time, I carried the shame of enjoying my own company. Now I have
decided not to do that anymore. Solitude is the place where I can become myself
without any judgment, where I can find peace. For a long time, society has taught me
that being alone was something to be ashamed of. But I no longer believe that. Perhaps
solitude is not the absence of love, but the beginning of understanding ourselves. It’s
my journey back to myself.

companion, a friend, or someone to confide in. I had the same belief for a long time and
accepted it as an undeniable truth, but someone once told me that, in the end, we are
all alone in this world. The statement may be grim, but the more I thought about it, the
more I realized it carried a quiet kind of wisdom. We came into this world alone and
fight many of our battles alone, and many of the battles that shape us are fought in the
depths of our minds.
Sometimes I like to play with words – like the word women. I look at the word and split
it into wo and men. That’s not how the word is formed, but it reminds me that language,
like people, carries hidden meanings we create for ourselves. Breaking the word, it
represents only half of mankind; the other half of it is lost. Then, considering the lost
half, we just have to add “wo” to “men”. The irony is that the word “wo “ adds meaning
to the word men, carrying emotions like worry, wonder, and woe - and gives our
humanity its emotional depth. Perhaps what was meant to be the afterthought is
actually the missing half of meaning itself. By taking “wo” away, we are left with only
men – alone, unaccompanied. And it leads to a belief that the word admits what cannot
be said aloud; that we were never meant to be whole alone
So, as a woman in this world, where everything is unpredictable, I believed I was
supposed to have a companion. But why does being sociable feel so difficult? I live in a
chaotic world, where noise is mistaken for connection and constant company is
celebrated as happiness. Yet, amidst all the chaos, I enjoy being alone. People love to

title: This World Feels More Like Yours Than Mine
author: Tasmia Habib
excerpt: I once read a quote that said, “This world feels more like yours than mine.”
imageAlt: Cover image for This World Feels More Like Yours Than Mine
content: I once read a quote that said, “This world feels more like yours than mine.”
This quote challenges the gender discrimination that women face every day. Even in the
workplace, where everyone should be judged by their work merit and abilities, women often face
unequal opportunities. Sexism and harassment from colleagues and superiors are common too.
Unfortunately they have to put up with this behaviour because speaking up can sometimes risk
their professional relationships, reputation, or even their careers. But why is the responsibility to
maintain a comfortable working environment often placed on the person being mistreated rather
than the person responsible for the misconduct?
When someone makes a rape joke and the people around him laugh, remain silent, or dismiss it
as harmless humour, they contribute to an environment where such behaviour becomes
normalised. This makes topics of sexual violence more of a amusing topic rather than a serious
one for many. This also leads to victim blaming and nitpicking towards the victim's attire and
lifestyle rather than the offence of the perpetrator. Rape victims, alive or dead, are often trolled
online. Sometimes commenters justify the crime by judging the victim's outfit or even the time
and place of the crime. A woman can't find peace and be free of judgement even after her
death.
Despite women and men being born in this world, they don't experience the same freedom. A
woman mostly has to think twice before walking alone at night. Sometimes they aren't even
allowed to because of fear. Often consider what she wears before stepping outside or question
whether an ordinary interaction could put her into danger or not. These precautions have
become a daily part of most women's lives almost as a second nature. Men of course have their
own struggles but women are burdened with bargaining their freedom and lifestyle with the
possibility of harassment and other violence. Why should something as simple as taking up
space in public demand so much careful navigation?
Women aren't asking for a world just for them. What they want is a world where they don't have
to think twice before stepping out of the house, where they don't have to look back constantly at
the sound of footsteps behind them. They want a world where they don't have to justify their
existence or dignity to anyone. A world where their rights aren't questioned or treated as a
privilege but recognised as basic human rights.
Until then I will continue to believe that this world belongs to men more than it belongs to
women.

title: Forgive me
author: Orisha
excerpt: Dear me,
imageAlt: Cover image for Forgive me
content: Dear me,

I say sorry too much but never to you, I forgave too many but never you, I solve problems of others but never yours, I ask about others but never ask you. I forgot in the chaos of helping others that you were the front of the line and that somehow over the years I lost your touch. This is my apology for all the broken days when I looked at you and told you to not be dramatic, to not create a scene and to not make yourself the center.

I know I messed up pretty badly and that this was not part of our plan. We wanted to dance when our song came up even though every song is ours but now i make you sit in the corner being afraid of moving freely even in your closed space. We wanted to talk loud being in a big friend group but now you cannot even talk with your family becoming the quietest in every room. You always wanted to go out and see the world from a poetic site but I made you feel like you gave up on those. I always knew you wanted to write a book to get those thoughts onto paper but again I made you leave the book unfinished just after 4 chapters. You wanted to feel confident, wanted to look yourself in the eye and live like Elle Woods but I always made you feel like you weren't enough.

Sorry might feel very small now.i ruined you by making you a version that always apologies even when you are the one hurt. That can always forgive others but never forget how it hurts. You became someone unrecognizable and somehow it was my fault because I saw you changing but never stopped to care. I along with everyone abandoned you making you feel like you don’t deserve to react, you don’t get to cry because that’s a crybaby and not very 19 year old like. I know a lot happened and I never gave you the chance to sit down and say,
“ It's not your fault. You can be mad, angry or frustrated and it’s okay. You don’t have to handle everything or make everything right it’s not your job”

And now you are so exhausted that you forgot to live for yourself. Forgot to write, the only thing that ever gave you the chance to speak, forgot to read the books that once gave you the experience of a thousand lives, forgot the little girl who used to see disney movies and wanted to be like them.
Therefore I promise you I’ll try better to put you first and tell you everyday that it’s your first time living too.
Yours truly
you
