title: My Very First Regret
author: AceMRI
excerpt: I sat in an expensive restaurant. Luxurious. Elegant. Important. Everything around
imageAlt: Cover image for My Very First Regret
content: I sat in an expensive restaurant. Luxurious. Elegant. Important. Everything around
was more than me. Perhaps, the only thing not… sat opposite. A she-wolf.
Orange-white fur. Calm and kind eyes. A smile that made me stare. She was
beautiful. The first ever beautiful I chose to acknowledge.
“This has been wonderful, Frater,” she said, her voice low. Perhaps a bit
strained.
I didn’t smile. Just nodded. She exhaled shakily, leaning forward toward me.
Then her face hit the table. A shudder ran through my body. Someone screamed. I
found myself rising from my chair, hands reaching out, trembling. For the first
time, I felt shaken.
“N-Nomi?”
To really understand… anything at all, let’s rewind time. A month should do.
Around the end of my junior year at college. But first, a little about myself. You
see, I was never your average Joe. In a bad way, I was a little weird. Though,
perhaps, saying a little weird is too modest.
Growing up, I enjoyed killing birds. Their chirping always annoyed me. I
threw stones, even squished a few to death myself. Obviously, my parents were
concerned, or rather, disgusted would probably be a more fitting word. In 6th
grade, I choked someone unconscious. Voluntarily. Expressionless. They wanted to
pick on me. It irritated me that he got away with just a neck brace. Damned
teachers. I got suspended. My parents argued that night, disowned me, and forced
me to leave. I didn’t mind. Neither did I care.
Some might be curious at this point. Why am I like this? Because I want to.
Perhaps, I realized too early that in this world, if you want something, you gotta
take it. And I didn’t like to be stepped on. Others don’t care about your comfort,
they care about theirs first. So you gotta make your own.
I lived in an orphanage most of my life, keeping my distance from everyone.
Anyone who did come talk to me scurried real quick. Otherwise, they met my fist
and ended up with a bloody face. The guardians there were kind enough to pay for
my school until 9th grade before I took over. By the time I was in college, I had left
long ago, already having a job and a full scholarship. Just… no one was walking
beside me. Did I regret my actions? No, not one bit. No sane person would ever
choose to walk beside me out of free will. And that was fine by me. Except…
Someone bumped my shoulder on the sidewalk going to college. A she-wolf,
smiling. A furry, more conventionally called. They appeared somewhere two
centuries ago when some guy decided to… ahem… at an apparently ancient altar
and had kids. Half-Breeds. Still feels weird though.
“Going all alone again, Frater?” Nomi asked, her tail wagging as she walked
beside me.
“Yeah.” My answer was quick. I didn’t really want to make small talk.
She pouted, then clung closer, wrapping an arm around mine. By now, I was
used to it and didn’t feel the necessity or the energy to step away. She sniffed my
coat.
“Is that a new perfume?”
“No.”
“Come on! It’s rude to ignore a girl holding your hand.”
I kept walking. She looked content just holding on. We walked through the
campus gates finally. People were already whispering. We simply walked by.
“Shouldn’t you be with your friends? They’ll stare at you if you don’t.”
“I am though.”
I raised an eyebrow. “I never said I was your—Ow.”
She punched my shoulder.
“Don’t you dare say that. Hmph!”
I rubbed my shoulder, sighing.
That’s Nomi. A she-wolf furry. Wolves were usually rough and tomboyish.
Not her. She’s quiet, but open. Smart, but gentle. She was the popular extrovert,
always hanging around or doing extracurriculars. But she was a bit naïve . I had to
pull her out of a few situations myself, as much as it annoyed me to do so. And
yes, that once caused a fight. They had to suspend me for a week.
We walked to class together, stopping at the door. She finally let go and
turned to face me. Someone from inside called her.
“Coming!” she said, then turned to me again. “Do you have it?”
I didn’t answer for a moment, then took out my bottle. “You mean water?”
Nomi smiled innocently. “Yes. Water.”
I handed her the bottle. She drank half of it before coughing violently. I
watched her without so much as a shudder. At least three girls rushed to support
her first. A crowd was already forming. Typical. She held onto the door for
balance, taking a shaky deep breath.
“Thanks,” she rasped, handing the bottle back. She managed a smile, visibly
trembling. “I’ll see you after class, okay? We get lunch together today.”
I frowned. “Lunch? Why?”
“You know why.”
She winked and headed inside, smoothing her dress. The students around
gave me looks before following her. I sighed and looked at the bottle, then threw it
in the trash and moved into class.
The hour was excruciatingly dull. I already knew these topics top-down.
Professor Sean called me up twice, expecting to embarrass me, only to be shocked
when I solved the problem in minutes. Out of the corner of my eye, I noticed Nomi
watching. She smiled when our eyes met. I set the marker down and turned away
from a fuming professor.
The class ended earlier than usual, coincidentally a few minutes after I
solved the second problem. I packed up and left first, hoping to go home. But of
course, Nomi blocked the way. Her arms crossed, tail flicking behind her. I forgot
to mention that wolves were ridiculously fast on their feet.
“Has no one ever told you it’s rude to walk out on a promise?”
I sighed. “I never said I promised.”
“Well. Doesn't matter.” She grabbed my arm and dragged me along. “We’re
getting lunch!”
“Hey! Slow down, I can walk!”
She dragged me along anyway.
We walked side by side down the streets. As always, she clung to me. It
annoyed me. Not because I was worried about people talking, because she was
probably the only person I genuinely didn’t understand. As we crossed the street,
an ad being displayed on a large digital billboard caught my attention. The picture
showed a doctor holding a small bottle of clear liquid. Underneath, there was a
bold text that said:
The cure for cancer! Testing now! If you need it, then call…
I stopped, halting her abruptly too. She turned to me, pouting.
“Hey! I almost—”
She noticed and followed my gaze to the billboard. Her ears drooped, and
tail stopped moving. I turned and walked again. Nomi came along without a word.
“Couldn’t you get that?” I asked.
“The cure?”
I nodded.
She chuckled. “We called. It’s too expensive.”
“You’re rich, though. Don’t you live in a mansion?”
“I do.” She held on a little tighter. “But it’s not enough.”
A low whine rumbled in her throat. She rubbed her stomach, trembling
again. I looked once, then kept walking.
“Maybe I can chip in.”
Nomi’s eyes widened, and her head snapped toward me so fast it looked like
that hurt. “Are you… offering to help?”
“Hell no,” I replied immediately. “It’s to get you off my back, or rather my
arm.”
Nomi stared for a moment, then laughed. I groaned. My fists clenched, but I
let go with a sigh.
Sometime later, we arrived at a rather empty diner, sat down, and ordered
drinks. I looked outside while she scrolled on social media. That billboard was still
clear from here. My phone rang. I answered without looking and waited as the
other person spoke.
“Coming,” I said, standing up.
Nomi’s ears quirked up. “Where are you going?"
“Parcel,” I replied, ending the call and stepping out of the booth.
I walked out of the diner. A man in a hoodie stood there, holding a small
blue package. I paid and opened it right there, pocketing the small bottle inside
before walking back in. The server stopped just short of bumping into me with his
tray of drinks while turning.
“Oh, s-sorry I—”
“Is this for table five?”
The server was caught off guard, eyes darting around. “I—yes.”
“Then I’ll take it. That’s me and… someone else.”
I took the tray without waiting for a confirmation, waiting until the server
left before setting the tray two tables ahead of ours. I took out the small bottle, and
emptied its contents into one drink, pocketing it again before walking to our table
with the tray. Nomi smiled, tail wagging as she set her phone down.
“Oh, Frater serving me? How romantic,” she said, leaning forward a little.
“Just thought it’d be more efficient,” I replied, passing her drink before
sitting with mine.
I watched her stir with the straw, staring as the contents mixed. When she
leaned down, my hand rose a little, then grabbed the table. She took a long sip,
sighing.
“Mm, this drink here is always the best. Don’t you agree, Frater?”
I turned to my drink, and nodded. “I guess.”
Nomi picked up the menu, humming. “What do you think we should order? I
heard their fried rice is amazing. The girls eat here often.”
“I don’t know. I’ll get whatever’s cheapest,” I replied, taking a sip of my
drink.
Nomi groaned. “Come on, offer some suggestions to this poor struggling
lady.”
I looked up from my drink, unimpressed by the puppy dog eyes she was
giving.
“Really?”
She sighed and crossed her arms. “That usually works,” she muttered.
I shook my head and went back to my drink.
We left the diner about an hour later. I was still sipping on my drink. Nomi
stretched as we walked through the doors. Her ears flicked a few times before
relaxing.
“I’m full! Now, wasn’t that fun?” she asked, smiling and leaning toward me.
I looked at the road instead. “Depends on your concept of fun. I was
bored—Ow.”
She punched my shoulder again. I sighed, not looking at her. The light
turned red. I was about to cross when her hand suddenly grabbed my shoulder.
“What the—”
I turned to her. She was gripping her stomach and shaking, gritting her teeth.
Her ears folded back. Her claws bared, digging into my shoulder. I winced. Then,
her eyes snapped to meet mine. Her pupils dilated. I stared for one second, then
quickly turned away, exhaling as I reached for my phone and dialed.
“H-Hello, I think I have an emergency,” I said as calmly as I could.
I sat next to an empty seat for a week straight. Occasionally, I stared at the empty
space, wondering. The bell rang. I packed my bag and walked out of class. Some
gossiping girls scurried by.
“Did you hear? Nomi’s been admitted to the hospital again.”
“Again?”
I didn’t pay heed to them. It wasn’t my job to care after all, right? I went
home and lay on my bed, doomscrolling. Random pictures and videos appeared on
my feed, but I found myself a bit distracted. Those eyes, the way she—my phone
rang, snapping me out of my trance. Unknown number. I answered and put it on
speaker.
“Hello?”
“Hey. Uh, is this Frater?”
“It is.”
“Oh, hey man. I’m Tyler. I know you don’t—”
“I know who you are, Tyler Smith. Just get on with what you want.”
There was a pause, and some muttering on the other side. Then, someone
cleared their throat.
“Right. So uh… Nomi asked us to call this number to tell you she was at
Advent Hospital. Room 305 right now.”
My hand gripped the phone tighter, subconsciously.
“That’s the ICU,” I muttered.
There was another pause.
“Y-Yea, man. If you wanted to see her—”
I ended the call before he could finish, bringing my hand up to cover my
eyes. For a moment, I laid there, busy with my thoughts. The sunlight felt
particularly annoying today. I got up, walked to the windows and closed the
curtains, staring at them. Her eyes, those dilated eyes, flashed before me. My fists
clenched. I turned, grabbed my phone from the bed and left. The walk to the
hospital was brief.
“I was looking for a patient. Nomi. A she-wolf,” I asked the front desk.
“Are you Frater?” the woman at the desk asked.
I nodded.
“Mm, she told us to expect you. Room 305. But she might not be open to
visitation just yet. You’re welcome to check.”
I looked around, then walked down a hallway. Someone stepped into an
empty elevator and held it open. But I walked by, taking the stairs instead. As I
reached the landing, I saw someone standing near her room. I stopped before him.
He spared me a glance before turning ahead again.
“Forgive me if I’m wrong. But are you Frater?”
I sighed. “Let me guess. Nomi told the entire hospital by now?”
The guy didn’t reply and simply gestured to the room. I turned, and for the
first time in my life, froze. Three people were trying to restrain her to the bed. She
was writhing and snarling. Her eyes were red, spit flying everywhere. Her screams
rattled the door, though they came muffled because of the soundproofing. I stared,
eyes wide, trembling even. Was this really… her?
“She’d been asking for you nonstop,” the guy said.
I couldn’t muster a reply.
The guy patted my shoulder. “Stomach cancer is difficult to deal with. Being
stage three with a weak immune system like hers doesn’t help either. But we are
trying our best. Come, let’s—”
I brushed the guy’s hand off rather roughly. My body tensed. I took a step
back, then another, then ran. Down the stairs and out of the hospital, not stopping
until I reached home and slammed the door. I planted my back against the wall,
panting heavily. Scenes flashed across my mind. It hurt. I grabbed my head,
covering my ears, trying to stop the ringing, but it just wouldn’t.
Night. 7:24PM. I sat beside her bed, calm and composed, a stark contrast to how
she looked. Her fur was all disheveled. Her eyes red-rimmed. She leaned against
the bedframe, looking out the window. A bouquet rested on the table beside her.
“Thanks for coming to see me, Frater,” she said, turning to me with her usual
smile. Her tail wagged.
“Don’t mention it,” I replied. “Someone asked me to bring flowers. That’s
why I came. Probably wouldn’t have otherwise.”
She pouted. “You really know how to hurt a woman’s feelings, don’t you?”
“Right now, you’re more of a child than a woman.”
“I am not! Y-you are!”
I looked at her, unimpressed by the worst comeback to exist for the next
centuries, probably. The corner of my eye caught the edge of the bandage peeking
from her stomach. She covered it quickly, as if sensing my gaze.
“The doctors said I’ll be fine. Nothing serious to worry about.” She sighed.
“Sorry if I worried you for nothing.”
“I never said I was worried—Ow.”
She punched my shoulder, crossed her arms and pouted, turning away
entirely.
“This is what I meant by being a little child,” I said, rubbing my shoulder.
“I am NOT a child!” she argued with a low growl, spinning right back
around to face me. “I am a mature and grown wolf!”
I sighed and stood up. “Well, you’re doing good. It’s best I leave. Later,” I
said, and turned.
She grabbed my hand. I stopped. Her hold was weak. I could easily break
free. But something in me refused to give me strength. So I looked over my
shoulder instead. She was blushing.
“I… just wait a minute,” she said, averting her gaze.
I waited a moment, watching her fidget.
“Just spit it out already,” I said.
“I’m trying!” She took a deep breath, holding my hand a little tighter. “I…
want us to go on a date. At the end of the month.”
“What?” It was an instinctive response, as if the very idea was absurd to me.
Nomi nodded, blushing hard. Silence passed between us for a moment. Her
tail was wagging wildly, and I could hear a very low whine from her throat. I
sighed again.
“Look, we have finals at the end of the month. It’s not possible,” I said,
about to take a step forward.
“I’ll pay for yours too!” she said quickly, tightening her hold further.
“Please, just… one more time.”
My leg stopped mid-step. My body tensed ever so slightly.
“Nomi…”
“Please, Frater. Consider it a last wish. I won’t bother you after that.”
I stayed still for a long moment, then pocketed my hands and took that step
forward. My arm slipped free from her grip even as she tried holding on, though I
didn’t leave yet.
“Fine,” I said.
I didn’t wait to hear a response and walked out of the room, but felt her
smiling behind me.
I went home and sat on my bed, thinking. Just one more time. One… last
time. The thought wasn’t so comforting, but her smile—I slapped myself. No,
there’s no person stupid enough to actually like me. Never. It’s just… dumb. She
just wants to get it over with. It’s a fleeting fantasy not worth pondering. At least,
that’s what I told myself.
I spent the next weeks mostly in preparation. Assignments, quizzes, and some
minor projects here and there. Everybody was becoming increasingly busy.
Though, my attention kept slipping, more than usual. I found my thoughts drifting
occasionally, though I brushed them off most of the time. The news of the date
spread like wildfire. But what irritated me were the whispers. The constant
muttering grated on my nerves as I walked the hallways. It took a lot to hold it in.
Nomi had to stay a few more days in the hospital before being discharged.
She, as usual, refused to leave my side. I couldn’t figure out why she lingered
beyond what she needed, and it frustrated me, though I found myself complaining
less and less. That irritated me too.
I walked down the hallway to the gym. Apparently, Nomi had a volleyball
match today. I sighed. Part of me wondered why I was doing this much. But I
didn’t feel enough energy to care. I entered the gym right as Nomi managed a nasty
block. The whistle blew. Her side won.
“Yes! Still have it girls!”
I stood by the door, watching them celebrate for a moment before gently
tapping my foot. Nomi’s ears twitched, and she turned. She smiled and rushed over
to me.
“Frater! How long have you been standing there?”
“A few minutes.”
“Ooh, did you see that last play? It was outstanding, wasn’t it?!”
“It was okay.”
Nomi crossed her arms. “Come on, you don’t have to be so… this.”
“What’s this?”
“You know! This,” she said, gesturing to me.
I stared at her for a moment, then took out my phone. “Well, too bad.”
“Nomi!” someone called.
“Coming!” she said, turning to me again. “Wait here, I’ll be back in a few
minutes, alright?”
“Hurry up,” I replied, scrolling on my phone.
She turned and winced, holding her stomach. Her ears folded back. I looked
up from my phone.
“I’m… fine,” she said, and hurried away.
I stared for a moment, then sighed and went back to my phone. She changed
into casual attire, and we left, walking down the hallway.
“Mmm!” Nomi stretched. “I missed so much these last few days. It’ll be a
nightmare to cover up.”
“It’s kinda your fault, you know,” I said, pocketing my phone.
“Really? I just got back from the hospital!”
“You were playing volleyball just now.”
“W-well, that’s—that’s different,” she argued, turning away.
Some guy tried shoving past me, but my shoulder didn’t move.
“What the—Hey! Watch it!” the guy yelled.
My fists clenched, but I kept walking. Nomi hung closer, holding onto my
arm.
“Oh, I get it. You think you’re the big man now that you’re dating her, huh?
You’re a nobody, and she’s a dumbass.”
I stopped dead in my tracks. Normally, this would be my turning point. But
something inside compelled me not to. A crowd was forming now. The attention
was like fuel to the fire. My knuckles were turning white. Nomi’s ears folded back.
“Frater, come on. Let’s go,” she urged.
I stood still a moment longer, then pocketed my hands and landed a heavy
step forward.
“Oh, that’s it.”
I heard rapid footsteps. The last of my restraints snapped. I whirled on the
spot. Nomi screamed and let go. My fist connected with his face, hard. The guy
staggered back and fell on the floor, his nose bleeding. The crowd gasped. I
breathed heavily, staring at him like a hawk locked on prey. My instincts took over
as I took a step toward the guy. Right then, Nomi jumped to hug me from behind.
“Stop!”
I gasped and looked over my shoulder, hand already on her head to pry her
off. Her gaze stopped me. My teeth gritted, but I relented.
“Alright, just… let go of me,” I said, turning around and trying to free
myself.
“Not until we are out safe!” she insisted, holding on tighter. Her ears flicked
a few times.
I groaned and walked out of the crowd with her. We walked out of the
campus building. I had relatively calmed down, but she refused to release me. Her
car was waiting at the gate. She finally let go and walked ahead, turning to me.
“Are you hurt?”
“No,” I replied, pocketing my hands again.
She sighed, then smiled. “That’s good to hear.” Her tail wagged. “Tonight at
8, Lily & Ember’s Moonlight. I took care of the reservations already. Don’t be late,
okay?”
“I’ll try.”
“Try isn’t enough. I need punctuality, Frater.”
I rolled my eyes. “You’re not my teacher.”
She chuckled and turned, but just when she was about to get in the car.
“Nomi,” I called.
She stopped and looked over her shoulder.
“Does it have to be—”
“Yes, Frater,” she interrupted. “Please. I promise it’s the last.”
She gave me one last smile and got in. The chauffeur closed the door and got
into the driver’s seat. I stood still as the car drove away, watching until it went out
of view before finally walking. My thoughts went back to the fight, but they were
interrupted by her again. Somehow, that gave me a headache.
I reached home and closed the door softly behind me, holding the knob for a
second before turning. A small package lay on the floor. I picked it up, staring a
moment.
“One last time…” I muttered and headed inside.
I don’t think I was ever this anxious. Or rather, this was my first time feeling
anxiety. It was frustrating to put together a last-minute attire, yet it somehow
turned out to be the best one I had. I felt uncomfortable and over-prepared in that
tuxedo. I had never worn formal attire. There was never any need to. I checked my
pockets one last time. Everything was there. It was time for the last sail, but
somehow, the thought didn’t quite comfort me like it used to.
The walk to the restaurant was long since I lived far from the city center. It
gave me plenty of time to think, and it still didn’t make sense. None of this did
anymore.
Why?
This unanswered question rang in my head continuously. I arrived about five
minutes early. The guy at the front welcomed me before checking my name and
letting me in. I deliberately walked up the stairs. The more I climbed, the heavier
my legs got. It didn’t take long to reach the 6th floor. The main area was vast. The
atmosphere was romantic and quiet despite being filled with customers.
Candle-shaped lights hung from the ceiling. Intricate designs accentuated the walls.
Vast windows showcased one of the best views in town. I exhaled shakily. An
employee walked up to me.
“Hello and welcome to Lily and Ember’s Moonlight, sir. May I have your—”
“Frater.”
He was caught off guard. I didn’t miss that small sneer on his face.
“Thank you. Please wait a moment.”
He scurried away and came back a moment later with a very fake smile.
“This way, esteemed sir.”
My eyes narrowed at the sudden care. What did she do this time? I
wondered. I followed him past a few tables. Then, the silence broke abruptly.
Heads turned towards the entrance. Whispers and mutters began as people stared
and pointed. I stopped and turned around. My eyes widened. There she was. Nomi,
walking out of the elevator, in a dress that perhaps, at least in my mind, put the
entire establishment to shame. A red that perfectly matched her fur, even though
they were vastly different colors. The dress clung to her every curve just right.
Every inch of her was groomed to perfection. She stopped before me with a smile.
I blinked and shook my head.
“Thank you for coming, Frater,” she said, her voice lower than usual. Her
eyes moved up and down. “You look… delectable~”
A shiver ran down my spine. This… is not what I am used to. For a moment,
I didn’t reply, expecting her to continue. But she didn’t, and just stared at me,
waiting.
“I… you too,” I blurted.
“Thank you,” she said, smiling wider. Her tail wagged.
A few people around us giggled. I tensed and shot the nearest couple a glare.
They turned away real quick. Then, she extended her hand.
“Shall we then?”
I nodded and gently, though hesitantly, took her hand. She walked ahead,
and we followed the server to our table. A window seat. We sat on plush chairs. I
closed my eyes and took a few deep breaths to compose myself. She giggled.
“Wow, I’ve never seen you this tense,” she whispered.
I averted my gaze. “Shut up. I’ve… never been on a date, and you know
that.”
“I know. But…” She rested her hand atop mine. “Loosen up. After all, it
might be our last, you know.”
I didn’t reply to her for a long moment, then sighed.
“Does it have to be…” I muttered.
“Hm? Pardon?”
“Nothing.”
She didn’t press, and instead turned to the view outside. The welcome drinks
came. But she didn’t turn. I looked around. Everything was quiet again, though
some stares lingered. Slowly, I took her drink and brought it under the table. My
hands shook a little. With one hand, I took a small bottle out of my pocket and
unhooked the cap. I was about to pour it in, but my hand paused. I stared at her
drink, then took a deep breath.
“Hm? Did they miss my drink?” Nomi said, looking around.
“No,” I said, quickly putting the drink in front of her again. “I saw this trick
online. You can heat their drink a little, and it tastes better. Thought it’d be worth
the experiment.” I shrugged.
“Oh? Let’s see how that holds.” She took the glass and gently sipped.
I shifted my legs, watching every gulp.
“Ah. Well, you weren’t wrong. It does taste good,” she said, finally putting
the glass down. “But I for one didn’t expect you to DIY for me.” She chuckled.
“It’s not for you,” I replied with a sigh that felt forced this time. “Just…
thought it would be better. I mean, it’s common sense—Ow.”
She punched my shoulder and pouted. I couldn’t stop a small, a very small
smile from peeking out this time, but quickly wiped it off.
“You’re acting like a child again.”
“Am not!” she snapped back with a low growl.
I sighed. “We should order.”
The evening seemed to pass quite quickly today. We ordered. We talked. We shared
moments. Reluctantly, I found myself wanting to, perhaps, stay a little longer. She
wasn’t overly romantic or anything. But I realized she never needed to be. I
realized… that I always had a hard time believing she was here. She was real. And
that she cared. No sane person would ever choose to walk beside me. That’s when I
thought. Perhaps she wasn’t sane at all. I might be guilty of smiling a little at that
thought. She was beautiful. The first beautiful I chose to acknowledge.
I leaned on my chair, having finished my food. She gently wiped her mouth
with a napkin, then looked at me. Her tail wagged slowly.
“This has been wonderful, Frater,” she said, her voice low. Perhaps a bit
strained.
I didn’t smile. Just nodded. She exhaled shakily, leaning forward toward me.
Then her face hit the table. A shudder ran through my body. Someone screamed. I
slowly rose from my chair, hands reaching out, trembling. For the first time, I felt
shaken.
“N-Nomi?”
Mutters and murmurs filled the place as people got up from their chairs. My
eyes shrank. I quickly rushed to her side, my breathing shaky.
“Nomi? NOMI?! NOMI WAKE UP!”
I jostled her. She wasn’t responding. Panic rose within me. My heart
hammered against my chest. I checked for a pulse. Thankfully, I found one, but it
was weak.
“SOMEONE CALL AN AMBULANCE!” I shouted over my shoulder.
Employees rushed to the spot. People gathered. I held on as best as I could,
trying to rouse her. My brain was empty. I didn’t know what to think or say. I
snatched her phone from the table and dialed the first number on her list. My phone
rang.
“S-Shit. F—”
I scrambled to end the call and quickly rushed through her contacts.
The ambulance arrived minutes later with her elder brother and father
already inside. They laid her on a stretcher and rushed her inside. They offered me
a seat. I took a step forward. Then, as if realizing myself, I said I didn’t want to
crowd the space. They thanked me for the thought, and the ambulance skidded
away. I stared as the car went out of view, breathless from that adrenaline rush. The
surrounding people muttered words of apology and encouragement before heading
back inside. I wasn’t exactly listening. I just turned and walked home.
My tuxedo, the whole attire, lay strewn across the floor. The silence of the room
felt deafening. I lay on the bed in normal clothes, eyes covered by my arm. The
clock struck midnight. I closed my eyes, wondering what was going down at the
hospital right about now. Part of me regretted not going.
I ran through the streets, panting. Arriving at the hospital, I sprinted up the stairs
without braking, bursting into Room 305. Nomi sat on the bed, looking out the
window, her fur groomed to perfection. Perhaps too much perfection. Her earlier
dress was swapped out for medical robes. Her ears twitched, and she turned to me
with a smile.
“Frater, you came. Come sit,” she said, patting the chair beside her.
I stood still for a moment, then walked in and closed the door. Everything
looked a bit too bright in here. My hand instinctively went for the light switch, but
hesitated and came back to my side. I sat down. Nomi turned to the window again.
“The doctors said I’ll be fine by the way,” she said.
I sat quietly for a moment, letting my breath settle.
“That’s… good to hear,” I replied, my voice low.
The silence stretched on. A clock ticked somewhere. I stared at the bed. She
sat so still that I felt uneasy.
“You must be tired,” she then said.
My body tensed. I didn’t reply for a long moment.
“Nomi…” I started.
“Yes?”
My hands trembled on my lap. “Nomi, I-I don’t want to kill you anymore,” I
said, my voice a bit strained.
Nomi didn’t reply immediately. She turned to look at me with a soft smile.
“I see. I got a little close to you, huh,” she said.
“That’s an understatement,” I said, staring at the floor, tears rolling down my
face at this point.
Another long silence followed as I sobbed quietly. Then, Nomi gently lifted
my head to meet my eyes.
“I’m sorry for your pain, Frater,” she said. “But you were the only person I
could’ve asked. The only person who I knew would agree to something suicidal
like this without judgement.” She brought a hand to her stomach. “I had been
fighting this for almost a year. The pain… had become unbearable. I couldn’t
sleep. I couldn’t eat. Sometimes, I could barely talk.”
She paused, exhaling softly. “I didn’t have the guts to kill myself. So I asked
you to do it with the poison I sent you. It was meant to be quick but…” She
chuckled. “Life has a funny way of striking back, doesn’t it? It took three times to
work.”
“I know.” I sniffled. “I agreed back then because—because back then you
were just another person to me. I thought the same for you as I did for everyone.
But you—you were not the same. You’re the only person who actually cared about
me, who didn’t walk away in disgust, who chose to walk with me, voluntarily, and
listen. I acted completely brash, and you still came back. You never needed to talk
to me anymore than your needs, but still you—you did. I-I can’t do this anymore,
Nomi. Please, there has to be another way.”
Nomi smiled again.
“There isn’t,” she said. “Cause it’s already over.”
My eyes widened. “W-What? N-no. Y-you’re right here. You said the doctor
said—I-I didn’t pour in the last vial!”
Nomi looked surprised. “You didn’t spike my drink at the date?”
I shook my head. “No. I was going to, but… I-I couldn’t bring myself to.
Not after I finally found someone who actually cared!”
A pause followed. Then she sighed. “I see.”
Something was ringing somewhere. It annoyed me. But I stared at her eyes,
as if trying to find an answer in them. She smiled again.
“Frater. You have my eternal gratitude,” she said, brushing a stray lock of
hair from my forehead. “The time I spent with you, however short, has been some
of the best of my entire life.” Her gentle hand came to rest on my cheek.
“W-what are you—”
“Remember something. You are a monster.” She leaned closer. Her voice
lowered to a whisper as our forehead touched. “But you are my monster.”
I gasped. My eyes shot open. I stared at the ceiling, my heart racing. I was at home,
sweating on my bed. My phone was ringing. I ignored it, trying to calm myself.
A… dream? The thought unsettled me.
My phone rang again. Reluctantly, I reached out and grabbed it. Unknown
Number. I answered and put the phone against my ear. Someone spoke from the
other end, hysterical and crying. None of what they said registered in my mind,
except one line.
She didn’t make it!
I didn’t hear further. The phone slipped from my hand and clattered to the
floor. One tear rolled down my face. Questions rang in my head.
Why?
I sat up and slowly got dressed. My gaze unfocused.
What should I do?
I freshened up and sat for breakfast. Another tear rolled down my face.
Why? Why… me?
My phone dinged. I contemplated whether I wanted to pick it up or not,
ultimately trudging to it and doing so. A message. From Nomi? I opened the chat
and found a video. I exhaled and hit play with a shaky thumb. Nomi sat on a chair
in her room. It felt so surreal to see her.
“Right. I’m filming this to admit that I, Nomi Silverton, being of sane mind
and body, confirm to have consented to being poisoned to death…”
Of course. She was smart. She wouldn’t want me to face issues. The rest of
the two-minute video covered legal details. But I just stared at her face. I watched
it again, just watching her. Then again, and again, and again, and—the screen
flashed low battery and shut off. I stared at the phone a moment longer, then tossed
it to the floor.
I walked out of my house and left the keys on the door, leaving my breakfast
unfinished. I walked and walked until I reached the bridge that stood several
hundred feet above the water, connecting two cities. The view looked…
mesmerizing. I climbed onto the railing without hesitation.
Someone behind me screamed. Cars screeched to a halt. People yelled.
Some tried reaching out. I didn’t care. Her face flashed before me. The
conversations we had replayed in my mind. If only I talked more. Lingered longer.
Thought twice, for once. Sought another way. If I had just… cared.
I didn’t even realize when my foot slipped and I was falling. But I didn’t
care. At this point, one might ask oneself. Did I have any regrets about my life?
Yes. Killing her… was my very first regret.

runs.text: I sat in an expensive restaurant. Luxurious. Elegant. Important. Everything around
was more than me. Perhaps, the only thing not… sat opposite. A she-wolf.
Orange-white fur. Calm and kind eyes. A smile that made me stare. She was
beautiful. The first ever beautiful I chose to acknowledge.
“This has been wonderful, Frater,” she said, her voice low. Perhaps a bit
strained.
I didn’t smile. Just nodded. She exhaled shakily, leaning forward toward me.
Then her face hit the table. A shudder ran through my body. Someone screamed. I
found myself rising from my chair, hands reaching out, trembling. For the first
time, I felt shaken.
“N-Nomi?”
To really understand… anything at all, let’s rewind time. A month should do.
Around the end of my junior year at college. But first, a little about myself. You
see, I was never your average Joe. In a bad way, I was a little weird. Though,
perhaps, saying
a little weird
is too modest.
Growing up, I enjoyed killing birds. Their chirping always annoyed me. I
threw stones, even squished a few to death myself. Obviously, my parents were
concerned, or rather, disgusted would probably be a more fitting word. In 6th
grade, I choked someone unconscious. Voluntarily. Expressionless. They wanted to
pick on me. It irritated me that he got away with just a neck brace. Damned
teachers. I got suspended. My parents argued that night, disowned me, and forced
me to leave. I didn’t mind. Neither did I care.
Some might be curious at this point. Why am I like this? Because I want to.
Perhaps, I realized too early that in this world, if you want something, you gotta
take it. And I didn’t like to be stepped on. Others don’t care about your comfort,
they care about theirs first. So you gotta make your own.
I lived in an orphanage most of my life, keeping my distance from everyone.
Anyone who did come
talk
to me scurried real quick. Otherwise, they met my fist
and ended up with a bloody face. The guardians there were kind enough to pay for
my school until 9th grade before I took over. By the time I was in college, I had left
long ago, already having a job and a full scholarship. Just… no one was walking
beside me. Did I regret my actions? No, not one bit. No sane person would ever
choose to walk beside me out of free will. And that was fine by me. Except…
Someone bumped my shoulder on the sidewalk going to college. A she-wolf,
smiling. A furry, more conventionally called. They appeared somewhere two
centuries ago when some guy decided to…
ahem
… at an apparently ancient altar
and had kids. Half-Breeds. Still feels weird though.
“Going all alone again, Frater?” Nomi asked, her tail wagging as she walked
beside me.
“Yeah.” My answer was quick. I didn’t really want to make small talk.
She pouted, then clung closer, wrapping an arm around mine. By now, I was
used to it and didn’t feel the necessity or the energy to step away. She sniffed my
coat.
“Is that a new perfume?”
“No.”
“Come on! It’s rude to ignore a girl holding your hand.”
I kept walking. She looked content just holding on. We walked through the
campus gates finally. People were already whispering. We simply walked by.
“Shouldn’t you be with your friends? They’ll stare at you if you don’t.”
“I am though.”
I raised an eyebrow. “I never said I was your—Ow.”
She punched my shoulder.
“Don’t you dare say that. Hmph!”
I rubbed my shoulder, sighing.
That’s Nomi. A she-wolf furry. Wolves were usually rough and tomboyish.
Not her. She’s quiet, but open. Smart, but gentle. She was
the
popular extrovert,
always hanging around or doing extracurriculars. But she was a bit naïve . I had to
pull her out of a few situations myself, as much as it annoyed me to do so. And
yes, that once caused a fight. They had to suspend me for a week.
We walked to class together, stopping at the door. She finally let go and
turned to face me. Someone from inside called her.
“Coming!” she said, then turned to me again. “Do you have it?”
I didn’t answer for a moment, then took out my bottle. “You mean water?”
Nomi smiled innocently. “Yes. Water.”
I handed her the bottle. She drank half of it before coughing violently. I
watched her without so much as a shudder. At least three girls rushed to support
her first. A crowd was already forming. Typical. She held onto the door for
balance, taking a shaky deep breath.
“Thanks,” she rasped, handing the bottle back. She managed a smile, visibly
trembling. “I’ll see you after class, okay? We get lunch together today.”
I frowned. “Lunch? Why?”
“You know why.”
She winked and headed inside, smoothing her dress. The students around
gave me looks before following her. I sighed and looked at the bottle, then threw it
in the trash and moved into class.
The hour was excruciatingly dull. I already knew these topics top-down.
Professor Sean called me up twice, expecting to embarrass me, only to be shocked
when I solved the problem in minutes. Out of the corner of my eye, I noticed Nomi
watching. She smiled when our eyes met. I set the marker down and turned away
from a fuming professor.
The class ended earlier than usual, coincidentally a few minutes after I
solved the second problem. I packed up and left first, hoping to go home. But of
course, Nomi blocked the way. Her arms crossed, tail flicking behind her. I forgot
to mention that wolves were ridiculously fast on their feet.
“Has no one ever told you it’s rude to walk out on a promise?”
I sighed. “I never said I promised.”
“Well. Doesn't matter.” She grabbed my arm and dragged me along. “We’re
getting lunch!”
“Hey! Slow down, I can walk!”
She dragged me along anyway.
We walked side by side down the streets. As always, she clung to me. It
annoyed me. Not because I was worried about people talking, because she was
probably the only person I genuinely didn’t understand. As we crossed the street,
an ad being displayed on a large digital billboard caught my attention. The picture
showed a doctor holding a small bottle of clear liquid. Underneath, there was a
bold text that said:
The cure for cancer! Testing now! If you need it, then call…
I stopped, halting her abruptly too. She turned to me, pouting.
“Hey! I almost—”
She noticed and followed my gaze to the billboard. Her ears drooped, and
tail stopped moving. I turned and walked again. Nomi came along without a word.
“Couldn’t you get that?” I asked.
“The cure?”
I nodded.
She chuckled. “We called. It’s too expensive.”
“You’re rich, though. Don’t you live in a mansion?”
“I do.” She held on a little tighter. “But it’s not enough.”
A low whine rumbled in her throat. She rubbed her stomach, trembling
again. I looked once, then kept walking.
“Maybe I can chip in.”
Nomi’s eyes widened, and her head snapped toward me so fast it looked like
that hurt. “Are you… offering to help?”
“Hell no,” I replied immediately. “It’s to get you off my back, or rather my
arm.”
Nomi stared for a moment, then laughed. I groaned. My fists clenched, but I
let go with a sigh.
Sometime later, we arrived at a rather empty diner, sat down, and ordered
drinks. I looked outside while she scrolled on social media. That billboard was still
clear from here. My phone rang. I answered without looking and waited as the
other person spoke.
“Coming,” I said, standing up.
Nomi’s ears quirked up. “Where are you going?"
“Parcel,” I replied, ending the call and stepping out of the booth.
I walked out of the diner. A man in a hoodie stood there, holding a small
blue package. I paid and opened it right there, pocketing the small bottle inside
before walking back in. The server stopped just short of bumping into me with his
tray of drinks while turning.
“Oh, s-sorry I—”
“Is this for table five?”
The server was caught off guard, eyes darting around. “I—yes.”
“Then I’ll take it. That’s me and… someone else.”
I took the tray without waiting for a confirmation, waiting until the server
left before setting the tray two tables ahead of ours. I took out the small bottle, and
emptied its contents into one drink, pocketing it again before walking to our table
with the tray. Nomi smiled, tail wagging as she set her phone down.
“Oh, Frater serving me? How romantic,” she said, leaning forward a little.
“Just thought it’d be more efficient,” I replied, passing her drink before
sitting with mine.
I watched her stir with the straw, staring as the contents mixed. When she
leaned down, my hand rose a little, then grabbed the table. She took a long sip,
sighing.
“Mm, this drink here is always the best. Don’t you agree, Frater?”
I turned to my drink, and nodded. “I guess.”
Nomi picked up the menu, humming. “What do you think we should order? I
heard their fried rice is amazing. The girls eat here often.”
“I don’t know. I’ll get whatever’s cheapest,” I replied, taking a sip of my
drink.
Nomi groaned. “Come on, offer some suggestions to this poor struggling
lady.”
I looked up from my drink, unimpressed by the puppy dog eyes she was
giving.
“Really?”
She sighed and crossed her arms. “That usually works,” she muttered.
I shook my head and went back to my drink.
We left the diner about an hour later. I was still sipping on my drink. Nomi
stretched as we walked through the doors. Her ears flicked a few times before
relaxing.
“I’m full! Now, wasn’t that fun?” she asked, smiling and leaning toward me.
I looked at the road instead. “Depends on your concept of
fun
. I was
bored—Ow.”
She punched my shoulder again. I sighed, not looking at her. The light
turned red. I was about to cross when her hand suddenly grabbed my shoulder.
“What the—”
I turned to her. She was gripping her stomach and shaking, gritting her teeth.
Her ears folded back. Her claws bared, digging into my shoulder. I winced. Then,
her eyes snapped to meet mine. Her pupils dilated. I stared for one second, then
quickly turned away, exhaling as I reached for my phone and dialed.
“H-Hello, I think I have an emergency,” I said as calmly as I could.
I sat next to an empty seat for a week straight. Occasionally, I stared at the empty
space, wondering. The bell rang. I packed my bag and walked out of class. Some
gossiping girls scurried by.
“Did you hear? Nomi’s been admitted to the hospital again.”
“Again?”
I didn’t pay heed to them. It wasn’t my job to care after all, right? I went
home and lay on my bed, doomscrolling. Random pictures and videos appeared on
my feed, but I found myself a bit distracted. Those eyes, the way she—my phone
rang, snapping me out of my trance. Unknown number. I answered and put it on
speaker.
“Hello?”
“Hey. Uh, is this Frater?”
“It is.”
“Oh, hey man. I’m Tyler. I know you don’t—”
“I know who you are, Tyler Smith. Just get on with what you want.”
There was a pause, and some muttering on the other side. Then, someone
cleared their throat.
“Right. So uh… Nomi asked us to call this number to tell you she was at
Advent Hospital. Room 305 right now.”
My hand gripped the phone tighter, subconsciously.
“That’s the ICU,” I muttered.
There was another pause.
“Y-Yea, man. If you wanted to see her—”
I ended the call before he could finish, bringing my hand up to cover my
eyes. For a moment, I laid there, busy with my thoughts. The sunlight felt
particularly annoying today. I got up, walked to the windows and closed the
curtains, staring at them. Her eyes, those dilated eyes, flashed before me. My fists
clenched. I turned, grabbed my phone from the bed and left. The walk to the
hospital was brief.
“I was looking for a patient. Nomi. A she-wolf,” I asked the front desk.
“Are you Frater?” the woman at the desk asked.
I nodded.
“Mm, she told us to expect you. Room 305. But she might not be open to
visitation just yet. You’re welcome to check.”
I looked around, then walked down a hallway. Someone stepped into an
empty elevator and held it open. But I walked by, taking the stairs instead. As I
reached the landing, I saw someone standing near her room. I stopped before him.
He spared me a glance before turning ahead again.
“Forgive me if I’m wrong. But are you Frater?”
I sighed. “Let me guess. Nomi told the entire hospital by now?”
The guy didn’t reply and simply gestured to the room. I turned, and for the
first time in my life, froze. Three people were trying to restrain her to the bed. She
was writhing and snarling. Her eyes were red, spit flying everywhere. Her screams
rattled the door, though they came muffled because of the soundproofing. I stared,
eyes wide, trembling even. Was this really… her?
“She’d been asking for you nonstop,” the guy said.
I couldn’t muster a reply.
The guy patted my shoulder. “Stomach cancer is difficult to deal with. Being
stage three with a weak immune system like hers doesn’t help either. But we are
trying our best. Come, let’s—”
I brushed the guy’s hand off rather roughly. My body tensed. I took a step
back, then another, then ran. Down the stairs and out of the hospital, not stopping
until I reached home and slammed the door. I planted my back against the wall,
panting heavily. Scenes flashed across my mind. It hurt. I grabbed my head,
covering my ears, trying to stop the ringing, but it just wouldn’t.
Night. 7:24PM. I sat beside her bed, calm and composed, a stark contrast to how
she looked. Her fur was all disheveled. Her eyes red-rimmed. She leaned against
the bedframe, looking out the window. A bouquet rested on the table beside her.
“Thanks for coming to see me, Frater,” she said, turning to me with her usual
smile. Her tail wagged.
“Don’t mention it,” I replied. “Someone asked me to bring flowers. That’s
why I came. Probably wouldn’t have otherwise.”
She pouted. “You really know how to hurt a woman’s feelings, don’t you?”
“Right now, you’re more of a child than a woman.”
“I am not! Y-you are!”
I looked at her, unimpressed by the worst comeback to exist for the next
centuries, probably. The corner of my eye caught the edge of the bandage peeking
from her stomach. She covered it quickly, as if sensing my gaze.
“The doctors said I’ll be fine. Nothing serious to worry about.” She sighed.
“Sorry if I worried you for nothing.”
“I never said I was worried—Ow.”
She punched my shoulder, crossed her arms and pouted, turning away
entirely.
“This is what I meant by being a little child,” I said, rubbing my shoulder.
“I am NOT a child!” she argued with a low growl, spinning right back
around to face me. “I am a mature and grown wolf!”
I sighed and stood up. “Well, you’re doing good. It’s best I leave. Later,” I
said, and turned.
She grabbed my hand. I stopped. Her hold was weak. I could easily break
free. But something in me refused to give me strength. So I looked over my
shoulder instead. She was blushing.
“I… just wait a minute,” she said, averting her gaze.
I waited a moment, watching her fidget.
“Just spit it out already,” I said.
“I’m trying!” She took a deep breath, holding my hand a little tighter. “I…
want us to go on a date. At the end of the month.”
“What?” It was an instinctive response, as if the very idea was absurd to me.
Nomi nodded, blushing hard. Silence passed between us for a moment. Her
tail was wagging wildly, and I could hear a very low whine from her throat. I
sighed again.
“Look, we have finals at the end of the month. It’s not possible,” I said,
about to take a step forward.
“I’ll pay for yours too!” she said quickly, tightening her hold further.
“Please, just… one more time.”
My leg stopped mid-step. My body tensed ever so slightly.
“Nomi…”
“Please, Frater. Consider it a last wish. I won’t bother you after that.”
I stayed still for a long moment, then pocketed my hands and took that step
forward. My arm slipped free from her grip even as she tried holding on, though I
didn’t leave yet.
“Fine,” I said.
I didn’t wait to hear a response and walked out of the room, but felt her
smiling behind me.
I went home and sat on my bed, thinking. Just one more time. One… last
time. The thought wasn’t so comforting, but her smile—I slapped myself. No,
there’s no person stupid enough to actually like me. Never. It’s just… dumb. She
just wants to get it over with. It’s a fleeting fantasy not worth pondering. At least,
that’s what I told myself.
I spent the next weeks mostly in preparation. Assignments, quizzes, and some
minor projects here and there. Everybody was becoming increasingly busy.
Though, my attention kept slipping, more than usual. I found my thoughts drifting
occasionally, though I brushed them off most of the time. The news of the date
spread like wildfire. But what irritated me were the whispers. The constant
muttering grated on my nerves as I walked the hallways. It took a lot to hold it in.
Nomi had to stay a few more days in the hospital before being discharged.
She, as usual, refused to leave my side. I couldn’t figure out why she lingered
beyond what she needed, and it frustrated me, though I found myself complaining
less and less. That irritated me too.
I walked down the hallway to the gym. Apparently, Nomi had a volleyball
match today. I sighed. Part of me wondered why I was doing this much. But I
didn’t feel enough energy to care. I entered the gym right as Nomi managed a nasty
block. The whistle blew. Her side won.
“Yes! Still have it girls!”
I stood by the door, watching them celebrate for a moment before gently
tapping my foot. Nomi’s ears twitched, and she turned. She smiled and rushed over
to me.
“Frater! How long have you been standing there?”
“A few minutes.”
“Ooh, did you see that last play? It was outstanding, wasn’t it?!”
“It was okay.”
Nomi crossed her arms. “Come on, you don’t have to be so… this.”
“What’s this?”
“You know!
This
,” she said, gesturing to me.
I stared at her for a moment, then took out my phone. “Well, too bad.”
“Nomi!” someone called.
“Coming!” she said, turning to me again. “Wait here, I’ll be back in a few
minutes, alright?”
“Hurry up,” I replied, scrolling on my phone.
She turned and winced, holding her stomach. Her ears folded back. I looked
up from my phone.
“I’m… fine,” she said, and hurried away.
I stared for a moment, then sighed and went back to my phone. She changed
into casual attire, and we left, walking down the hallway.
“Mmm!” Nomi stretched. “I missed so much these last few days. It’ll be a
nightmare to cover up.”
“It’s kinda your fault, you know,” I said, pocketing my phone.
“Really? I just got back from the hospital!”
“You were playing volleyball just now.”
“W-well, that’s—that’s different,” she argued, turning away.
Some guy tried shoving past me, but my shoulder didn’t move.
“What the—Hey! Watch it!” the guy yelled.
My fists clenched, but I kept walking. Nomi hung closer, holding onto my
arm.
“Oh, I get it. You think you’re the big man now that you’re dating her, huh?
You’re a nobody, and she’s a dumbass.”
I stopped dead in my tracks. Normally, this would be my turning point. But
something inside compelled me not to. A crowd was forming now. The attention
was like fuel to the fire. My knuckles were turning white. Nomi’s ears folded back.
“Frater, come on. Let’s go,” she urged.
I stood still a moment longer, then pocketed my hands and landed a heavy
step forward.
“Oh, that’s it.”
I heard rapid footsteps. The last of my restraints snapped. I whirled on the
spot. Nomi screamed and let go. My fist connected with his face, hard. The guy
staggered back and fell on the floor, his nose bleeding. The crowd gasped. I
breathed heavily, staring at him like a hawk locked on prey. My instincts took over
as I took a step toward the guy. Right then, Nomi jumped to hug me from behind.
“Stop!”
I gasped and looked over my shoulder, hand already on her head to pry her
off. Her gaze stopped me. My teeth gritted, but I relented.
“Alright, just… let go of me,” I said, turning around and trying to free
myself.
“Not until we are out safe!” she insisted, holding on tighter. Her ears flicked
a few times.
I groaned and walked out of the crowd with her. We walked out of the
campus building. I had relatively calmed down, but she refused to release me. Her
car was waiting at the gate. She finally let go and walked ahead, turning to me.
“Are you hurt?”
“No,” I replied, pocketing my hands again.
She sighed, then smiled. “That’s good to hear.” Her tail wagged. “Tonight at
Lily & Ember’s Moonlight
. I took care of the reservations already. Don’t be late,
okay?”
“I’ll try.”
“Try isn’t enough. I need punctuality, Frater.”
I rolled my eyes. “You’re not my teacher.”
She chuckled and turned, but just when she was about to get in the car.
“Nomi,” I called.
She stopped and looked over her shoulder.
“Does it have to be—”
“Yes, Frater,” she interrupted. “Please. I promise it’s the last.”
She gave me one last smile and got in. The chauffeur closed the door and got
into the driver’s seat. I stood still as the car drove away, watching until it went out
of view before finally walking. My thoughts went back to the fight, but they were
interrupted by her again. Somehow, that gave me a headache.
I reached home and closed the door softly behind me, holding the knob for a
second before turning. A small package lay on the floor. I picked it up, staring a
moment.
“One last time…” I muttered and headed inside.
I don’t think I was ever this anxious. Or rather, this was my first time feeling
anxiety. It was frustrating to put together a last-minute attire, yet it somehow
turned out to be the best one I had. I felt uncomfortable and over-prepared in that
tuxedo. I had never worn formal attire. There was never any need to. I checked my
pockets one last time. Everything was there. It was time for the last sail, but
somehow, the thought didn’t quite comfort me like it used to.
The walk to the restaurant was long since I lived far from the city center. It
gave me plenty of time to think, and it still didn’t make sense. None of this did
anymore.
Why?
This unanswered question rang in my head continuously. I arrived about five
minutes early. The guy at the front welcomed me before checking my name and
letting me in. I deliberately walked up the stairs. The more I climbed, the heavier
my legs got. It didn’t take long to reach the 6th floor. The main area was vast. The
atmosphere was romantic and quiet despite being filled with customers.
Candle-shaped lights hung from the ceiling. Intricate designs accentuated the walls.
Vast windows showcased one of the best views in town. I exhaled shakily. An
employee walked up to me.
“Hello and welcome to
Lily and Ember’s Moonlight
, sir. May I have your—”
“Frater.”
He was caught off guard. I didn’t miss that small sneer on his face.
“Thank you. Please wait a moment.”
He scurried away and came back a moment later with a very fake smile.
“This way, esteemed sir.”
My eyes narrowed at the sudden care. What did she do this time? I
wondered. I followed him past a few tables. Then, the silence broke abruptly.
Heads turned towards the entrance. Whispers and mutters began as people stared
and pointed. I stopped and turned around. My eyes widened. There she was. Nomi,
walking out of the elevator, in a dress that perhaps, at least in my mind, put the
entire establishment to shame. A red that perfectly matched her fur, even though
they were vastly different colors. The dress clung to her every curve just right.
Every inch of her was groomed to perfection. She stopped before me with a smile.
I blinked and shook my head.
“Thank you for coming, Frater,” she said, her voice lower than usual. Her
eyes moved up and down. “You look… delectable~”
A shiver ran down my spine. This… is not what I am used to. For a moment,
I didn’t reply, expecting her to continue. But she didn’t, and just stared at me,
waiting.
“I… you too,” I blurted.
“Thank you,” she said, smiling wider. Her tail wagged.
A few people around us giggled. I tensed and shot the nearest couple a glare.
They turned away real quick. Then, she extended her hand.
“Shall we then?”
I nodded and gently, though hesitantly, took her hand. She walked ahead,
and we followed the server to our table. A window seat. We sat on plush chairs. I
closed my eyes and took a few deep breaths to compose myself. She giggled.
“Wow, I’ve never seen you this tense,” she whispered.
I averted my gaze. “Shut up. I’ve… never been on a date, and you know
that.”
“I know. But…” She rested her hand atop mine. “Loosen up. After all, it
might be our last, you know.”
I didn’t reply to her for a long moment, then sighed.
“Does it have to be…” I muttered.
“Hm? Pardon?”
“Nothing.”
She didn’t press, and instead turned to the view outside. The welcome drinks
came. But she didn’t turn. I looked around. Everything was quiet again, though
some stares lingered. Slowly, I took her drink and brought it under the table. My
hands shook a little. With one hand, I took a small bottle out of my pocket and
unhooked the cap. I was about to pour it in, but my hand paused. I stared at her
drink, then took a deep breath.
“Hm? Did they miss my drink?” Nomi said, looking around.
“No,” I said, quickly putting the drink in front of her again. “I saw this trick
online. You can heat their drink a little, and it tastes better. Thought it’d be worth
the experiment.” I shrugged.
“Oh? Let’s see how that holds.” She took the glass and gently sipped.
I shifted my legs, watching every gulp.
“Ah. Well, you weren’t wrong. It does taste good,” she said, finally putting
the glass down. “But I for one didn’t expect you to DIY for me.” She chuckled.
“It’s not for you,” I replied with a sigh that felt forced this time. “Just…
thought it would be better. I mean, it’s common sense—Ow.”
She punched my shoulder and pouted. I couldn’t stop a small, a very small
smile from peeking out this time, but quickly wiped it off.
“You’re acting like a child again.”
“Am not!” she snapped back with a low growl.
I sighed. “We should order.”
The evening seemed to pass quite quickly today. We ordered. We talked. We shared
moments. Reluctantly, I found myself wanting to, perhaps, stay a little longer. She
wasn’t overly romantic or anything. But I realized she never needed to be. I
realized… that I always had a hard time believing she was here. She was real. And
that she cared. No sane person would ever choose to walk beside me. That’s when I
thought. Perhaps she wasn’t sane at all. I might be guilty of smiling a little at that
thought. She was beautiful. The first beautiful I chose to acknowledge.
I leaned on my chair, having finished my food. She gently wiped her mouth
with a napkin, then looked at me. Her tail wagged slowly.
“This has been wonderful, Frater,” she said, her voice low. Perhaps a bit
strained.
I didn’t smile. Just nodded. She exhaled shakily, leaning forward toward me.
Then her face hit the table. A shudder ran through my body. Someone screamed. I
slowly rose from my chair, hands reaching out, trembling. For the first time, I felt
shaken.
“N-Nomi?”
Mutters and murmurs filled the place as people got up from their chairs. My
eyes shrank. I quickly rushed to her side, my breathing shaky.
“Nomi? NOMI?! NOMI WAKE UP!”
I jostled her. She wasn’t responding. Panic rose within me. My heart
hammered against my chest. I checked for a pulse. Thankfully, I found one, but it
was weak.
“SOMEONE CALL AN AMBULANCE!” I shouted over my shoulder.
Employees rushed to the spot. People gathered. I held on as best as I could,
trying to rouse her. My brain was empty. I didn’t know what to think or say. I
snatched her phone from the table and dialed the first number on her list. My phone
rang.
“S-Shit. F—”
I scrambled to end the call and quickly rushed through her contacts.
The ambulance arrived minutes later with her elder brother and father
already inside. They laid her on a stretcher and rushed her inside. They offered me
a seat. I took a step forward. Then, as if realizing myself, I said I didn’t want to
crowd the space. They thanked me for the thought, and the ambulance skidded
away. I stared as the car went out of view, breathless from that adrenaline rush. The
surrounding people muttered words of apology and encouragement before heading
back inside. I wasn’t exactly listening. I just turned and walked home.
My tuxedo, the whole attire, lay strewn across the floor. The silence of the room
felt deafening. I lay on the bed in normal clothes, eyes covered by my arm. The
clock struck midnight. I closed my eyes, wondering what was going down at the
hospital right about now. Part of me regretted not going.
I ran through the streets, panting. Arriving at the hospital, I sprinted up the stairs
without braking, bursting into Room 305. Nomi sat on the bed, looking out the
window, her fur groomed to perfection. Perhaps too much perfection. Her earlier
dress was swapped out for medical robes. Her ears twitched, and she turned to me
with a smile.
“Frater, you came. Come sit,” she said, patting the chair beside her.
I stood still for a moment, then walked in and closed the door. Everything
looked a bit too bright in here. My hand instinctively went for the light switch, but
hesitated and came back to my side. I sat down. Nomi turned to the window again.
“The doctors said I’ll be fine by the way,” she said.
I sat quietly for a moment, letting my breath settle.
“That’s… good to hear,” I replied, my voice low.
The silence stretched on. A clock ticked somewhere. I stared at the bed. She
sat so still that I felt uneasy.
“You must be tired,” she then said.
My body tensed. I didn’t reply for a long moment.
“Nomi…” I started.
“Yes?”
My hands trembled on my lap. “Nomi, I-I don’t want to kill you anymore,” I
said, my voice a bit strained.
Nomi didn’t reply immediately. She turned to look at me with a soft smile.
“I see. I got a little close to you, huh,” she said.
“That’s an understatement,” I said, staring at the floor, tears rolling down my
face at this point.
Another long silence followed as I sobbed quietly. Then, Nomi gently lifted
my head to meet my eyes.
“I’m sorry for your pain, Frater,” she said. “But you were the only person I
could’ve asked. The only person who I knew would agree to something suicidal
like this without judgement.” She brought a hand to her stomach. “I had been
fighting this for almost a year. The pain… had become unbearable. I couldn’t
sleep. I couldn’t eat. Sometimes, I could barely talk.”
She paused, exhaling softly. “I didn’t have the guts to kill myself. So I asked
you to do it with the poison I sent you. It was meant to be quick but…” She
chuckled. “Life has a funny way of striking back, doesn’t it? It took three times to
work.”
“I know.” I sniffled. “I agreed back then because—because back then you
were just another person to me. I thought the same for you as I did for everyone.
But you—you were not the same. You’re the only person who actually cared about
me, who didn’t walk away in disgust, who chose to walk with me, voluntarily, and
listen. I acted completely brash, and you still came back. You never needed to talk
to me anymore than your needs, but still you—you did. I-I can’t do this anymore,
Nomi. Please, there has to be another way.”
Nomi smiled again.
“There isn’t,” she said. “Cause it’s already over.”
My eyes widened. “W-What? N-no. Y-you’re right here. You said the doctor
said—I-I didn’t pour in the last vial!”
Nomi looked surprised. “You didn’t spike my drink at the date?”
I shook my head. “No. I was going to, but… I-I couldn’t bring myself to.
Not after I finally found someone who actually cared!”
A pause followed. Then she sighed. “I see.”
Something was ringing somewhere. It annoyed me. But I stared at her eyes,
as if trying to find an answer in them. She smiled again.
“Frater. You have my eternal gratitude,” she said, brushing a stray lock of
hair from my forehead. “The time I spent with you, however short, has been some
of the best of my entire life.” Her gentle hand came to rest on my cheek.
“W-what are you—”
“Remember something. You are a monster.” She leaned closer. Her voice
lowered to a whisper as our forehead touched. “But you are
my
monster.”
I gasped. My eyes shot open. I stared at the ceiling, my heart racing. I was at home,
sweating on my bed. My phone was ringing. I ignored it, trying to calm myself.
A… dream? The thought unsettled me.
My phone rang again. Reluctantly, I reached out and grabbed it. Unknown
Number. I answered and put the phone against my ear. Someone spoke from the
other end, hysterical and crying. None of what they said registered in my mind,
except one line.
She didn’t make it!
I didn’t hear further. The phone slipped from my hand and clattered to the
floor. One tear rolled down my face. Questions rang in my head.
Why?
I sat up and slowly got dressed. My gaze unfocused.
What should I do?
I freshened up and sat for breakfast. Another tear rolled down my face.
Why? Why… me?
My phone dinged. I contemplated whether I wanted to pick it up or not,
ultimately trudging to it and doing so. A message. From Nomi? I opened the chat
and found a video. I exhaled and hit play with a shaky thumb. Nomi sat on a chair
in her room. It felt so surreal to see her.
Right. I’m filming this to admit that I, Nomi Silverton, being of sane mind
and body, confirm to have consented to being poisoned to death…
Of course. She was smart. She wouldn’t want me to face issues. The rest of
the two-minute video covered legal details. But I just stared at her face. I watched
it again, just watching her. Then again, and again, and again, and—the screen
flashed low battery and shut off. I stared at the phone a moment longer, then tossed
it to the floor.
I walked out of my house and left the keys on the door, leaving my breakfast
unfinished. I walked and walked until I reached the bridge that stood several
hundred feet above the water, connecting two cities. The view looked…
mesmerizing. I climbed onto the railing without hesitation.
Someone behind me screamed. Cars screeched to a halt. People yelled.
Some tried reaching out. I didn’t care. Her face flashed before me. The
conversations we had replayed in my mind. If only I talked more. Lingered longer.
Thought twice, for once. Sought another way. If I had just… cared.
I didn’t even realize when my foot slipped and I was falling. But I didn’t
care. At this point, one might ask oneself. Did I have any regrets about my life?
Yes. Killing her… was my very first regret.

title: "Christmas Carols"
author: Labiba Hasan
excerpt: Mrs. Howard turns 68 this year.
imageAlt: Cover image for "Christmas Carols"
content: Mrs. Howard turns 68 this year.
Like every year on Christmas, she wakes up early today. There has been no particular reason, yet, she
looks at her reflection in the bathroom mirror a little longer on this day. She observes her wrinkles, her
crinkled skin, beauty marks. But of all that she tries to find someone in her own reflection.
She wraps her cardigan and walks down the stairs.
The house is a two -storey urban villa. It is one of the oldest in the block. The paint is fading, the door
still has an antique doorknob, the mahogany desk near the study has a beautiful greek lamp, the 1975
Honda in the garage. All the neighbours now call that car “the old Howard car”.
Mrs. Howard takes a simple breakfast. Some toasts with an omelet. She goes to study with a hot-
steaming cup of coffee. The room smells like old books and wood with a faint smell of fresh
caffaine.She sets the cup on the large mahogany table in the centre. It is now maybe 34 years old. The
first expensive purchase her husband made after they moved here. She dusts it a little and her hand
stops at a place on the table. It was a drawing her daughter made when she was a kid. She loved pandas.
That day she and her husband went to a friend and left their daughter with a babysitter. The babysitter
fell asleep and her daughter took the chance and went into the study. By the time they came back the
study was a wreck. Her husband, Edward got quite upset about the table but soon melted away when
his daughter surprised him with a drawing the next day.
Mrs.Howard chuckles to herself, “ Oh Lucy! What a naughty kid you were!”
She finishes her coffee in the study. Then she goes to the living room where the decorated Christmas
tree is placed. She looks at it closely. The bulbs are deep red with silver shine just like Edward likes.
Lucy loves the golden neon lights wrapped around the tree. She looks at the top. Something is missing.
Oh! She forgot to place the star-shaped light on the top. Lucy used to call it Mr.starry as a child. She
finishes the decoration and hurries to the bedroom. She changes into formal clothes. The morning
prayer is about to start.
She reaches the church. It is a bit more crowded than usual today. She enters and greets other people
and spots a familiar face. Janet as usual saved her a spot in the front. She sits beside her.
“You look beautiful today ,” says Janet with a smile.
“ We are already old. You should be over that phase, Jenny!”
Janat laughs. “ Oh, don't get me started. I am still as beautiful as ever. But do you know Oprah from
our department, whose daughter got married last year? Well, now she is the granny of a beautiful baby
girl. You can call her an oldie grandma now. Haha. There they are! Baby Agnus's first Christmas. Let's
go and congratulate them.”
Janet goes to greet them. Mrs.Howard stares at them a little longer. Oprah’s daughter carrying her
daughter. Such a beautiful sight. She suddenly remembers the first Christmas after Lucy was born.
Edward bought her a beautiful flowy yellow dress. Her baby chuckles bustling in the Church.
Soon the prayer starts.
The choir ended in two hours. Mrs.Howard talked with the other ladies. They were planning to go to a
coffee shop nearby and asked her to accompany them. She politely refused and bid them a good bye.
She has to prepare the meals for the dinner. Edward likes medium rare steak and Lucy loves risotto. She
has to make a stop at the grocery store. She notices the old bakery near the nursery. She, Edward and
Lucy had a tradition. Always visit the local bakery on Christmas evening. But things change with time.
But today she has decided to buy the strawberry frost cupcake. Lucy used to be crazy about it.
The town covered in snow looks like a big white paper. The weather sends chills even inside the coat.
Mrs.Howard took the cupcake and a hot chocolate and sat beside a lakeside bench. The lake is frozen.
But the old willow tree near the lake is still here. She remembers this is the exact place where Edward
proposed to her. She shared the news about Lucy here also.
The store is walking distance from the home. She first goes through the meat items. Then the pasta
section. Edward loves sirloin steak. In the fruit sections one column is filled with fresh, juicy red
plums. She recalls a very vivid memory from her own childhood. Edward and she used to go to the
same school. There used to be a plum tree on the way to their home. She really wanted to take some
but the tree was owned by someone. In the following afternoon Edward climbed the fence and stole
some plums but was later caught by the owner's wife. His father stopped him from going out for 1
whole week. Later he again went there and brought the plums for her.
She stares blankly at the plums and just walks away.
It was evening by the time she reached home. Even walking a small distance is hard at her age. She
starts preparing the meals.
While it is getting ready she goes to the garden. The garden looks like an ancient temple, where life has
been absent for decades. But the Snowdrops bloomed so beautifully this year. Edward had a weird
obsession with Snowdrops.. Celebration, condolence or sometimes without reason he carried
Snowdrops.
She went to Lucy’s room and picked her favorite dusty pink sheets. The white Snowdrops on the table
with pink sheets looked like dreamy candy floss. She picked some scented candles with vanilla scent and
then set the table for three. Edward’s Chinese porcelain.
The room is filled with a sweet vanilla scent, along with the aroma of freshly made steak and pasta.
Mrs.Howard doesn’t sit. She fetches two pieces of paper and envelopes. She starts writing the first
letter:
To my daughter
(Who never got to grow up)
My dear, my moon, my sweet and most beautiful daughter in the world. Lucy, do you know the doctor
told me that I might forget things from now on. Even people, faces and names!! I don't believe it. How can
mommy forget Lucy's face?
You had the prettiest hazel eyes. Your stunning ginger hair, soft as silk threads. You know Oprah is a
grandma now. If you had a daughter, who would she look like? You or me.
Your daddy used to say you resembled me so much. I always look at the mirror and think, would you have
looked like this if you had grown old?
Nah, maybe a more graceful woman than me. More elegant and delicate like an autumn leaf.
Mommy made risotto today. The cupcake from the bakery doesn't taste as good as before…..
Merry Christmas Luciana Howard, my precious baby.
I will write to you again.
Mrs.Howard stops writing. Her hands are trembling. Pen has been her closest friend in her 30 years of
teaching career. But her hands are shaking while writing a simple letter. “ Age maybe…” she retorts to
herself. She carefully folds the letter and puts it in the envelope. She starts writing the other one:
To my husband,
Who promised to stay,
Dear, I have learnt how to fix a broken chair, how to keep my keys safe. I can go to the doctors by myself
now. I drive pretty well now. They say to get a new car. But that car still holds the scent of your dusky
perfume. I haven't eaten plums in a long while.
Do you know it is easy to replace actions but not the people behind it. I still carry you in thoughts and
heart. How can some forget a person when your whole life was built around them? I wanted to grow old
with you so badly…….
Take care of Lucy.
25 December, 1995. 6:23 pm.
The room has a suffocating smell. Winter chills made the cold room colder. There is a bee in the room.
Maybe a beeswax is somewhere nearby. It is stuck in the room for 17 minutes. Searching for a door. It
mistook the glass window for a clear path. It tries and bumps into the window again and again. Thup!
thup! thup!........
Mrs Howard? Mrs????
Mrs.Howard looks at the officer calling her name. He hands her two zipper bags. One with a blood
soaked sage green shirt. And one with a lavender dress, a white hairband and a air of glasses, all
drenched in blood.
“ Edward….. Lucy…….”
“ The estimated time of the crash was 12 pm. The Injureds were sent to the nearest hospitals but one of
them was spot dead and other died in the emergency section. We contacted you through the emergency
contact. You will receive the bodies by tonight. We are really sorry for your loss.”
Mrs.Howard puts the pen on the table and puts the letters in a separate box. A box full of letters.
She keeps the door slightly open and pours some tea, one by one, in three cups.

crinkled skin, beauty marks. But of all that she tries to find someone in her own reflection.
She wraps her cardigan and walks down the stairs.

Honda in the garage. All the neighbours now call that car “the old Howard car”.

caffaine.She sets the cup on the large mahogany table in the centre. It is now maybe 34 years old. The
