title: The Moonlit Night
author: Labiba Hasan
excerpt: A crow sits on the flickering pole light
imageAlt: Cover image for The Moonlit Night
content: A crow sits on the flickering pole light
Engulfing the silence of the night.
Old lady Bentham sits by the window
Her breath feels heavy yet hollow.
Upper in the red building
daughter of the smiths stays awake
Her eyes sing the song of spring while looking at the keepsake.
The wind blows away the time
The night grows deeper;
The night grows deeper.
A man is walking on the road;
His left shows the dark-silent city
His right covers the vastness of the sea.
His walk is slow,
Every step counted,
The long coat covers his silhouette,
His cold eyes glare from under the hat.
There is something,
about the perfection he holds.
Like he has lived the same day
for years and years.
Tonight something changes.
The road he walked everyday;
He knows how many lamps are there,
How many benches by the road,
Which houses remain lit
Even at the dead of night,
Where the black alley cat sleeps,
Where the homeless George sits in his sleepless nights,
He memorized the town,
like formulas on sheets.
But today an unfamiliar figure stops him on the track.
A Red chair by the Sea.
The man looks at it,
His judgement questioning the reasons of the chair being here,
But some things are better not questioned.
He sits there,
Facing the endless ocean.
The cold,freezing air brushes against his face,
The sound of waves crashing against the shore
Reminds him of a time.
His mother’s tales.
How she used to tell him a story about a poet who lived near the sea.
He admired the moon,
He wrote poems praising her charm.
He told her stories to the sea.
The charming princess she is,
The dazzle of her light
lighting the night sky.
One day the Sea asks the forbidden,
“ O the princess of heavenly galaxy, walk an eternity with me like parallels.
The moon whispered,
“I belong to the heavens, and my light touches every corner of the earth. Tell me, my dear Sea,
what could you offer someone who was born among the stars?”
The Sea then said, “ I'm bound to earth for eternity. Inside me lies a whole universe. O, my
lover, you illuminate the universe,let me reflect the light of yours.”
The SILVER Princess swayed,
The earth, showered with pearl rains,
Witnessed the heavenly descent.
The Poet watched the union, silently on the land.
In the ethereality, he wrote his last poem.
This time, neither about the Moon, nor about her charm.
This time about the life that can be passed by just seeing the world.
The poem tells, just sit and see.
To wait a little longer, to breathe a little longer.
The Man stands,
The breeze made his hat fall,
The coat is loosened,
The hair is rather messy.
The coldness in his gaze melts like snow;
He walks again,
This time his steps move in a rhythm,
In which he once walked,holding his mother's hand.
A rhythm, he always knew, but forgot to remember.

title: A Love That Looks Like Me
author: Tea Time
excerpt: Narcissism, a term that has recently become popular on social media, caught my
imageAlt: Cover image for A Love That Looks Like Me
content: Narcissism, a term that has recently become popular on social media, caught my
attention some days ago. However, back then, I had no idea about the tragic Greek
myth regarding Narcissus behind what seemed to be such a cool personality trait.
Narcissus was the son of Cephissus, the river god, and Liriope, a water Nymph.
Narcissus possessed extraordinary beauty from his divine parents, however, a famous
blind prophet, Tiresias, had given a vague oracle to his mother- “Only if Narcissus
does not know himself, can he live a long life.”
As Narcissus reached his golden days of youth, his beauty turned legendary, and his
number of admirers multiplied despite his emotional distance. He rejected everyone
who expressed romantic interest in him, including the mountain nymph named Echo
who was helpless in expressing her longing for Narcissus because of her curse.
While hunting one day, Narcissus discovered a spring whose water was so clean that
he could view himself precisely. He himself was bewitched by the glimmer of the
handsome man staring back at him, and he instantly fell in love with the reflection. He
could see the beautiful creature on the water, but whenever he attempted to touch it, it
disturbed the aquatic surface, causing the image to tremble.
Ultimately, he realized that it was his own mirror image, and that gave him the taste of
unrequited love. He became his own lover, the reflection of himself was the very thing
he passionately yearned for. At one point, he became so mesmerized by his own
charm that he deserted all mundane activities, and stayed by himself in the spring,
savoring the bitter feeling of loving someone who could never return his affection. He
could not bring himself to break free from it, and with the turning of the seasons, he
died by the spring where his dead body was replaced by a white flower called
Narcissus.
Now the scepticism that arises is that is loving oneself such a sin that one has to
experience death because of it? If I put myself first, if I am my greatest priority, then
is it my mistake for being detached from others’ feelings since at the end of the day, it
is only me who stays by me through thick and thin?
Throughout the history of humankind, anything that had happened was fueled by
desire and greed, whether it was the Trojan war or the cold war. Everyone wanted
their fair share of fame and fortune, which inevitably paved the way for destruction
and insanity.
When I am mindful of my individuality, separating myself from negative energy and
the avarice of other people, that cannot paint me as a selfish person for looking after
myself. For instance, my mom, she gave away her ambitions just so she could take
care of her household, and I could swear that somehow along the way, she could not
help regretting this decision that she took impulsively that time. From her story, I had
my lesson about the art of self-love. No matter how much I offer myself to others, it is
never enough because human thirst knows no boundaries. On the contrary, if I retain
my own novelty and do not let them stain it, then at least I do not have to tolerate the
insurmountable weight of remorse.
Time heals all, and I can bleed yet heal at the same time when I know that I believe in
myself. Because in the end, all we do is pretend albeit being caught between caring
too much and not caring enough. The echo of everything unsaid and the taste of such
tender tears linger like the fragrance of dried flowers inside the forgotten pages of my
life, never quite there although hurting. Given that knowing me might lead to loving
me less, I would rather be nothing, for it lasts forever. The invisible thread of gold
would inevitably tie me to someone if it is meant to be.
Similarly, Narcissus was enamoured with his own beauty, and he did not wish to get
associated with any romantic relationships. Thus, if he denied everyone and simply
gave all his attention to himself, how can he be guilty for being withered by his very
own presence?
He might be reckless in his way of rejecting others, or even inflecting the anguish of
heartbreak upon his admirers like Echo. My interpretation is that even though he
apprehended at some point that he might die being his one and only beloved, even so
he continued his devotion. Therefore, if loving myself means losing others' definition
of affection, then so be it.

title: The Sentimental Value of a Daughter from a Well-off Family
author: Nabila Anjum
excerpt: They paint the walls black
imageAlt: Cover image for The Sentimental Value of a Daughter from a Well-off Family
content: They paint the walls black
Then light a lamp.
And blame the light
For why there’s no light.

In the dystopian thriller, Children of Men (2006), for eighteen years, no babies had been born until a refugee in a British refugee camp gives birth to a daughter. Before her birth, the mother had a boy’s name in mind. After her birth, amid the exchange of gunfire with the army, a refugee rights activist, who conspired to use the baby for his political cause, begged, “We need the baby. We need him.” Probably the most sentimental scene in the film, which is otherwise quite restrained in its emotional expression, is when the soldiers and the activists cease fire to let the baby out, some reach out to touch the baby’s foot; it’s a miracle, after all! Although, by default, we might have expected the miracle to be a boy, when we, the audience, hear, “It’s a girl,” we tear up because a girl has sentimental value.

Some might say, “Well, that’s one point for girls over boys”, while I can’t help but see girls having just as much sentimental value as an antique piece kept for display. Usually the financially well-off are fond of such pieces while the less well-off would rather pawn them. Unlike the former, the latter might rush to marry their daughters off or get them to work in somebody else’s household, or at a garment factory, or send them off to the Middle East- anywhere but home. Poverty can make daughters burdensome while wealth can make them objects of prestige. Swap their economic positions, and their sentiments toward their daughters would swap too.  After giving birth to my brother, my mother didn’t want another child, but my father insisted. He wished for a daughter, and then I was born. Aww- that’s a cue for you to tear up! By contrast, his sister in the village had five daughters before finally having a boy on her sixth attempt. Despite their first child being a boy, why’d my father wish for a daughter? Would he want the same had he and his sister swapped places?

While a woman coming from money has much easier access to empowerment, i.e. higher education, how empowered she is depends on the sentimental value her parents put on her. She is as valued as the most expensive possession in their house; that possession can be an antique piece of furniture, or jewellery, or a clock, or a lamp, or a vase. But an antique piece doesn’t cause as much inconvenience as a conscientious daughter. That’s where the conflict begins. You see, some daughters are happy being a vase, while a conscientious one asserts her humanity only to be dismissed and discover that she is merely a vase.

My father’s an anaesthesiologist, so, when I was around seven, I made a deal with him: I’d go to the village on Eid-ul-Adha, if and only if he anaesthetised the cow before having it slaughtered. I got into the car believing the anaesthetic equipment was in the trunk. But when we arrived, my father pouted and put on a baby voice, “If I anaesthetise the cow, then we might all pass out after eating its meat.” Although he didn’t bother to explain scientifically why he couldn’t do it, he posted my proposal on Facebook emphasizing how sympathetic his daughter was towards animals. Aww- fuck that!  Around the same time, I started reciting the Quran. It is such a holy book that the highest shelf was designated for it that I couldn’t reach without standing on a stool wearing an ‘abaya’- which was too big for me- what a maneuver! So I accidentally dropped it once. As a result, my parents had to feed the poor in the village to make amends for my sin. I liked the result, so I dropped it again. The moral of the story is, I don’t hold anything sacred. And I refuse to be held sacred, like some book on a shelf, to the point that my humanity is seen as profane.

A few years later, I was sexually abused… three times. And each time, I sought justice at the cost of my parents’ convenience, and thus risked losing the non-transactional love that I had been so generously given. “We’ve never left your needs unmet,” they said, without addressing the elephant in the room. And instead of apologizing to me, they begged Allah for forgiveness lest they be further punished for failing to raise a daughter as she should have been raised, adding, “We did everything we could.” No, well-off parents do everything they are willing to do. They are willing to pay my bills, but holding an abuser accountable has social and psychological costs that they are simply unwilling to pay. One of the abusers was a relative, and my parents had practical reasons to maintain that relationship.  Maintaining  the relationship was more convenient than holding him accountable. The other two abusers were nobodies, and to even acknowledge that a nobody dares to touch their property is to admit that they are not as revered in the society as they thought they were. Lest such shame reduce their life expectancy- in other words, their relevance in society- they deny it ever happened. Denial was more convenient than holding the abusers accountable. Thus my sentimental value as a daughter reaches its limits when it becomes inconvenient.

The reader at this point might have interrupted, if they could, to say, “Alright, alright, we get it. Rich girls have problems too.” Sure, but that’s not my point. I intend to illustrate the phenomenon of the sentimental idealization of a daughter by her parents- the attachment to the idea of having a daughter, and to what that daughter represents, rather than relating to her as a person with needs, flaws, desires, and agency. Whether she is possessed like an object or revered as a divine entity, either way, her human experiences are denied. Furthermore, because such idealization is contingent on convenience, it’s not a secure basis for a daughter’s relationship with her parents. To be clear, I’m not claiming that parents cannot love their daughters. Some surely do. I hope so! Rather, I’m arguing that sentimental idealization can be easily mistaken for love even though the two are fundamentally incompatible; they cannot coexist.

As so-called women’s empowerment has become a symbol of status, the parents expect their daughter to be well educated and well paid, while treating her like a showpiece anyway. That is to say, despite her modern aspirations, she must look traditional. On top of the period cramps, she’s worried that the blood might show while she’s presenting; she’s worried that the worry might show making her look less presentable. And yet, despite the stress caused by modern aspirations, a woman from a respectable family can’t smoke like a man with similar aspirations.

Daughters from well-off families do smoke. I do, but I must hide it from my chain-smoking yet respectable father. But if I have to hide parts of myself, then I’m not being seen and understood as my whole self. One must be seen and understood to be loved. Otherwise, who do you think you love? To make things more inconvenient,  I can’t just go out for a walk in a T-shirt and trousers without an ‘orna’ around my neck, and even if I dress in accordance with my parents’ standard, “what do you mean she just went out for a walk?” they might ask. Just because the antique piece now studies and works, they can’t let it have fresh air or a smoke to relieve the stress it imagines having. When my experience of stress is denied, my stress is amplified. When my need for relief is denied, the need is amplified. Meanwhile, I’m expected to function and perform, both as an empowered woman AND as an antique vase. How can a woman grow up in a family with such contradictory principles without being divided into pieces? How can she remain sane?
I often see mice running about in our clean and well-lighted house.

title: why are you crying? it's just a book
author: Zahraa Zee
excerpt: I have spent entire evenings crying over people who don't exist. I have been reluctant to close
imageAlt: Cover image for why are you crying? it's just a book
content: I have spent entire evenings crying over people who don't exist. I have been reluctant to close
books, reluctant to leave the worlds inside them, reluctant to accept that I had reached the last
page. And yet, one afternoon, when my younger sister came to tell me a story, I couldn't spare
her a minute.
I was on the sofa with my headphones on and my tablet in front of me. My exam was in roughly
two hours. She just wanted to tell me something funny.
I didn't take off my headphones.
Instead, I complained to my dad, over her head, that she always came to talk to me when I was
studying. My sister groaned and walked away.
But I never found out what the story was about.
I don't think I was being unkind. I was preoccupied, and I didn't want to be disturbed.
I know that afternoon from both sides.
By thirteen, I was devouring books. This was partly a love of novels, but I also relished being
transported elsewhere, especially when I didn't want to be where I was. After hours immersed in
a story, I would emerge feeling as though I had travelled. On occasion, I had no desire to return.
It's a kind of loneliness that is hard to describe, because on the surface nothing would seem
wrong. I had friends. People liked me. I was seen as the sweet one, the diligent one, the one
who was nice to everyone. I was certainly not left out, nor banished to some dramatic corner of
the classroom. I simply wasn't always someone's first choice.
Everyone liked me. Nobody would've picked me.
I found that much harder to explain than I expected. How could I be lonely when I wasn't alone?
How could I feel so separate from people who were perfectly happy to have me around? When I
tried to word it out loud, the answer I got was, 'You have siblings. Why are you lonely?'
I had no convincing counter-argument. All I knew was that I craved a friendship where I wouldn't
have to remind anyone I existed. One in which my absence would be felt.
I wanted room for the little things I had to say. Not major life events or matters requiring a
considered reply. Merely the passing thoughts I wanted someone else to hear.
Books were easier, in a way. They didn't require me to work out where I was standing. I could
open one and be somewhere else entirely.
Once, when I was caught crying over one, I was asked: 'Why are you crying? It's just a book.'
It's a question I still hear in different forms. Why grieve for someone who never existed? Why
feel a strange reluctance to close a book, when all it takes to return to that world is to open it
again?
I understand the question. I also find it slightly irritating.
Of course it's a book. But it is also a whole world you have poured hours into. You come to know
the people in it intimately: the way they speak, the things they will never say aloud, the habits
they don't realise they have. You know what they have been through. You remember
conversations that the other characters might have already forgotten. Over time, people who
were once just names on a page become familiar in a way that is difficult to convey to anyone
who hasn't met them.
Then, eventually, there are no more pages.
It was with 1Q84 by Haruki Murakami that I felt this most acutely. I wasn't waiting for anything
else to happen. I had simply settled into the narrative and its inhabitants. Until the last page, I
could put the book down and get on with my day, knowing I could slip back into that world
whenever I liked. Once it was over, closing the cover felt like leaving home.
Sometimes the sadness isn't about losing a character at all. It's about losing the ordinary
experience of living inside the pages. You have come to rely on this 'home', and now you are
expected to leave it and return to your own room, your own afternoon, your own unfinished
work.
That is what makes reading so peculiar. It is a solitary activity that can make you feel
surrounded. You spend long periods alone, occupied by the lives of people who have never
occupied a room with you.
At thirteen, I needed this more than I cared to acknowledge. I was still working out where I fit,
and keen to be liked. I thought kindness meant being equally available to everyone: never
leaving anyone out, never being too much of anything. I was adept at being pleasant. Less so at
saying what I wanted.
Whether reading was an escape from all this, or simply a place to put the things I couldn't say, I
still can't tell. At that age, I didn't have the words for any of it.
I'm no longer thirteen. I can say what I want now.
Still, I need somewhere to disappear. I reach for a novel when I'm distressed, frustrated, weary,
or just unwilling to deal with whatever is going on around me. Sometimes I want to know how it
ends. Just as often, I'm content to stay a little longer in the company of its characters, whatever I
think of them.
Would I have laughed at my sister's story, had I removed my headphones? It might have been
entirely ridiculous. It might have lasted thirty seconds. Perhaps she would have trailed off
halfway through. Perhaps I would have smiled. Perhaps not.
I still don't know what she wanted to tell me. I remember the sofa, the headphones, the exam. I
remember her groan. The only thing missing is the story.
After she left, I returned to the paragraph I had been reading.
Although,
I don't remember that paragraph either.

title: A Groundbreaking Theory. (Source: Trust Me Bro)
author: Paravin
excerpt: A couple days ago, I read what may have been the worst piece of writing I've ever
imageAlt: Cover image for A Groundbreaking Theory. (Source: Trust Me Bro)
content: A couple days ago, I read what may have been the worst piece of writing I've ever
forced myself to comprehend in my entire life. And it got strikingly positive reviews.
Mind you, it was so terrible that it shoved me out of my writer's block to ask you a single
question.
Why the hell are men rewarded for scraping up the basement sludge of hell and serving
it on a plate?
Because only a man who thinks he's simultaneously the Aristotle, Nietzsche,
Dostoevsky, and every other smart, romantic thinker of our generation (in a way, he is,
I'll get to that), would mistake his half baked shower thought as some kind of socio
philosophical breakthrough. Of course, in reality, it's just the same manosphere
misogynistic bullshit that takes every opportunity to reduce humans, specifically women,
into some kind of biological machine excluded from the grasp of nuance. To be fair, it's
not modern essayists who have invented the concept of excluding emotional nuance
when interacting with a topic relating to women, the overly romanticized male
philosophers that came before them made sure to lay down the floorboards for this to
be the norm.
Thousands of words that come together to paint a picture of bioessentialist haven– for
anyone lucky enough to have avoided that corner of the internet, bioessentialism is just
the fancy, academic-sounding way of saying 'biology is destiny'—the belief that men and
women are hardwired with fixed, unchangeable traits from birth, conveniently leaving
zero room for personality, upbringing, or basic free will — simply to reduce women down
to less-than-human creatures that surgically remove their frontal cortexes the second a
man with “masculine energy” enters the room. Because as we all know, women aren't
human beings with preferences and past experiences that shape what they value in a
person, women are programmed to like x and dislike y! Women stay in abusive
relationships not because of psychological, social or financial circumstances, but
because their stupid female brains are overwhelmed by the masculine energy of the
abuser!
I can't mention the specific piece that radicalized me but I don't think you need to know
it intimately to understand this scenario. The internet is full of men who think their one
thought of the day is something no one has ever even come close to thinking of. It's
almost always some bioessentialist nonsense backed by statistics and percentages that
are also unable to completely touch upon the nuance of their origins. Or they'll try to
dissect a topic that was stripped to its bare bones 17 years ago. Don't worry they'll miss
the point of the dissections anyway.
Because no, Chad, divorce rates weren't lower in the ‘50s because women were more
obedient and pure, there was no option for it to even be a possibility for the millions of
abused housewives.
I want to bring back the piece that inspired this cokeless coke rant. I'm sorry I keep
bringing it up; it's just so appalling to me how these lone wolf thinkers think they are
entitled to the readers' time. As a writer, I understand wanting to fully scope out your
position so people can see where you are. But as a reader, I don't fucking care when
you realized that women were either pure amazing traditional housewives or slutty trash
whores, and how you can't get laid by either. I promise you your involuntary celibacy
was clear to us two paragraphs ago. Can't even say don't beat a dead horse because at
this point in time, the only memory we have left of it is a single electron.
I can't lie to you, the only force that pushed me to finish that God-awful think piece, was
the sheer horror that it was real. A grown ass man sat there, wrote this multiple
thousand word essay with no thesis in sight, only to end it on a high note of
bioessentialism. If it was satirical, it would've been the perfect reflection of the male ego.
Unfortunately, the satire was the friends we made along the way consoling me so I don't
rip out my eyebrows from the insanity that crawled out of the screen and into my head.
Enough about the radioactive side effects of reading modern philosophy by the men of
our generation, let's talk about how vintage it really is. Remember when I said in a way,
these thoughtless thinkers are Aristotles of our time? You may be confused by that
sentiment. However, his philosophies of ethics and logic were specifically inapplicable to
women. Why? Because he himself said so! According to Aristotle, women lack full
reason. Not to mention his views on race, slavery existed long before him, however his
contribution to its justification probably extended its lifetime by at least a couple
centuries.
He's the forefather of bioessentialism, labelling women as “mutilated men”, blaming the
existence of women on genetic deformities and using that as his reasoning for seeing
women as lesser than. Now isn't that familiar?
Our intellectuals do not only hold the logic of Aristotle, but also the self improvement
angles of Nietzsche. After the daily dose of Übermensch, which is Nietzsche's 19th
century version of looksmaxxing, they may recreate his belief that women are incapable
of depth. Don't think that one will take too much effort, as women are endlessly
described by these absolute geniuses as the reflection of large language models when
asked how many r’s in the word strawberry. The smell of testosterone is just too
overwhelming for us! So obviously women = stupid AIs.
Nietzsche was also a textbook rejected alpha. After multiple rejections from intelligent
and capable women such as Lou Andreas-Salomé, he became the fox unable to reach
the grapes. Just as the fox consoled himself by telling himself the grapes were too sour
anyway, Nietzsche too told himself he's too smart and alpha for women who are all
shallow.
Oh but, make sure to mention you're not a misogynist, you believe in equal rights. As
long as those rights only apply to women you deem worthy. The beautiful dead wife
shown through candid videos of the film camera. The pure, tragic muse frozen in amber,
like Nastenka in Dostoevsky's most popular work, White Nights—worshiped not as a
real, messy human being, but as a four-night therapy session designed to cure a lonely
man's isolation before disappearing into memory. Now that brings that classic
Dostoevsky vibe.
The brilliants never really died, they just sprinkled their worst parts into our peers.
Actually, their brilliance excluded 50% of the population. Now it doesn't sound as
inspiring does it? Many will argue that these thinkers were the product of their times and
social norms. I believe that as the weakest defense. They were smart enough to invent
theories about physics and society, write tragic books about emptiness, but not smart
enough to recognize the fleshbags that are slightly different to them as human beings?
It reminds me of how fervently internet celebrities’ past counts of racism or sexism are
defended by the shield of “it was 10 years ago!”. Did women not have feelings 10 years
ago? Was racism not oppressive 10 years ago?
The greats are defended because their bigotry supposedly never really affected the
things they were right about. They were right 6/10 times, the 4 fails were flukes.
However, the 4 wrongdoings didn't just disappear into the void. Those 4 flukes went
through mitosis and created the modern manosphere.
I can almost hear the calls of the not-so-rare misogynistic man bird… I think it's saying,
“Well, how come there were no women philosophers then?” Ah, the ear-grating sound
of stupidity. It's not that women really are 2D characters with no thoughts uninvolved
with men (shocking, I know I couldn't believe it), it's that these greats barred women
from ever even standing on the podium. Academia had never been inclusive, even more
so for the unfortunate women who thought of the theories we now regard as the best of
humanity years before a man did. Their cage is now a defense against their existence.
Since the greats and the institutions that lick their feet pushed women away from being
thinkers, it is now gospel those women never even existed.
Speaking of, institutions will never fully recognize how wicked these idolized folks were,
or how lackluster the modern misogynists’ writing can really be. They are all owned by
the descendants of these greats or one of their lackeys. It's a man and man world! Or
whatever the saying is. So no amount of unpolished, offensive, or downright stupid
rhetoric will stop the glorification of men’s bare minimum efforts. Tomorrow we'll see an
essay by a man entitled “Why racism is a bad!” In which the thesis will be “racism bad
because actually we should all hold hands and worship billionaires” with 46 typos and at
least four logical fallacies and it will be regarded as raw and real.
The philosophers of then at least had some breakthroughs worth mentioning, the male
philosophers of today are awarded for genuine mediocrity (and watch this piece get
docked points for saying so— bazinga!). The criminal (essay) who inspired this
investigation (also an essay) is an exact example of such a scenario. Actually, scrap

runs.text: A couple days ago, I read what may have been the worst piece of writing I've ever
forced myself to comprehend in my entire life. And it got strikingly positive reviews.
Mind you, it was so terrible that it shoved me out of my writer's block to ask you a single
question.
Why the hell are men rewarded for scraping up the basement sludge of hell and serving
it on a plate?
Because only a man who thinks he's simultaneously the Aristotle, Nietzsche,
Dostoevsky, and every other smart, romantic thinker of our generation (in a way, he is,
I'll get to that), would mistake his half baked shower thought as some kind of socio
philosophical breakthrough. Of course, in reality, it's just the same manosphere
misogynistic bullshit that takes every opportunity to reduce humans, specifically women,
into some kind of biological machine excluded from the grasp of nuance. To be fair, it's
not modern essayists who have invented the concept of excluding emotional nuance
when interacting with a topic relating to women, the overly romanticized male
philosophers that came before them made sure to lay down the floorboards for this to
be the norm.
Thousands of words that come together to paint a picture of bioessentialist haven– for
anyone lucky enough to have avoided that corner of the internet, bioessentialism is just
the fancy, academic-sounding way of saying 'biology is destiny'—the belief that men and
women are hardwired with fixed, unchangeable traits from birth, conveniently leaving
zero room for personality, upbringing, or basic free will — simply to reduce women down
to less-than-human creatures that surgically remove their frontal cortexes the second a
man with “masculine energy” enters the room. Because as we all know, women aren't
human beings with preferences and past experiences that shape what they value in a
person, women are programmed to like x and dislike y! Women stay in abusive
relationships not because of psychological, social or financial circumstances, but
because their stupid female brains are overwhelmed by the masculine energy of the
abuser!
I can't mention the specific piece that radicalized me but I don't think you need to know
it intimately to understand this scenario. The internet is full of men who think their one
thought of the day is something no one has ever even come close to thinking of. It's
almost always some bioessentialist nonsense backed by statistics and percentages that
are also unable to completely touch upon the nuance of their origins. Or they'll try to
dissect a topic that was stripped to its bare bones 17 years ago. Don't worry they'll miss
the point of the dissections anyway.
Because no, Chad, divorce rates weren't lower in the ‘50s because women were more
obedient and pure, there was no option for it to even be a possibility for the millions of
abused housewives.
I want to bring back the piece that inspired this cokeless coke rant. I'm sorry I keep
bringing it up; it's just so appalling to me how these lone wolf thinkers think they are
entitled to the readers' time. As a writer, I understand wanting to fully scope out your
position so people can see where you are. But as a reader, I don't fucking care when
you realized that women were either pure amazing traditional housewives or slutty trash
whores, and how you can't get laid by either. I promise you your involuntary celibacy
was clear to us two paragraphs ago. Can't even say don't beat a dead horse because at
this point in time, the only memory we have left of it is a single electron.
I can't lie to you, the only force that pushed me to finish that God-awful think piece, was
the sheer horror that it was real. A grown ass man sat there, wrote this multiple
thousand word essay with no thesis in sight, only to end it on a high note of
bioessentialism. If it was satirical, it would've been the perfect reflection of the male ego.
Unfortunately, the satire was the friends we made along the way consoling me so I don't
rip out my eyebrows from the insanity that crawled out of the screen and into my head.
Enough about the radioactive side effects of reading modern philosophy by the men of
our generation, let's talk about how vintage it really is. Remember when I said in a way,
these thoughtless thinkers are Aristotles of our time? You may be confused by that
sentiment. However, his philosophies of ethics and logic were specifically inapplicable to
women. Why? Because he himself said so! According to Aristotle, women lack full
reason. Not to mention his views on race, slavery existed long before him, however his
contribution to its justification probably extended its lifetime by at least a couple
centuries.
He's the forefather of bioessentialism, labelling women as “mutilated men”, blaming the
existence of women on genetic deformities and using that as his reasoning for seeing
women as lesser than. Now isn't that familiar?
Our intellectuals do not only hold the logic of Aristotle, but also the self improvement
angles of Nietzsche. After the daily dose of Übermensch, which is Nietzsche's 19th
century version of looksmaxxing, they may recreate his belief that women are incapable
of depth. Don't think that one will take too much effort, as women are endlessly
described by these absolute geniuses as the reflection of large language models when
asked how many r’s in the word strawberry. The smell of testosterone is just too
overwhelming for us! So obviously women = stupid AIs.
Nietzsche was also a textbook rejected alpha. After multiple rejections from intelligent
and capable women such as Lou Andreas-Salomé, he became the fox unable to reach
the grapes. Just as the fox consoled himself by telling himself the grapes were too sour
anyway, Nietzsche too told himself he's too smart and alpha for women who are all
shallow.
Oh but, make sure to mention you're not a misogynist, you believe in equal rights. As
long as those rights only apply to women you deem worthy. The beautiful dead wife
shown through candid videos of the film camera. The pure, tragic muse frozen in amber,
like Nastenka in Dostoevsky's most popular work, White Nights—worshiped not as a
real, messy human being, but as a four-night therapy session designed to cure a lonely
man's isolation before disappearing into memory. Now that brings that classic
Dostoevsky vibe.
The brilliants never really died, they just sprinkled their worst parts into our peers.
Actually, their brilliance excluded 50% of the population. Now it doesn't sound as
inspiring does it? Many will argue that these thinkers were the product of their times and
social norms. I believe that as the weakest defense. They were smart enough to invent
theories about physics and society, write tragic books about emptiness, but not smart
enough to recognize the fleshbags that are slightly different to them as human beings?
It reminds me of how fervently internet celebrities’ past counts of racism or sexism are
defended by the shield of “it was 10 years ago!”. Did women not have feelings 10 years
ago? Was racism not oppressive 10 years ago?
The greats are defended because their bigotry supposedly never really affected the
things they were right about. They were right 6/10 times, the 4 fails were flukes.
However, the 4 wrongdoings didn't just disappear into the void. Those 4 flukes went
through mitosis and created the modern manosphere.
I can almost hear the calls of the not-so-rare misogynistic man bird… I think it's saying,
“Well, how come there were no women philosophers then?” Ah, the ear-grating sound
of stupidity. It's not that women really are 2D characters with no thoughts uninvolved
with men (shocking, I know I couldn't believe it), it's that these greats barred women
from ever even standing on the podium. Academia had never been inclusive, even more
so for the unfortunate women who thought of the theories we now regard as the best of
humanity years before a man did. Their cage is now a defense against their existence.
Since the greats and the institutions that lick their feet pushed women away from being
thinkers, it is now gospel those women never even existed.
Speaking of, institutions will never fully recognize how wicked these idolized folks were,
or how lackluster the modern misogynists’ writing can really be. They are all owned by
the descendants of these greats or one of their lackeys. It's a man and man world! Or
whatever the saying is. So no amount of unpolished, offensive, or downright stupid
rhetoric will stop the glorification of men’s bare minimum efforts. Tomorrow we'll see an
essay by a man entitled “Why racism is a bad!” In which the thesis will be “racism bad
because actually we should all hold hands and worship billionaires” with 46 typos and at
least four logical fallacies and it will be regarded as raw and real.
The philosophers of then at least had some breakthroughs worth mentioning, the male
philosophers of today are awarded for genuine mediocrity (and watch this piece get
docked points for saying so— bazinga!). The criminal (essay) who inspired this
investigation (also an essay) is an exact example of such a scenario. Actually, scrap
that; calling that steaming pile of crack shit mediocre is an insult to normalcy.

author: The untamed rabbit

imageAlt: Cover image for The Burning House
content: ‘Your father was a good man my child, you must step into his shoes now. God will make your lives easy for his sake.’ -The last mourner at the funeral promised pressing Rafsana’s hands but neither she nor her grandmother believe it would keep hunger out of their tin walled home.

At the day’s last hour, the silence and darkness inside run as deep as the grave she left her father in. They remain in darkness; they cannot afford light neither in this home nor in their lives now. Yet her father’s kindness has arranged them food for the funeral and a grave for himself.

The dirty dishes and food left by the guests remain unattended on the table, the cushions of the sofa misarranged. Yet grief has hollowed them to even look around or at each other, silently they retreat to different rooms. Rafsana takes over her father’s room as she has taken his place as the guardian of this house at 24. She lies on the bed as a soft blue light slips through the window behind her softly caressing each corner of the room. Eyes closed, left alone with the voices in her head in this silence around her she takes a deep breath and nearly surrenders to sleep. Until the thunderous crash of a steel dish hitting the dining room floor jolts her awake.

She sees the dish by the table on the floor just when she steps out of her room. She picks it up and places it on the table, hisses of a cat alert her to look at the backdoor of her house. She shoos it away and it goes outside through the hole at the end of the backdoor it came from. But she knows it is of no use; it will find its way back here as she used to feed it. It has no choice but to. Whether that be a human or a mere pet for their stomach they don’t forget the hands that feed them even if it is the one that drives them away, they bear with it, she knows it will too, it will come back.  She covers the food and cleans as much as she could and paces slowly back to her room.

‘It hasn’t been a day in my absence, and the house is a mess.’ Perched at the edge of the right side, foot of the bed facing the window wrapped in a white cloth he spoke to her – his voice horrifying, low pitched rasp, deep and husky like a broken creek beneath a door. One-foot rested bend on the bed and the other swaddling constantly by it. The room feels a bit colder. She keeps her calm demeanor and walks inside the room and sits over the head of the left side of the bed diagonally facing him. A bald man, medium build, wrapped in a white fabric, even in the blue light she can see his pale blue face, all life and benevolence left his face, eyes fixated on her and a gruesome smile from ear to ear.
‘You notice the house but never noticed the mess you made of our lives.’ She keeps her calm and looks blankly at him.
‘That’s not how you talk to someone who fed, clothed and took care of you! Do you!’

He stands up and sits in front of her at the edge of the left foot of the bed facing her horizontally. He maintains that gruesome smile, Rafsana’s eyes still fixed on him, she maintains her composure to mask her pounding pulse, grips tight on her shivering right hand with her sweaty left one. She takes a gulp to wet her dry throat. His eyes lock onto every flinch and breath of her with a demonic satisfaction in knowing, even in death his hold over her and the terror he inspired still grips her tight.

‘The food, the cloth and the roof you preach of kept me alive, but I never lived. You did it too feed your ego, to feel like a saint. You punished me for her sin; you kept me in the cage that mother walked right out of.’ She loses her calm; there is nothing but anger and hatred in those tear-filled eyes of hers.
‘I loved you my child, if I hadn’t disciplined you, you would’ve become just like that shameless and unfaithful woman who sold my reputation to be with her lover.’

‘Just so that I don’t become a monster, you became one instead. Discipline?’ she lets out a bitter hollow laugh. ‘You tore down my mind, my limbs behind closed doors. Everyone thought you were a saint while dadu and I bled and cried on these floors.’

‘Ungrateful wretch.’ He hisses, his voice echoing like scrapping metal. ‘I was the one who raised you when she left, I was faithful for this family, after I sacrificed my life, you chocked me, you repaid me by taking mine.’

‘Even when you breathed you were a monster, you would’ve killed grandmother, I did that to save her. When your body fell to the ground I did regret it.’ she says. Her voice steady, refusing to flinch even when his humanly feature, the mask that he wore in front of her twist into something horrifying with rage.
‘I don’t anymore neither am I afraid. You are dead. I should have done it differently, I have sinned. But I did it, I ended all the abuse and torture with both my hands; I ended it with you.’

‘I spent my life to raise you, to make sure you wouldn’t be your mother. You didn’t, you became something far worse. I can’t let you live to drag my name through the mud the way she did. If I am in the ground, you belong there too.’

The temperature in the room grows suffocatingly colder, his translucent figure flickers closer until his hands press onto her neck and chock her against the headboard of the bed frame. Her screams cut off to a strangled squeak, her vision blurs, she tries to pull in air through her mouth, but she could only gasp for it. A single teardrop falls down her eyes as she is about to give up and leaves a final gasp. Yet suddenly his grip loosens and, in that moment, a beautiful sound of loud recitation of a holy verse lessens her pain, her heartbeat stabilizes, it’s her grandmother approaching them from the open door. Her father covers his ears rolling in the floor, screaming in absolute agony. She keeps reciting and approaches closer. She keeps reciting until there is no trace of her son’s damned soul in the room and he disappears in ashes leaving a faint scream, the temperature of the room warms up.

She runs to Rafsana, throws her arms around her, hugging her like she would never let go. Rafsana finally finds the warmth and love she had spent her whole life searching for. With him gone the burning house finally cooled down. Behind them the morning sun breaks through the window, spills across the room, wrapping them both in its light.

A hand that barely feeds can never satisfy a soul starved of affection, no coat can warm a child the way two loving arms can. All that can keep a child alive, it takes love and warmth for it to live. Even on days when this place will have little food to spare, they will still have each other – and perhaps being loved the way you were meant to be is all what someone really needs.
(Image credit – Hold on by Liliia Kodunova, Jackson’s art prize)
